IF you want to find out how great a boastful. • man is, let him tell it himself. SomE officers always show the white feather when they are in full dress uniform. " A MAN should always live within his income," says a financier, "even if he has to borrow to do it." "I THINK I will have autumn leaves on my new hat," said she. "I am glad of it," returned he, " for autumn leaves are falling." A MAN having fallen from his berth in a sleep- ing car, hurt his knee rather badly, a in a sleep- claimed that he waa lame from his bertnd at once SOME people sneer at the Siamese for h. the elephant. But in this country worshipping paid every year just for the privilegemillions are the ele-ph of "seeing MOST UNREASONABLE !—He :—" I believe if it hadn't been for my money you would never have married me." She :—" II it had been I Could you expect it ?" A GENTLEMAN found the water at a public Aathing establishment so dirty that, on going out, he asked the man in charge :—" I say, friend, where do strangers go for a wash after bathing „ here ?" BROWN—" You see those two sheep over there? Spell the pair in one letter." Bass—" Give it up." Brown—" W." Bass—" Very good, Brown—only one of them happens to be a ram." "flow are you, Smith? How are all the girls your way? Are you sweet on that Miss Jones as you used to be ?' "Oh, no! I've left that off seine time." "Had a quarrel ?" "No. Married her last month." AN American who had been in the far East told a French lady that Hindoo girls are taught to think of marriage as soon as they can talk. She replied: "French girls are not. They don't require teaching." . A WAY TO MAKE HIM SMILE. —Editor—" I Can- not Make Him Smile" (reading title of her poem). "You want to make him smile very bad, eh ?" Miss Violet (with indignant inflection)—" Sir !" Editor—" Show him your poem." "AND them's what folk calls handsome, are they ?" said a Leicestershire farmer, as he watched a couple of hansom cabs rolling down the Strand. "Well, I wonder what they'd think if they could see a new waggon with red wheels." A Goon story is told of Sully, the painter, a man distinguished for refinement of manners as well as success in art. At a party one evening Sully was speaking of a belle who was a great favourite. " Ah," said Sully, "she has a mouth like an elephant." "Oh ! Mr. Sully, how can you be so rude ?" " Rude, ladies, rude? What do you mean I say she has got a. mouth like an elephant . because it is full of ivory." FIRST BRIDESMAID: "You'll never tell ?" Second bridesmaid : "Of course not. I never do, you know." First bridesmaid: "Well, she told me— in strict confidence, understand—that, though Jack was .poor, they were going to travel all summer and stop at. the best hotels, and that they got the money by selling their wedding presents. Now, I wonder if. my spoons are paying part of the ea- penses." Dunma the short time that Lord Byron was in Parliament, a petition, setting forth the wretched

condition of the Irish peasantry, was one evening presented,: and very coldly received by the " here- . ditary legislative wisdom." " Ah, said Lord Byron, "what a misfortune it was for the Irish that they were,not born black ! They would then have had plenty of friends in both houses." WHEN Goldsmith once talked to Johnson of the difficulty of living on very intimate terms with anyone with whom you differed on an important topic, Johnson replied, "Why, sir, you must shun the subject as to which you disagree. For instance, I can live very well with Burke; I love his know- - ledge, his genius, his diffusion and effulgence of conversation; but I would not talk to him of the Rockingham party." IN a continental sea-side watering-place there

• was a reading-room kept by an Englih lady, who, , on the strength of her position, supposed herself to be connected with literature. Lord Macaulay passed through the town, went to the reading-room, . and wrote dawn his name in the subscription 13ok. His money was returned to him with the remark, "No, my lord, we literary people must not take money from each other." AT an evening party, Dumley was introduced to ;8, young lady, and after a remark about the weather he said, gallantly: "And have I really the .pleasure of meeting the beautiful Miss Smith, whose praises .are being sounded by everybody ! " -". Oh no, Mr. Dumley," the lady replied, "the •beautiful Miss Smith to whom you refer is a cousin of mine." "Oh, that's it? Well, I thought there .must be a mistake somewhere," said the gallant Dumley.—New York Sun. SOME years ago a man whose marriage had been •published in a paper with his name wrongly spelled called to have it corrected. He said he was one .of that class whose name never appeared in a news- paper but twice during the course of their lives— once when they are married, and again after death. As he could not see to having the name given cor- rectly on the last occasion, he was very anxious it should be right on the first. ONCE, when. John Kemble played Hamlet in the -country, the gentleman who enacted Guilderstern was 01 imagined imagined himself to be a capital musician. Hamlet asks him, "Will you play upon this pipe ?" My lord, 1 cannot." "I pray you." "Believe Inc, I cannot." "I do beseech you." "Well, if your Lordship insists on it, I shall do as well as I can;" and to the confusion of Hamlet and the great amusement of the .audience, he played ,God save the King." AT a meeting of the Fife Magistrates some years after 1745, a Whig gentleman gave as a toast "The Duke of Cumberland." David Beatoun, of Kilcon quhar, a zealous Jacobite, immediately after pro- posed "James Sibald, the butcher of Colnesburgh;" to the great indignation of his Whig neighbour, who said he must decline to do so much honour to a common tradesman. "Sir," said Kilconquhar sternly, "I've drunk your butcher, and you'll either drink mine or be put over the window."— Chamber's Journal, THE proverb, "The drunken man aye gets the drunken penny," was probably never so truly verified as in the case of two tipplers in Lock- winnock. They had exhausted funds and credit, yet still they might be seen describing right angles in their course towards home. One day, having failed in all their schemes for raising the necessary funds, "Gang awa' in, Peter," said John, "and see gin they'll gie us credit for a gill." "Na, John, wad it no be likelier that ye wad get it; ye're far better acquaint ? " "It would be u:eless," replied John.; "I'm ower weel kent."

THE little town of I— was many years ago deluged by the overflowing of its beautiful river, and the occupants of the houses on its banks were only able to escape with their lives. So rapid was the rising of the water that those who lived in the upper flats of the houses had to be rescued by boats from their perilous position. One of those was found, when succour came, in an attitude of prayer, importuning hif;h heaven in the following terms :-- " Lord, thou saidst thou would never again drown us with a flood, but I am getting very doubtful." "Way, how wonderfully lifelike," said Mr. Der- rix, gently caressing a bumblebee which reposed among the artificial flowers and insects of his wife's new bonnet. "If it was.a, garden flower I'd swear at was al—G-r-eat Cesar-r !' he suddenly shrieked, inserting a wounded finger in his month and danc- ing around like a whirling dervish. "Why, the blamed thing is alive." A WELL-KNOWN beauty has one drawback; her hands are the colour of boiled lobster. Some one happened to mention her name to a celebrated wit, who said, "She is very pretty: I see only one fault in her; her hands ore a trifle too—bashful ?" Mr. Gladstone is troubled by his friends even in Biarritz. Every day's post brings him numerous epistles from Continental admirers. At home the difficulty is easily dealt with; but it will be readily understood that it is wiser to open and read every missive that arrives at a place like Biarritz. Some important cirlmunicatio,n may arrive, and in con- quence the Premier is privileged to peruse many very extraordinary epistles. The Continental let- ter writers forward some requests which really are astonishing.

Again the Labour Commission has postponed its meeting.and thus all chance of its report being pre- sented at the commencement of the session has been destroyed. In Labour circles especially the dissatis- faction which prevails with regard to the delay is particularly keen, and an amendment to the Ad- dress will in all probability be moved when the House reassembles. In view of the pressing charac- ter of the unemployed and other social questions.it is hardly to be wondered at that some impatience should begin to be n3anifested. I believe it is now over a year since the Commission completed the hearing of evidence.

If it be true that "happy is the wooing that is not long a-doing," Sir Philip and Lady Currie should have a good time in store. Tile new Ambassador to Constantinople, who has long been looked upon by mothers with marriageable daughters as an eligible bachelor, has lost no time in determining that the Embassy at Pera should be graced by an Ambassa- doress. His engagement to Mrs. Singleton ("Violet Fane") was only announced on Monday; on Wed- nesday they were quietly married at All Saints', Ennismore-gardens.

Signor Valera, the indeNtigable London repre- sentative of the Italian Secolo, has succeeded in se- curing the views of a considerable number of Bri- tish members of Parliament on the imprisonment of the Sicilian Labour leader. -Mr. Burns, Mr. John Wilson, Mr. Woods, and Mr. Kerr Hardie are among those who have written expressing dissatisfaction with the action with the action of the Italian Cabinet, and disapproval of the institution into Sicily of martial law.

No one cared to oppose Mr.llenry Fowler at Wol- verhampton in 1891 We now hear that the Tories mean to put up NI r.Ritchie against him. Surely this is adding insult to insult and injury to injury. No deserving politlcian ever suffered such shabby treatment at the hands of a party ter whom he worked and toiled as Mr. Ritchie has. He was a Cabinet Minister. rle successfully piloted through Parliament one of the few measures on which the last Tory Government can plume themselves— though they do not. Bet they have handed over seat after seat to unknown 'prentice handa,and now they propose to set hit n a hopeless task. "Blow, blow, thou winter wind thou art not so unkind as —Tory ingratitude.'

Italy is in a troubled state ; but the discontent of the people is not levelled against the Pope, but the Government. Therefore, it is very improbable that there is any truth in the rumour referring to Pope Leo's contemplated departure for Spain. Circum- stances will have become very grave indeed when the present Head of the Catholic Church is induced to surrender the Vatican. Once before, the Popes left Rome, and the Church was ruled from Avignon for a period of seventy years. But they again re- turned to the ancient See. A flight to Spain—for it would be nothing else—would mean much to the present Pope, who is now eighty-four.

Lord Salisbury is back in town, and has taken up his quarters at his handsome residence in Arlington- street. At noon on Friday his colleagues in the Upper Chamber met him to talk over their attitude towards the Parish Councils and Employers' Lia- bility Bills. The report of active hostility to the leading provisions of both measures—which appar- ently would give satisfaction to Tory organs such as the "Standard"--may at once be discredited. I am told that in conference with Mr. Balfour a list of some half dozen amendments has been drawn up, which will embody the views of the Conservative 'party as a whole, and that these and these only will receive any countenance from the official Peers. By the way, it is becoming more and more probable that a compromise will be arrived at on the con- tracting-out question by delaying the operation of the bill as regards existing societies for a period of three years.

It is now stated that the Princess of Wales has definitely decided to withdraw in future from all attendance at Society functions. The gossips have of course, their own reason for this decision, but it' may be taken that Her Royal Higness's state o f health renders it undesirable, that she should be subjected to any worry or excitement of any kind. It is no secret that during the last year she suffered constantly and acutely from severe mental depres- sion, and that the various trips abroad have had little or no effect. As at present arranged, the Princess will spend a considerable portion of the present year in the South of France.

The Prince of Wales, about whose health there is also talk, is back in London, having taken New- market on his way. But Sandringham is to be re- cruited by the presence of the Duke and Duchess of Teck, who on Friday go e.O WII on a visit to their daughter and son-in-law.

The arrest of Jahez Spencer Balfour continues to be the sensation of the hour. It is not yet possible to ascertain the exact time when his return may be looked for, but the belief in official circles is that at least two months must elapse before he can be placed upon his trial. I may note that the most startling rumours are in circulation as to the effect whicki may ultimately be created by the Balfour trial. His defence will, I believe, be that the col- lapse was due to unfortunate speculations and in- vestments, and the charge of fraud will, it is ex- pected, be vigorously denied. Should Balfour only decide to tell the whole story the public may be prepared for revelations more startling and sensa- tional in their nature than any that have yet been made. Among those who know the real position of affairs some important resignations of official posi- tion are momentarily expected.

It is significant of the very widespread convic- tion of Jabez Balfour's astuteness that so many people one meets are profoundly sceptical of ever seeing him in this country, and would not need much encouragement to make them even doubtful whether the news of his arrest is true. Balfour is 80 well up in all the niceties of legal and illegal arrest that unless we are extremely fortunate he is sure to slip through some of the loopholes and meshes of the law.

I understand that the question as to the name by which the various territories south of the ZrlMbesi in2luded within the charter of the British South Africa Company are in future to be known is engag- ing some attention. North of the Zambesi the British sphere from Lake Nyassa on the east to the furthest limits of the Barotse valley on ths west is officially designated " British Central Africa,' and Nyassaland is " the British Central African protec- torate" in all official documents. But sfauth of the Zambesi there is no official name for the Chartered Company's territory, since Matabeleland, Mashona- land, and such names refer to distinct portions of country, and cannot be taken to apply to all the territory included in the charter. I believe that in South Africa, where Rhodes-worship is now at its height, there is a widespread desire to commemor- ate Mr. Rhodes's connection with the painting of this part of Africa red on the maps by adoping the name " Rhodesia." A newspaper published in Sal- isbury has adopted as its name the " Rhodesia Herald, so that to some extent the settlers have become acquainted with the name. Another sug- gestion is to christen the region " Zambesia ;" while still another is to commemorate the great work done by the famous missionary-explorer in giving the name " Livingstonia " to the country in and for which Dr. Livingstone did so much.

Althoug apro are when one is engaged in household duties, as was the case a few years back—yet they can never be cousidered.wholly out of fashion, and new shapes are continually making their appearance. One of the best materials for a serviceable yet smart- looking apron is coloured linen trimmed either with flax lace or'embroidery. Pale blue linen, for example, :makes up charmingly with full, wide skirt-piece, edged with two liin. bands of coarse 4ru guipure insertion laid on the material. This is gathered to a pointed band, and the bib—if it can he so called—consists of two 21n. straps of , linen, on which insertion is laid, these straps' being connected by two short bands similarly trimmed, and hnished. n ,the shoulders with little butterfly bowi, oi pale blue ribbon. Then as to millinery. Hats of fashionable shape, in ivuy shade of felt, can be procured now for a imail sum and this, let me tell you, includes the band of ribbon and bunch of feathers at the side w all which such head-gear is now being trimmed- -1 the cuming boat-shaped felts promise to hold their own right on into the spring, and where economy is an object, I strongly recommend their adoption.. ,

This is of black velvet, trimmed, with black moire velvet and plumes. Bonnets are of varied shape, but a pretty model is made on a buckram chape, edged with a ruche of shaded green sequin jet. The natural wings are in shades of green, and the bows of shot rose and green velvet, but plain velvet may be used and the colouring varied as desired. Another dainty little bonnet, made on a buckram shape, is one in which a combination of coloue may be employed, or the shape may be covered with coloured velvet, with the aigrette to correspond, and the remainder of the trimming consist of jet. Some of the prettiest costumes for winter wear are such as favour the amateur dressmaker, and require no especial care in fitting. For instance, a black moire skirt, made perfectly plain, and the edge lined up with stiff muslin' and one of the new balayeuses of silk corded with colour. With this a little &may° of moire, the fronts and neek finished with a deep full rever, edged narrow jet. This zouave is useful on other, gowns, and' is very easily made and fitted.

A costume which is charming and lady-like, is of rifle, green cloth, trimmed with beaver. The cloth must be of a fairly good quality, or the weight of the fur may cause it to hang badly. The skirt is out in full "umbrella" shape, and up each seam is sewn a piping of beaver far. This fur is quite inexpensive when bought in such narrow strips. If the fur be nice and full, a quarter of an inch will be wide enough for these pipings. That is to say, the skin should be a quarter of an inch; this will make the fur about half an inch wide, as it spreads on either aide. The deep baNued jacket is tight-fitting, with high collar, and a couple of well --ct capes, cut on the cross, which causes them to "flute" slightly at the outer edge. Beaver, in a wider width, trims this coat as illustrated, while a beaver muff forms a charming finish. This is well lined, and is made with the fur arranged to fit over the edges of the muff and to gather closely round the hands. A large green felt hat is worn with the above, lined with black velvet, and trimmed with a band and loops of pale blue velvet, while at the back and front of this c'f,ai ming chapeau are set upstanding pompons of beaver fur, foraling a becoming contrast to the blue :4nd gree

A pretty and useful blouse bodice is of brocaded Chite silk, and to set really well the bodice should be made without a lining—that is to say, all except the sleeves should be so treated. These must be linei, partly for the sake of the extra strength so obtained, and also to facilitate the arrangement therefore. For instance that graceful and out- standing double pouf could hardly be adapted satisfactorily without being caught here and there to a close-titting lining. The back is then cut on the cross, and drawn in to the waist by a reeving. string. The full fronts are gathered into the shoulder seams, crossed over the figure, and tied on the left hip. Full falling frills of any cream- colouted lace are added to the elbow sleeves. Yours lovingly, JENNIE.

Dents in Furniture. If the bruise be small, soak it with warm water, and hold a red-hot iron near the surface, which should be kept wet; the bruise will soon disappear. For larger bruises proceed as follows: Wet the part with warm water; double a piece of brown paper five or six times, soak it in the warm water and lay it on the place; apph on that a warm, but not hot, flat-iron till the moisture is evaporated. If the bruise be not gone, repeat the pro- cess. After two or three applications, the dent or bruise will be raised to the surface.

--- Washing and Wringing Machines. At this season of damp and frost all kinds of domestic: machinery should be overhauled and thoroughly cleaned and dried. Remove all the old grease from the cog • , wheels and bearings of wringing, mangling and washing machines, and apply fresh oil. Any bright steel parts, after being dried, should be wiped over with vaseline or kerosene, for, if damp is allowed to remain long and get into the metal, it will require a consid,rable amount of labour to restore its original brightness.
Very Modern Servant Girls.

After the failure of the registry offices to supply my wants, I advertised for " a strong country girl." The numbers who answered my advertisement seemed cer- tainly encouraging, and I congratulated myself—a little too hastily, as it afterwards turned aut. All the appli- cants represented themselves as giants of strength,para- gons of virtue, and of unflagging industry. I engaged the most promising, who, among her other virtues, boasted that she had never had a day's ill-health. At the end of three days I found her weeping in the pantry. "What's the matter, Ellen ?" I said. "Oh, m'm,please, my legs is all of a tremble, and I think my 'ealth is bound to suffer if I stay. The fogs, they make me feel fainty-like." "But I thought you said you were so strong." "Well, m'm, I've 'eard say as 'ow the strong- est goes off soonest." I administered some sal volatile, and did the little work there was to do myself, sending the patient to bed. Next day I sent her out for an hour's run in the fresh air. She went out at 10 am., and did not return for twelve hours. At ten at night the invalid walked in smiling. She did not stay long after this. From experience of Ellen and the three girls who followed her, I have come to the conclusion that many girls come up from the country just for a week or two's jaunt in London, and get the fares for the pro- posed jaunt from the ladies who are foolish enough to engage them. Ellen and her successors seemed sur- prised that any work at all was expected of them. One of them proposed to leave after a week, saving plaintively—" I couldn't live, m'm, where there ain't more things kep'." Another, the second day, began to remark," This ain't my work," which remark she made unceasingly, until requested to leave. All these dam- sels seemed highly-educated, but one, named Amelia, "took the cake" in the matter of education, if not in house work. "Why, where did you learn to sweep ?" I asked her one day, seeing her raise clouds of dust with a broom. "Well, m'm, I ain't had much experience of sweeping, but 1 can do crool-work and play the planner beautiful." " Well," I said incautiously, "it's a pity you don't take lessons in sweeping from little Jane next door. I don't know about her crewel-work, but she keeps the house like a new pin." " That girl !" Amelia cried contemptuously, flourishing her broom. "I've been at school with 'er. Why, the girl's a perfect fool. She was past twelve year old, and couldn't move the decimal point." I was bound to confess that thou:zit , much more than twelve years old myself, neither could 1 I move the decimal point—whatever that may be.— " Cassell's Family Magazine."
THE ALLEGED POLLUTION OF THE MERSEY BY WIDNES CHEMICAL WORKS.

Mr. Joseph Walton, Q.C., applied ex parte on Fri- day morning last week, to a divisional court of the Queen's Bench, consisting of the Lord Chief Justice and Lord Justice Day, in the case of the United Alkali Company, Limited, and Francis Odell Simp- son, acting on behalf of the Conservators of the River Mersey, that the appeal which was pending from the de- cision of the justices of Widnes might stand over till the Easter sittings, so that a strong court might be formed, the question at issue being one of great impGrtance. The learned counsel stated that the matter would come be- fore the court in the form of a special case stated by the justices at Widnes, who had convicted the appellant for the alleged offence of throwing some chemical waste in- to the river Mersey. It was not suggested that the waste was offensive in any way, but the conservators felt that they had the right to prevent it being thrown into the river. The justices found, as a fact, that the throwing of the waste into the river did not affect or in- jure navigation. The question at issue was whether the conservators had the absolute right to prevent it or not. The learned counsel stated that the case was one of great importance to the chemical industry at Widnes.—The court acceded to the application.

CHAPTER xxxiii. A BROKEN LOVE-DREAM. Alighting from the phteton, Verlie And Noddy he hastily up the gravelled walk. Emily Lennox was profuse in her thanks when they told her what they had brought for her sick friend. "I thank you—for her sake, more than words can express," said Emily, as she invited them into her humble apartment, taking the parcels from them. " Is the poor girl so very bad?" asked Neddy. "Yes," replied Miss Lennox, "she is suffering from the worst form of brain fever. It would I make you cry to sit by the bedside for any length of time, and listen to her delirious ravings—it , would, indeed. She clasps her little white hands, and with ,the bitterest of tears falling like rain down her face, she pleads with some imaginary person to spare her the love of some one whose every heart-throb should be for her and no one else. That is the one burden of her pitiful prayer by day and by night." "Her lover should be sent for, if you know who he is," said Verlie, pityingly. "That is the worst of it. I do not know his name, or, in fact, where any .of her friends are '-" and she related to them how and where she had met the young girl who called herself Miss Dean. Neither Verlie nor Neddy could understand a sorrow so great that a young girl like themselves should seek death when the bright world was so fair. "I can understand a lover turning from a plain, homely, unattractive woman; but how any man ' could turn from this young girl would be a mystery to me. She is so beautiful, so sweet, with all the graces of a young lady of the highest culture." "You interest me greatly in this beautiful . stranger," said Verlie, watching mechanically the process of the white surah silk being tried on and fitted to Neddy'e superb, supple, slender form. "I should like very much to befriend her. I—l am so happy myself, it pains me to see other young girls wretched. Could I see your protegee ? " An, Heaven pity us how slight a thing in this life might avert a cruel fate. Had Emily Lennox granted Verlie Sefton's request, one of the darkest tragedies that ever startled a quiet community would have been averted. "I am sorry to be obliged to refuse you," said Miss Lennox. "The doctor left a sleeping potion for her, which I have just given her, hoping it will induce steep. She would start from her couch at the opening of a door. The sound of a footfall awakens her.' "In that case it would be wrong to disturb her. I will come again soon, however, and I hope then to be permitted to see her," said Verlie, as she and Neddy rose to depart. Daring the drive back to Renwick Villa Verlie was unusually thoughtful. This by no means suited gay, talkative, lively Neddy. "A penny for your thoughts, Verlie," she cried. "I have been talking to you for the last half hour, and I'll wager a pair of kid gloves or tickets to to-day's matinee, that you haven't heard a word I said. "I may as well own up at once and plead ,guilty to the charge. I haven't been listening, IN eddy. I was thinking of that poor sick girl in the cottage we have just left, who must be breaking her poor heart over some faithless, unworthy lover. Ah, how thankful I should be, Neddy, for the love of such a noble man as Rutledge Chester !" "What should you do if you were to lose him now, I wonder ?" cried blunt little Neddy. Vedic turned as white as the pale blossoms she wore on her breast. "It would kill me. That's all, Neddy," she an. sawed, in a low voice. "Don't mention such a , posAbility." "lhere ! I'm always saying something to bring tears to your pretty blue eyes," sighed Neddy. "On, if somebody would invent a bridle for the tongue what a blessing it would be! Why, the patentee would make a fortune in no time. It would be one of those useful articles that's needed in every household." No one could be down-hearted long where merry, fun-loving Neddy was, and she soon had Verlie in the beet of spirits again. On the drive homeward they passed Captain Lansing. Since the memorable night. of the lawn tete he had carefully avoided Verlie. He raised his hat with a stiff bow as the two girls whirled by, and in that moment a sudden and startling secret became known to Verlie. Turning to look at Neddy, she noticed with astonish- ment that her pretty, dimpled face was suffused with blushes, and the dark eyes were wistfully following the young captain's handsome figure, with a light in them Verlie had never seen there before.
cam

Like a flash the truth came to I'erlie Sefton. ,iPoor little Neddy—beneath her mask of gaiety —was quite as much a victim to a hopeless love- dream as the poor soul lying ill in the cottage which they had just left. Yee, she could plainly see that poor little Neddy's heart had gone out unsolicited to the gallant, dashing, handsome captain, who, in turn, loved her instead of Neddy. Ah what strange freaks fate plays with human lives and loves ! Never dreaming Verlie had the faintest idea of her secret, Neddy asked, with apparent in- difference : "Is Captain Lansing coming to the wedding, do yoa suppose ?" "I hardly think so. Still, I shall endeavour to persuade him to come and act as one of the grooms- men." " I have always had a fancy that he cared for you, \Tel lie. Is it true, do you think?" she asked, wistfully, turning sharply towards Verlie. " I think that is merely your imagination, Neddy, dear," replied Verlie, gently and evasively. "He wae at one time a great friend of Ratledge's, you know." "Why aren't they friends now?" incrtiired Neddy, suspiciously. "I suppose young gentlemen friends are like girl friends—they have their little differences once in a while; don't speak, and then make up again," This view of the matter seemed to please Neddy, and proved quite satisfactory. "Then you must be mediator, Verlie, between the two," she declared. "Captain Lansing is such a nice young man to have at our entertainments, you kkow." "I'll do my best," agreed Verlie. In the depths of her heart she pitied bright, beautiful Noddy, for, she well knew, adding fuel to the flame of Neddy's love by being thrown into the constant society of the agreeable captain would be cruel to Neddy in the end, for she would never win him. As long as he lived his heart would hold but one love, one idol ; that idol, lie had told her, was herself ; and the love of a life-time that filled his heart was his hopeless love fr her. But Verlie would not have pained Noddy by telling her this for worlds. Hope is such a sweet, grateful panacea for a yearning, hungry heart. Rutledge Chester had walked leisurely down the avenue, and half-an-hour later, dropping in at his club, the first person whom he met was his old 14;aitial. Coat.* ',.4......aLkailisa,

div.p: "He wds so happy with the whole world," Rut- ledge told himself, impulsively, " tlict he ought to make overtures of friendship to his old chum, who had lost what he had won."

All the world seemed joyous, for was he not in the coming fortnight to claim his darling Verlie as his bride? "Lansing," said Rutledge, touching,him lightly on the arm, and addressing him in the old, familiar way, "would you mind walking a short distance with me? I should like to let by-gones be by-gones. I would be pleased to renew the old friendship." Captain Lansing laughed a harsh, bitter laugh. He drew back haughtily, paling to the lips, his eyes flashing fire. _

"Go yorir way Rutledge Chester," he cried, fiercely. "You insult me by imagining I could be friendly with the man who has wrecked my life, and stolen from me the only woman whom I could ever love." "I am sorry you look at it in that way," replied Rutledge, with pained gravir,y. "If you had been successful in winning my Verlie's love, I should have bowed to it as the will of Heaven." _ _ _

A sneering laugh fell again from Captain Lan- sing's lips. "I make no pretense of being a saint;" he re- torted, bitterly; "and, I own frankly, I hate you with all my heart, and I Jive for the one hope of revenge ! " he cried, rashly, scarcely heeding, in kis bitterness, the words he was using. "I hate you so desperately," he went on, reck- lessly, "that, if I could snatch Verlie Sefton from your arms at the very altar, I should do it, no matter what the cost might be. I would rather see you lying deid at my feet than hear you call the oily child I could ohly love your bride." Every one in the clubroom heard the horrible words, and there came an hour in which they remembered them all too well. "It is useless to ask you to come to our wed- ding, then ?" ankel Rtit:eflge, sorrowfully. "I am much grieved, Lansing." "You know that is false, every word you have uttered," cried Lansing " You laugh at my defeat, and come here to taunt me with your approaching marriadze. I warn you—take care ! beware how you goad me on. I tell you there is fi limit to my forbearance in this cafe." "Captain Lansing, you forget yourself," said Rutledge, h augh ly._

The -captain-,„uriced %vitt) a muttered curse, and, without ewiting one backward glance at the hand- some, pained face of the more fortunate lover, strode angrily down the marble steps and on down the avenue.

"Of course his rival's angry words meant nothing," Rutledge told himself, with a forced laugh. Whether they (lid or not we are soon to see. Ali, if Rutledge could but have foreseen the horrible future I

CHAPTER XXXIV. TIE DEUE,6I4: OF FATE. " laovr I him? 'Though scorned and slighted, Thrown like wortnless weds apart, Feel'inv seared, afLction bli4hted, Love him ?—y6s, with all my heart! With a passion niperhurnan— Constabcy„ thy name is woman !" The arr6.ogernents for the fatal marriage were nearing c•nopletion. Ratte;lge had endeAvoured to persuade Verlie not t, have the al!-important ceremony performed in , Black- for f.i4htiiols,!; but in this 8110 was not tc foi,olren from her resolution.

"I love the old, dark stone pile, with the white- capped waves curling about it," she answered, softly. "Do not try to oppose me, Rutledge." The pretty bridesmaids were delighted at the novel, romantic idea.

"It was decidedly out of the common," they declared, unanimously. "Let the marriage take place at the lighthouse by all means." Rutledge had therefore t set to work, sparing neither pains nor money, to make tho pia,ee a veritable fairy bower for the great occasion. Although Mark Sefton had been raised to great wealth and afdaence, he could never be induced to give up possession of the old light- house. It had been placed in the care of a trusted assistant.
It was the merriest party that ever boarded a steam yacht that stepped on board the Island Queen that 20th day of June. The ceremony was to take place two days later —on the evening of the 22ud.

How proud Nella Sdtou was of her beautiful daughter Verlie. As she watched her standing on deck by Rutledge Chester's side, she noted how fond they were of each other; and in that moment a thought of Uldene, who had come between them, came to her. Ah, how strange it was that these two young girls had been destined to love the same man. During the whole journey, the memory of Uldene haunted her. She could not tell why. She could not forget a remark Uldene had once made, which, at the time, although spoken in jest, had made a great impression upon her. The subject under discussion had been a young lover who had married a year after the death of a pretty sweetheart, who had pined away beeline, her guardian had separated her from this lover.

"lie should never have married. He should have been true to her memory while his life lasted 1" Uldene had cried, her cheeks flushing, and her great, dark, glorious eyes gleaming like stars. Adding, excitedly: "If I had been that girl, I should have come back from my grave to have snatched him from another altar. They could not bury me so deep but what I should have risen."

The words haunted the mother's anxious heart, try hard as she could to forget them. " Uldene is lying cold and dead in her grave," she murmured, gazing down into the blue waves. "She can never come between Verne and her love again."
wThere was a merry party waiting at the light- house to receive them, and welcome the bride-elect back to her old home.

"''Mid pleasures and palaces though we may roam, Be it ever so humble, there's no place like home," murmured Verlie, with tears in her pretty blue eyes, as she walked up the well-remembered path, surrounded by her friends. Early the next morning the bridal trousseau—a marvel of art—axived. Neddy Temple was alone with Verlie when it was unpacked. "Oh, do try it on, dear," she cried, enthusiasti- cally. "I cannot wait patiently until to-morrow evening to see the effect. Do try it on. That's a darling." Against her better judgment, Verlie allowed herself to be persuaded into donning it, even to the tiny white kid slippers, tie orange wreath and filmy veil. "You will look like an angel, Verlie," declared Neddy, impulsively throwing her arms around her friend, and kissing her rapturously. "Rutledge will be the happiest man in the world when he leads you to the altar. Your fair, dazzling loveliness will bewilder the adoring fellow." "Flatterer !" laughed Verlie blushing, " I shall take take my death of cold in the breeze you're giving me." The laughter of the two girls was suddenly cut short by the entrance of the old housekeeper. "You did not hear me knock, I reckon, -Alla Verlie. I thought—" The sentence never was finished.

"Good Lord ! " gasped the old woman, holding up her hands in dismay, and staring with all her might at the slim, graceful figure that wheeled around from the mh.ror. "Oh, Lord, if she hain't got on her weddin' gown an' all the fixin'o! May the saints preserve us from the uiducky omen Oh, poor lamb—poor lamb! Take 'em off. quick ! " "What on earth do you mean, my good woman exclaimed Neddy, sharply, seeing that all the colour had fled from Verlie's cheeks, and left them pale aE marble.
"I mean that's unlucky to try on a weddin' gown, and all the fixirfs, on the day before the wceldin'," answered the old woman, bluntly. "No good ever cornea of it."

"That's all old women's nonsense," declared Neddy, giving her a knowing wink behind Verlie's back, and holding up her little white hand with a warning gesture. "Come, now, Mn. Dunn, own up that you just said that to have a little fun with Verlie. Why, the girl actually thinks you are in dead earnest.'
Evidently the blunt old housekeeper was too obtuse to catch IsTeddy's meaning. "It's the truth, miss," she stoutly declared, solemnly. "I'd as soon hey seen her a stanciin' there in her shroud."
"You horrible creature!" cried the exasperated Neddy, "It's positively wicked to croak of evil. Why you make oae's b:ood run cold ! Thank goodness I've too much good sense to believe in omens."

" You're a rattle-brained piece, with no sense to speak of to spare," mumbled the old woman, quitting the room, and banging the door after her. Neddy's sharp ears had heard, however, and a wicked, rolheising laugh floated after her. - Ned 4 WM just the airl to talk. Varlie out of

what she had heard; and in half an hour's time, surrounded by her girl friends, she had quite for- gotten the unpleasant occurrence. On that same day—aye, that very hour—a strange scene was being enacted in the little cottage in which hapless Uldene had found shelter. The delii Wm of :ever wnich had kept her senses enthralled had at last subsided, and she opened her dark eyes to consciousness. For one moment the large pathetic eyes studied the white, anxious face bending over her. "Where am I?" she cried, starting up from her couch in the greatest bewilderment. ftw. "You have been ill for ninny days," answered Miss Lennox, pushing the heavy, dark" curls from • y the white face on her pillow. "Do you not remember me, my dear?" At the sound of her voice memory rushed back to Uldene's busy brain in an instant. "I remember all," she murmured, faintly. "You say I have been ill many days," she said, wonderingly. "Quite two weeks," declared Miss Lennox. "The bridetnaid dress came in to me to make on the day you were taken so ill. It was finished and delivered a week ago." "And the marriage," gasped Uldene, pale as death. "Has that taken place yet?" "It is set for the evening of the 22nd, I be- lieve," answered Miss Lennox, "and is, contrary to expectation, to take place somewhere down South at the bride's old home. It is to be a grand affair. Immediately after the ceremony, the happy couple aVill,start for an extended tour through Europe. So the papers say. Ah, well, to he happy in this life is not for all of us," continued Miss Lennox, with a deep sigh. "For example, I will read yon an article in the paper immediately following the- one I have jest mentioned. It is quite racy," she declared, drawing her chair up closer by the bed- side. "The headline reads: A scandal in High Life.' It will be sure to interest yon." Miss Lennox was a good little woman, but, like all her sex, she delighted in a spicy scandal, and she supposed, of course, it would interest her protegee. The sum and substance of the article was :

A handsome stranger had married a beautiful heiress, and for a time all went happy as a mar— riage bell. Suddenly a second wife appeared upon the scene, whom he ha, I believed to have been lost at sea on a steamer which had been wrecked, and the beautiful heiress found out to her cost that she was no wife.

"It must he a terrible calamity to be placed in such a predicament," cried Miss Lennox, energeti- cally. "Poor young bride It was a thousand pities to blight her future so, for, of course, she had no claim II Fni him when it was learned he had another wife living."
A sudden thought came to Uldcne, so startling it almost took her breath away. How strangely like her own story was this. She said :

"When the poor wife whom he believed dead found him wedded to another, she should have gone quietly away out of his life forever." "By no means," declared Miss Lennox, amazedly. "Why, she would be committing one of the gravest of crimes by keeping silent against both God's laws and man's; for the second marriage would be illegal, and she would be aware of that fact, while the husband and the bride were innocent of all intention of wrong. Why, did you ever hear of such a case, my dear ?" asked Miss Lennox, curiously. "No—yes. I—that is—no, certainly not," stammered Uldene, confusedly. All that long summer night Uldene was face to face with the terrible thought: Should she let the marriage go on, or should she not? She had drifted into a terrible position, and did not know how to extricate herself from it. She had awakened to the awful reality that her hus- band was going to marry another, while she herself was still alive—she, his lawful wife. She had wrecked his life and Verlie's once before. If she wrecked it a second time, how they would hate her! But--
If she could but warn Rutledge that it must not be.

But he would want proofs as to why he must part from the bride he was about to lead to the altar; and the only proof which would bear the least weight would be to present herself in the flesh before him.
"Oh, God, teach me what to do, which way to turn I" she aobbed, wringing her hands wildly together.,

WE MIGHT JTAYE ESCAPED ANY DAY. There was once a man who,on account of his religious convictions, was arrested by a despotic government and thrown into prison. Looking at the strong stone walls that shut him in, he naturally concluded that he must spend the rest of his days in this lonely and dismal place. Yet wretched as the prospect was, there was some com- fort in the thought that he was a victim of oppressions and not undergoing punishment as a violator of any good and righteous law. All the same he would have been glad to get out, as he had a right to do if he could. Nevertheless there he stayed and languished for six- teen years. At nearly the end of that period it occurred to him one day to climb up on a projecting stone in the wall and take a peep through the window above his bead. He did so, and found the iron bars removable and the sash not fastened. An idea struck him of course. Why not escape? He opened the window, jumped six feet to the ground, and loft that district immediately. He might have done so at any time during his protracted occupancy of the place, if he had only heen blessed with a more inquiring mind and not taken so much for granted.:
Now here comes an incident both like and unlike that of the martyr ; like it because there was loss of free action, unlike it because the sufferer was not imprisoned as he was.

The story is in the form of a letter, one of those letters we all prefer to get—short and made up of short words. The writer, a lady, says : " For the last sixteen years I have been greatly afflicted with billious complaints and weakness. I was always tired, weak,. and low-spirited. I had no appetite, and when food was placed before me I could not touch it. For days I could scarcely eat any- thing. At times I was troubled with sickness and heav- ing at the stomach, spitting up a thick phlegm. I had a troublesome cough, with pain at my chest and diffi- culty of breathing. I got very weak and could scarcely drag myself in and out of the shop. In December,lB9l, I began to take a medicine I had heard well spoken of by many of my customers, called Mother Seigel's Cura- tive Syrup. After I had taken only a few doses I felt relief, and 1 had not used the medicine for a fortnight when I felt better than I had done for years. Thus iencouraged, I kept on with it until I was restored to good health. My son Arthur had suffered off and on for a year from pain and heaviness after meals, with a i sinking feeling at the pit of the stomach. He was induced to try Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup and the result was the same as in my.own case. I know several persons in this district who have been cured by the Syrup after all other means had failed. You are at liberty to publish my letter if you think it might be of benefit to others afflicted as I was. Yours truly, (signed) (Mrs.) M. Ward, 1711, Ilkeston-road, lisdford, Notting- ham, April Ist, 1892."

We congratulate Mrs. Ward upon her deliverance from a distressing and dangerous disease. What a pity she did not sooner learn how easily and certainly she could be cured. Sixteen years is too large a slice out of one's life to be spent in bodily and mental misery. Very few of us can have wealth in any case, but health should be a blessing con.mon and universal as sunshine. And it might be if everybody knew how to preserve it when they possess it, or to regain it when lost. This lady's disease was of the digestive organs—indigestion and dyspepsia—the most afflictive and perilous ot all because it involves every function of the body, scattering its poison at every point through the medium of the blood. Nearly all ailments are nut the differently named results and symptons of this prolific parent of evil. That the remedy she mentions shorild have cured her will not sqrpr4e those who know its well-founded repwtation. Many worse cases constantly yield to it. Our friend the martyr abode in his cell a weary time because he was ignorant of the simple way out. If the reader of these lines is a captive to disease he has no excuse for remaining so. In her short and honest letter our correspondent points to the open door.

div.head: COMMON SENSE.
div.p: COMMON SENSE.

No use pouring a collegiate education into the upper story unless the ground floor of the brain contains com- mon sense. By exercising good, sound, common sense and judgment Mr. Thomas Hall, of 7, Westbury-street, South Stockton, succeeded in extricating himself from an unpleasant and serious situation. "For a long time I was under medical treatment for inflammation of the bladder and liver complaint, from which I was a sufferer. My urine contained albumen, blood and mucous, and I was in almost constant pain. I suffered from violent sickness, cough at night with heavy per- spiration, pain in head, pain across the loins, fickle appetite, a continual tickling sensation in the throat, and tongu4 thickly coated. As other treatment and remedies failed, I determined to try Warner's Safe Cure. Improvement was noticeable from the initial treatment; in two months time my urine was entirely free from albumen and blcod, and presented a healthy appearance, and the symptoms above referred to had disappeared. I consider that Warner's Safe Cure saved my life, and shall never cease praising and recommending it."

div.head: WARRINGTON ANGLERS' ASSOCIATION ANNUAL MEETING.
div.p: WARRINGTON ANGLERS' ASSOCIATION ANNUAL MEETING.

The annual meeting of the Warrington Anglers' Association was held in the Masonic Room, St. Austin's Chambers, last night week. The chair was occupied by Mr. Mawson, the president. There was a good attendance of members. The Chairman said .that the Committee could not give a very extra- ordinary report for the past year as they had so many ups and downs. The loss of the Latchford and Runcorn canal was a great disappointment. They had placed 8,000 fish into the canal which by the time the disaster took place would have increased to hundreds of thousands. It was, however, no use crying over spilled milk. They must look to the future. They must get a cheaper rate of travelling on the London and North-Western railway, and also impress upon the Cor- poration when they next went before Parliament that they must not forget that the ratepayers should get the right of fishing in their own waters. SECRETARY'S REPORT. Mr. P. KNIGHT, the Secretary, read his annual report in which he stated that the Coiemittee were gratified to state that the association had improved very much dur- ing the year, the membership having increased from 120 to 249 during that period, and the general status of the association had advanced in a very marked degree. They had succeeded in acquiring a portion of the old river at Lymm, which was already fairly well stocked with roach, perch and pike, the latter abounding in such numbers as to practically prevent the propagation of other coarse fish. They, had relaxed their rules some- what to allow of their being reduced, and in this they had been fairly successful, a considerable number of fine pike having been taken from it. There was an excellent supply ot fresh water to be had from Sow Brook, and it was intended to clear the banks and water from bushes, weeds, lac., and by the end of the close season they hoped to have an excellent fishing ground. They were in treaty with the agent of Lord Shrewsbury with a view to acquiring the fishing rights in a portion of the River Gowy (locally known as Trafford Brook), and from the nature of the correspondence, they had reason to believe they would be successful. At the same time, it must not be overlooked that this would entail considerable expense in the way, of rent, watching, ,te. They had received some excellent offers of assistance, and would require the ce-operation of every member of the Asso- ciation to enable them to complete the arrangement. This, as was well known was an excellent stream both for t-out and coarse fish. They had also had a correspondence with the manager of the Bridgewater Canal in reference to the fishing rights,and, though the result had not been satisfactory, if it were thought desirable to proceed further, they would re-open the question hen they had reason to be- lieve they would succeed. In July they had the first angling contest under the auspices of the association, at which a number of members competed for 14 prizes, the first being a splendid gold medal presented by the president, Mr. Mawson, and 13 other prizes' ranging from £1 to 2s. 61. and though the " takes" were not large, the competition was somewhat spirited during the last hour. The Runcorn and Latchford Canal had turned out a dead loss to them. This was to be regretted, as, besides los- ing all the fish by the bursting of the bank, and the pollution from the Ship CanaLthey had expended nearly £22 in rent, watching, and stocking. It was not pro- posed to proceed further with it,at least not for a year or two. In accordance with rule 13, they were enabled to offer 9s. in prizes for the first three fish in each class, which was a fair prize list considering the amount of the subscription. A full list of prize winners would be sub- mitted later. They found that several of the rules were not quite clear, and required alteraeion. The monthly meetings would be held on the third Tuesday in the month in future, and the meeting place would be in the Roebuck Inn. The question of cheap travelling on the London and North-Western and Great Western railways Still remained in an unsettled condition. From the na- ture of the correspondence it was apparent that these railways were disposed to extend the privilege to the Association, but the London and North-Western were negotiating with the Lancashire and Yorkshire railway with the view of extending the privelege to the whole of Lancashire, Yorkshire, and Cheshire,and until a decision was arrived at, the question must remain in abeyance. This was rather hard, as there was not a single station on the Lancashire and Yorkshire railway they wished to travel to. Toe London and North-Western have given a pledge to the provincial association that any associa-1 tion becoming affiliated with them would have the con- , cession granted, so that it was difficult to see how they ' departed from their pledges. The committee expressed their thanks to the members for their generous support during the past year, and hoped they would place the Warrington Association in the foremost ranks of the angling organizations of the country. The treasurers' report showed that the receipts amounted to £42 18s 11. d, and the expenditure £39 Os. Bd. which left a balance of £3 18s. 3d. The report was passed unanimously. The election of officers was then proceeded with. Mr. Mawson expressed a wish to retire from the presidency, but he ultimately decided to retain the office at the unanimous request of the meeting. The following were chosen as vice- presidents : Councillors Heaton, Roberts, and L. Green- Messrs. J. Lyon Whittle, Jenkins, W. Taylor, W. A. Proud, Joseph Mottram, T. Turner, Wm, Bodle, R. Rem?, C. White, S. Wellhead, J. L. Tunstall, W. H. Podrnore, W. Woods, and W. Skelton. The following Committee was elected : Messrs. E. Porter, J. Bancroft, A. Cook, S. Hartshorne, H. Kent, J. Garnett, F. Emson, Shaw, C. Ba,keter, J. Roberts, and J. Yarwood. Mr. Knight was re-elected secretary, and Mr. W. Bolton, treasurer. The distribution of prizes was then proceeded with. the following were the prize winners : Messrs. James Truc,kley, Edward Porter, Lawrence Sparrow, Peter night, Wm. Bodle, Chris. Basketer, Wm. Wood, Joseph John Forster, Wm . Bate. James Bancroft, Charles Shaw, anti Samuel Foulkes, senr.
THE INTERNATIONAL PRIZE! FIGHT.

The international" glove fight between Corbett and I.Nlitchell came off on Thursday, at Jacksonville, Florida, In the presence of four thousand persons. It lasted nine MiQutes. Mitchell was dreadfully punished in three rounds, and Corbett was declared the winner and the champjooaf the world. As soon as the pugilists quitted the ground they were arrested by the Sheriff, but qleased on giving bonds for their appearance in court.
NEWTON-LE-WILLOWS CRICKET AND
BOWLING CLUB.
ANNUAL MEETING.

The annual meeting of the Newton-le-Willows Cricket and Bowling Club was held in the Pied Bull Hotel, Newton, on Wednesday evening. There was a large number of Committee-men and members present, and the chair was occupied by the presi- dent, Mr. J.Smith, of Wigan. The Chairman said that he must offer his humble apology for his seeming neglect in not attending to his duties during the past year. His business ramifications prevented him from doing what he should like to do, so that he would tender his resignation, and ask them to appoint someone else who could devote more time to the office. He felt the honour of being president of the club, and he regretted that he was not able to attend to his duties.

TREASURER'S REPORT. The Treasurer (Mr. W. El. Hindlev) next gave the statement of accounts for the year 1893. They started the yearwith a balance of £25 14.5. 51. The total re- ceipts for the year had been v. 86 us. id., and the ex- penditure had been £lB5 9s. id., which left a balance of £1 2s. There had been considerable expenditure upon the bowling green this year, or the balance would have been very much greater.—The treasurer's report was adopted on the motion of Mr. E. Fairclough, seconded by Mr. Singleton.

It may,says the London Correspondent ot the Man- chester Guardian:" now be regarded as certain that the °PPosition to the Parish Councils Bill in the House of Lords will be of a somewhat unheroic character. The attendance in the House on Thursday night was smaller than the Whips expected,and there were no signs of any r"g controversial interest in the measure. Lord alisbury's speech is everywhere interpreted as pointing to a policy of amending the bill in detail rather than to any intention of striking at any of its essential ,Principles. As a matter of fact, there will be a large number of amendments, and it is in order that these may be prepared that the Committee stage h been deferred until next Thursday. A great many of Ml.tbem will be purely drafting amendments, as the 'ti th es of the measure in e House of Lords believe that they have discovered a number of inconsistences in the bill as it has come up, most of which are obviously due to the Mult.itudi mous points on which chances were intro- mu: d to awe effect to the compromise with the Opposi- lo Tliere is not the least prospect, however, of pro- opnngoed: discussion in Committee. The expectation of the din'nes`tion Whips is that this stage will be disposed of by Peet time on Friday, and in any case there is no pros- it will last beyond Friday night.

div.head: PATRONS. OP THE CLUB.
div.p: PATRONS. OP THE CLUB.

On the motion of the Chairman, seconded by Mr. R. Brierley, the five patrons, Lord Newton, Mr. T. W. Legh, M.P., Colonel McCorquodale, J.P., Mr. T. J. Gillespie, J.P., and Mr. A. C. McCorquodale, J.P., were re-elected.

div.head: ELECTION AE PRESIDENT.
div.p: ELECTION AE PRESIDENT.

Mr. R. Brierley proposed the re-election of Mr. J. Smith as president for the ensuing year. He had reasons to believe that Mr. Smith would be able to give a little more of his time to the club during the coining year.— Mr. Wilkinson seconded the motion which was carried with applause.—The President in responding, thanked the club' very much for the honour they had conferred upon him for the second time. He would promise that he would do all he could to attend to the duties of the office. (Applause.) Business of course must be attended to before pleasure, but he would try to devote as much time to pleasure as president of the club,as he could dur- ing the next year. (Applause.) ELECTION OF WE-PRESIDENTS. Mr. Liptrott proposed, and Mr. Bateman seconded the election of the following gentlemen as vice-presidents, Messrs. J. Fairclough, J.P ,R. Stone, J.P., R. Brierley, J. W. Glover, H. J. Longton, and J. Marshall.—The motion was carried unanimously.

div.head: ELECTION OF TREASURER.
div.p: ELECTION OF TREASURER.

Mr. Bateman i;;;O-ssed the re-election of Mr. W. H. Hindley as treasurer.—Mr. Speakman in seconding said that the accounts for the past year were highly satisfac- tory, and were very creditable to Mr. Flindley person- ally. He did not think they could improve upon him in any way.—Mr. Brierley also spoke highly of Mr. Hindley's abilities, and the motion was passed unanimously.

div.head: ELECTION OF SECRETARIES.
div.p: ELECTION OF SECRETARIES.

The retiring secretaries were Messrs. T. Fairclough and J. Cooke. Mr. Fairclough expressed a wish to retire, and Mr. Speakman thereupon proposed the elec- tion of Messrs. J. Cooke, and E. Grace.—Mr. E. Fair- dough seconded the motion which was passed.

ELECTION OF CAPTAINS. Mr. Hindley proposed the re-election of Mr.J. Cooke to the post of captain of the first Cricket team. He thought that it was the best thing that could be done at the pre- sent time. He hoped Mr. Cooke would see his way to take it another year.—Mr. T. Wilkinson seconded the motion which was unanimously carried. Mr. T. Wilkinson was elected captain of the second team on the motion of Mr. E. Fairclough, seconded by Mr. Percival. Messrs. C. H. Bodmer, G. Fairclough, J. Liptrott, and E. Fairclough, were unanimously re-elected bowling cap- tains for the ensuing,vear, on the motion of Mr. Single- ton, seconded by Mr. Brierley. Messrs. A. Andertoc, J. Latchford, and J. W. Glover, were elected tennis captains, on the motion of Mr. E. Fairclough, seconded by Mr. W. H. Hindley.

div.head: GENERAL COMMITTEE.
div.p: GENERAL COMMITTEE.

Ten gentlemen were nominated to form a general com- mittee. As there were only nina required, a vote was taken with the following result :—Dr. H. Watkins, 33 votes; Mr. Bateman, 32 ; Mr. W. Speakman. 30 ; Mr. J. Singleton, 29 ; Messrs. W. Dudgeon and T. Harrison,2B ; Mr. R. Brierley, 26; Mr. R. Brunton, 24 ; and Messrs. J. Simpson and G. Boyer, 23 each. The first eight were declared elected, and the names of Messrs. Simpson and Boyer were again submitted tl the meeting, with the re- sult that Mr. Simpson was electe,l by 21 votes to 16.

GROUND COMMITTEE. The following gentlemen were elected as members for the ground committee, on the motion of Mr. J. Liptrott, seconded by Mr. Bateman : Messrs. F. Brierley, W. Longton, J. Sankey, T. Wilkinson and T. Howard. ELECTION OF AUDITORS.
Messrs. Borer and Parks were elected auditors on the proposition of Mr. Singleton, seconded by Mr. E. Fair- dough.
GROUNDS MAN.

Mr. Frank Hutchins was elected grounds man on the motion of Mr. R. Brierley. Everyone was satisfied at the manner in which things had been kept during the past season. QUESTION OF A CRICKET PROFESSIONAL. Mr. Hindley said that he thought that a man should be engaged as a coach to the young players of the club. He thought that a situation might be found for a suit- able man, who could be engaged by the club at V. per week as a coach. The want of a coach was very much felt at the present time. There were many promising cricketers in the club who ought not to be neglected. He thought that the funds of the club would bear the extra expense. He moved that steps be taken in this direction.—Mr. R. Brierlev second& the motion, and endorsed everything that Mr. Hindlev had said. He had been connected with the club for over a quaiter of a century, and he remembered the time when the club stood equal to Manchester. Me hoped the time would not be far distant when they could challenge that club again. (Applause.)—Mr. Liptrott supported the motion as also did Mr. Wilkinson, and the motion that the com- mittee should move in the matter was carried unani- mously.
THE LANCASHIRE AND CHESHIRE HOWLING ASSOCIATION.
Mr. E. Fairclough moved and Mr. Hindley seconded, that the club again join the Lancashire and Cheshire Bowling Association during the coming season.—Car- ried.

NEWTON DIVISION BOWLING ASSOCIATION. Mr. Liptrott proposed that the club again enter the above association. They did not get as far into the competition last season as they would like, but this year the various grounds would probably be in a better state than last year. He understood that this was so in Haydock, Golborne, and North Ashton.—Mr. Speakman seconded.—Carried.

QUESTION OF TENDERS. Mr. T. Fairclough proposed that tenders for licensed victuallers be invited for refreshments on Saturday after- noons during the season—Mr. Elindley seconded—Mr. Parks moved an amendment that tenders be not invited and Mr. Cooke seconded the motion.—After a prolonged discussion the amendment was carried by 33 votes to five.
NEW MEMBERS. The following were elected new members :—Messrs. G. Owen, Dorman F. INagg. Dr. Street, A. Boshell, J. Kean, P. Fletcher, Laithwaite and E. Clarke. APPOINTMENT OF DELEGATES.

Mr. E. Fairclough was appointed delegate,and Messrs. Bodmen, and I. Bateman, representatives to the Lanca- shire and Cheshire Association on the motion of Mr. T. Fairclough, seconded by Mr. Hindley ; and Mr. Lip- trott was appointed delegate and Messrs. T. Fairclough and W.H. Hindley representatives to the Newton Divison Association. After the conclusion of the business, a convivial meet- ing was held in which songs, Sze., were given and the company broke up at a late hour in the evening.

div.head: AN IRISH INCIDENT.
div.p: AN IRISH INCIDENT.
A " LIVE "CORPSE.

- • -- An extraordinary ease of mistaken death is reported from Drogheda by the" Irish Times." A young man named Garrigatt had, as was supposed, expired, and was being" waked" by his bereaved relatives and friends, when the grave clothes began to move and the" corpse ' to show signs 51 animation. The more timid of the on- lookers fled from the house and refused to return. Strong men grew pale and hastened from the room. Women wailed and clapped their hands in an agony of terror. Within a short time all doubts weie dispelled, and the young man woke out of his trance.

AUTHORITY.

The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton workhouse, on Tuesday. Mr. J. Mclntyre presided, and there were present the Revs J. W.N. Tanner and J. Hanby, Messrs.J. Knowles, H. E. Heywood, E. Aaron, J. Pickering, C. W. Davenport, C.T.Whitley, J. Stokes, T. Lewis, A. Greenway. S. Woodward, J. M. Williams, J. Brandreth, A. Browne;. J. Ashtrm (clerk), G. Ashton (deputy clork), J. Farrington (nuisance inspector); and Dr. Adams (medical offi- cer).

HALTON PAROCHIAL COMMITTER. At a meeting of the Halton Parochial Committee a letter was read from the Local Government Board with respect to the drainage into Halton Brook, and Mr. Far- rington was requested to prepare a full report stating the number of houses drained into the sewer, the num- ber recently connected therewith, and the construction of the sewer and settling tank, and genert lly as to the effect on the brook. The Clerk read the provisions of the Public Health Acts, 1875 and 1894 and the orders of the Local Government Board empowering them with increased powers, and submitted a draft of the bye laws, which it was decided should be approved and adopted, and that they be forwarded to the Local Government Board for confirmation.—The minutes were approved, and on the motion of Mr. Aaron it was further resolved that similac bye laws be adopted for Weston. —Mr. Aaron said they did not want a Parcchial Com- mittee at Weston, and the Clerk said the bye laws could be applied direct from the Authority. APPSRTON PAROCHIAL COMIUTTEM. At the meeting of Appleton Parochial Committee on Friday afternoon,,the 19th January, the Clerk (Mr. J. Ashton) read the provisions of the Public Health Act, 1875, and the Public Health Acts Amendment Act, 1890, which by orders of the Local Government Board •dated respectively the 4th day of July, 1689, the 3rd day of January, 1890, the 17th day of October. 1892, and the 10th day of October, 1893, are declared to be in for in the contributory place of Hull and Appleton and sub- mitted the drafts of byelaws with respect to (1) the cleansing of footways, pavements, removal of house re- fuse, ashpits and cesspools ; (2) the prevention of nuisances arising from filth, dust, ashes, and rubbish and the prevention of the keeping of animals on any premises so as to be injurious to health ; (3) new streets and buildings ; (4) slaughter-houses ; (5) offensive trades; (6) alteration of buildings. After a ,lengthy discussion, the subject was adjourned until a meeting to be held on Friday the 26th inst. It was resolved that application be made to the Local Government Board for an order in- vesting the Authority with the powers of Section 154 of the Public Health Act,1875, with reference to the pur- chase of premises for the improvement of streets and of Section 172 of the same Act with reference to the making of byelaws for licensing horses, &c., for hire and that it be pointed out to the Local Government Board that the Authority have been invested with such powers as re- garded the contributory place of Frodsham, and that taking into consideration the rapid growth of Stockton Heath and Wilderspool in the contributory place of Appleton it was quite as essential that the Authority should be invested with such powers as regarded the contributory place of Hull and Appleton; and further that it would he a great advantage if the Authority were invested with like powers as regarded each of the said contributory places not only that thereby the same set of byelaws would be applicable to each but a considerable expense, would be saved in the printing of such byelaws. —The minutes were approved on the motion of Mr. Davenport. TEIE SCARLET FEVER OUTBREAK.

THE CLOSING OF KINGSLEY SCHOOLS. The Rev. A. P. Reynolds, vicar of Kingsley, wrote under date January 11th, respecting the reopening of Kingsley schools, that he had seen Mr. Woodward, and had a conversation with him on the subject of his reso- lution at a meeting of the Board on the 9:11 inst. Mr. Woodward informed him that his resolution was chiefly based (1) on the assumption that if the day schools were reopened the Sunday schools would also reopen, and the managers of the latter are not able to exercise the extreme caution always observed in the day schools; (2) that the day schools would suffer no pecuniary loss from the enforced closure. Disposing of no 1, they had mutually agreed to keep the Sunday schools closed for the present. As regarded no 2, Mr. Woodward was labouring under a misapprehension, which he had explained to him. He asked was there sufficient ground for this further order to close. Dr. Adams said "If the Kingsley schools are reopened great care will require to be exercised in seeing that no children attend from infec- ted houses." At the present time he believed there were just two houses infected from neither of which, of course, were children corning to the schcols. Where two or even three or four houses infected, if they could be found a sufficient justification for closing a school with an average attendance of 160, of whom 148 were in attendance that week, and the remainder absent for no reason whatever in connection with infectious disease. He had no sympathy with the resistance of lawful authority, but felt that he must on behalf of the mana- gers enter the strongest protest against this further order issued at the time when the disease seemed to have been stayed in its progress. and when, with the exception of two or three houses where patients were rapidly nearing convalescence, there is no widespread epidemic. He felt that he was taking some responsibility in keeping the schools open, but on hearing from the Education Depart- ment, as he doubtless would, he wculd place the feecs before them—The clerk said he therefore eent the report to the Education Department.—Mr. leoodward : The vicar closed the schce Is immediately on receipt of that letter, and they remained closed to this day.—Mr. Hanby said they had no right to be troubled with these letters. Any correspondence must be with the Educa- tion Department, and not with the authority,—Mr. Woodward said he had found that the compulsorily closing of the schools would entail some loss not upon the managers of the school but upon the teacher himself. He thought it only fair, if they, acting for the public weal, compelled schools to be closed, they should see that so far as they had the power, no pecuniary loss followed their action. (Hear, hear.) He was told that in the case of the closing of the schools, some two years aeo,at Kingsley, through an epidemic of measles the Master lost something like £l6 through a reduction in the examina- tion grant, which depended upon the report of the In- spector and must be affected by the continued closing of the school. He moved that a repreeentation of this matter be made to the Education Department.—Mr. Aaron seconded and added that enen the Weston schools were closed through an epidemic of measles they ha 4 the best grant ever the school. had had before.—Mr. Bran- dreth : I don't think u-e should interfere with the matter at all.—The Clerk : I don't think you will gain anything by doing as Mr. Woodward suggests.—Mr. Woodward thought the basis of allowance to the schools might fairly be placed upon the last grant taken in conjunction with the attendance for two years.—Mr. Hanby: On the other hand, I don't think one case can be shown where there has been loss or hardship, when the schools have been closed by the order of a local authority. The Govern- ment Inspector takes consideration of these matters when he makes his report.—Mr. Woodward: I have already instanced a case in which the master himself has lost £l6 one year from the examination grant, not the capi-

div.head: REMARKABLE DISCUSSION AT THE WARRINGTON BO::. vr. GUARDIANS.
div.p: REMARKABLE DISCUSSION AT THE WARRING- TON BO::. vr. GUARDIANS.

At the fortnigntly meeting 'of ;tne Warrington Board of Guardians, held at the Workhouse on Wednesday, lir. G. Ratcliffe presiding, a somewhat remarkable discussion took place, on the washing of paupers' linen. Mr. Hibbert said before the ordinary business of the Board was proceeded with he desired to ask a question, and it was one to which he should want an answer. He wanted to know whether, when a pauper came into the Workhouse with a dirty shirt,one all covered with blood —he should be sent out with his shirt in that state.

- The Chairman: You must raise the question when the House Committee's minutes have been read. Mr. Hibbert : A man from Earlestown has been turn- ed out in that condition. It was disgraceful. The Chairman : He is a bad character. I saw him when he came out. He was" cadging" of me. Mr. Hibbert ; That's all right. The question I want settling is whether his shirt ought not to have been washed.. I want the answer of our clerk.

The Chairman: You had better -ask. the question when the minutes have been read. After the reading of the minutes Mr. Hibbert said : Now then, will you allow me to speak now. I want the Clerk to answer. The affair is a disgrace to the Work- house and to us. Can you tell me who was responsible. I The Chairman: I cannot answer you. Mr. Hibbert : Well, I want to know. It is a disgrace- ful affair. The man looked like a butcher's shop—cover- ed with blood. _

Mr. Heaton : I take it that the man was some we eke in the hospital. He was then put in inmates clothes and hi a old clothes were given back to him upon coming out. It is not the place of any official to wash clothes for an inmate, they only have to disinfect them. Mr. Hibbert Is that so Mr. Clerk.

The Chairman : I don't know. I think— Mr. Hibbert : I want to know from the Clerk what are the regulatioas on the matter. Mr. Shaw : The regulations do not instruct the offi- cials to wash linen. If the inmate ask permission he is allowed to wash his linen himself. The Chairman: This man had been fighting at Earles- town. He had been before the Bench, and I think it would have been wiser had Mr. Hibbert brought the matter before the House Committee.
Mr. Hibbert : House Committee be hanged ; they don't care a straw for either the man or his shirt. I want an answer.

Mr. Davies : I take exception to Mr. Hibbert's re- marks about the Committee. They are uncalled for. Mr. Hibtert : They are true. Mr. Ward, master, explained that when a person came into the House he was given inmates clothes, and his own taken from him and disinfected in the oven. The officials were certainly not expected to wash a pauper's clothing.

Mr. kibbert : Oh! well that shirt ought to be put in the oven and some gravey stewed from it. (Laughter and" Oh! Oh !") May I ask the Clerk whether there is no law upon the matter, to prevent a man being turned out in such a disgraceful manner.

The Clerk: There is no law upon the matter. It is purely a matter of sentiment. If a man gets his cloth- ing into such a beastly state it is not expected that the officials should wash it for him. He wears other cloth- ing whilst in the House, but there is no doubt that had he asked for permission to have the shirt washed it would have been given. It was taken from him, how- ever, at the porter's office, and neither the Master nor Matron saw the shirt, so that they are exonerated from any blame that might even have attached itself to the matter.

div.head: Mr. Hibbert expressed himself satisfied with the explanation and the subject dropped.

WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians was held at the Workhouse on Wed- nesday. There were present :—Messrs. G. Ratcliffe (in the chair), R. Heaton, J. Muir, J. Clarke, R. .Owen, H. J. L,mgton, A. J. Jolley, A. Jolley, S. Davies, W. Balharry, H. Ilibbert, W. Houghton, J. Dignum, W. Turton, J. Swinton, Mather, W. Fair- dough, E. Aukland, Warburton, J. Hill, J. Dobson, Dr. Paterson ; J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (assis- tant clerk), C. H. Ward (master), H. M. Mines (superintendent).

The Clerk stated that he had forwarded on ail papers bearing upon the matter to the Local Government Board.
