The Clerk -read a letter from the Registrar General expressing regret that the Guardians did not agree with him as to the desirability of uniting the Newton-in- Makerfield and Winwick sub-districts. He, however, was not disposed to press the proposal. He enclosed the usual form for the appointment of a successor to the late Mr. Turner, registrar for the Winwick sub-district. The CLEM( stated that he had received several applica- tions for the vacant post.—Mr. Longton propssed that the Board go into Committee on the matter.—Mr. A. Jolley urged that it should be considered by the open Board.—Mr. R. Heaton pointed out that the subject was referred back from the meeting held a month ago, so that the Guardians representing Croft, Arbury. and Win- wick might recommend a candidate to the Board. If those Guardians had come prepared with the name of a candidate he proposed that the Board proceed with the appointment. The choice of a candidate was accordingly left to the Guardians for the district., and Mr. Mather proposed Mr. Peter Birchall, pointing out that he was a most suitable man for the post, and lived in the centre of the district.—Mr. Longton thought that Mr. Birchall be- ing a relative of one of the Guerdians there might be some delicacy in the matter, and to give the Guardians an opportunity of voting he would propose Mr. W. Sweetlove, Winwick Post Office, for the post.—Mr. A. J. Jolley seconded.—Mr. Owen thereupon bedded to pro- pose Mr. Daintith, while at the same time having no ob- jection to Mr. Birchall.—Mr. Muir seconded. The three applications were then read to the B@iard.—Mr. Longton said he was quite certain that Mr. Sweetlove was a most suitable man for the place. He enjoyed the confidence and respect of the whole of the inhabitants ot Winwick and Croft.—Mr. Mather said he quite agreed with what had been said about Mr. Sweetlove, but he worked at the Vulcan Foundry and was away all day.—The Clerk observed that weever was appointed must have a de- puty, and it was competent for Mr. Sweetlove to recom- mend his v,ife to the office.—The three names were sub- sequently put tc the meeting, and the voting resulted as follows .—Daintith 2, Sweetlove 5, and Birchall 14. Mr. Birchall was accordingly elected.

tatiop grant.—Mr. Hanby: Did thiq Authority close the schnol,—Mr. Woodward: No.—Mr. Hanby: It is a different thing altogether I am only talking of cases closed by this Authoritv.—Mr. Woodward said he pressed his motion.—Mr. Bran-dreth moved an amendment that no action be taken until it was ascertained that there had been a loss.—After further discussion it was unani- mously decided that the Clerk write to the Education Department and ask if a school could possibly lose through obedience to the instructions of a bacal Authority. THE VICAR OF NORLEY AND HIS COMMUNICA- TIONS. _ AMUSING DISCUSSION.

The clerk read the 'following letter from Dr. Adams, medical officer of health, under date January 12, says, "In reply to yours of the tenth inst., re Norley schools, I can only state what I told Mr. Nun at my interview with him, that while it was true that no fresh cases were being reported in Norley, yet that the children from houses in which other children might yet be "peel- I ing "after scarlet fever might form carriers of infection I if allowed to mingle with ethers in school, and hence my recommendation in last report, that, if opened,great care should be exercised in excluding children from infected houses. No fresh cases are, yet reported. I dont think anything is to be gained by making a fight of the matter with Mr. Nun as to the re-opening,but the sanitary condition of the schools should be amended as in my report." The doctor now informed the authority that. there had been no fresh cases reported at Norley since the last meeting, but there had been seven fresh cases reported in connection with the Kingsley outbreak, most of the cases were in houses already reported upon. The Clerk said he had received a long letter from the Vicar of Norley since the meeting commenced.—Mr. Hey- wood : Are we obliged to hear all this. This communi- cation ought to be sent to the Education Department, I take Hanby : Yes.—The Clerk: I wrote to the Vicar that the matter must be attended to or it would be reported to the Education Department.—Mr. Hanby: Any complaint against our instriactions must be sent to the Education Department.—Mr. Woodward : The Vicar of Norley has sent me a letter, Mr. Chairman ; I have not opened the letter. I will leave it for you. I dont want to act with animus in this matter. lam acting on behalf of the public weal.—Mr. Heywood: If you mean to open that see it it is the same length before you read it. (Laughter.)—Mr. Woodward: If it be the request of this Board that I open the letter I will do it. —A member (entreatingly) : Please don't (laughter).— The Chairman :Is it your pleasure that we read these letters. I take it that our clerk has gone through his letter.—The Clerk: No I have not. (laughter).—Mr. Stokes : I move that it be read.—Mr. Pickering seconded —Mr. Williams moved a negative. The authority had decided that certain work must be done at Norley schools and it had not been carried out.—Mr. Nun had resolutely set himself against the authority on this mat- ter.—Mr. Hanby ; I beg to move that the Education Department be made acquainted with the fact that Nor- ley schools were ordered to be closed and are not closed. —Mr. Brandreth : We have an objection to the sanitary condition of the schools which is equally important as closing the schools for fever.—The clerk said on the 6th inst he wrote Mr. Nun stating the authority expected the medical officers instructions to be carried out. If he had any other alterations which he thought would be preferable, he must submit a plan for the approval of the authority. Perhaps his suggestions were contained in this letter.—Mr. Woodward : I think it is derogatory to have a cavil with Mr. Nun upon this question.—Mr. Stokes :We have no evidence that he is cavilling at all. It was decided by 6 votes to 5 that the letter be read. The Clerk read the letter as follows :—" Norley Vicar- age, January 22,1894. Gentlemen,—A paragraph which appeared in a Chester paper of the 12th inst., compels me to request that in all fairness Mr. Woodward's incor- rect statement at your last meeting—(viz. : The Vicar of Norley had asserted that the sanitary arrangements at the school were perfect but now proved by further investigation to be quite the contrary) be withdrawn or at least modified. No such thing had been even implied much less was perfection asserted in any communication of mine. To protest against sweeping charges of insani- taryness brought against the school, which Ido re-affirm are not justified by facts, is not quite the same—is it ? as declaring the buildings, etc., perfect according to modern requirements (or—possibly sometimes mere fads). For my own part, I frankly own that the build- ings are not what I could wish them to be, or what they ought to be in a parish like Norley, and my efforts to make the school both efficient and sufficient have not escaped some opposition and misrepresentation. My sympathies, in the main are with the Education Department and the Sanitary Authorities in their endeavours to make schools what they should be—but in justice to my co-managers, I am bound to traverse the exaggerated statement and unfounded charges levelled against our school, and in the interests of managers, teachers, par- ents and scholars to publicly protest against the methods of the Sanitary Authority, as exemplified in this case. Your Inspecter stated that he adhere,/ to his report; what was it ? Drains blocked were not) ; —(theY large quantity of foul liquid in ashp(it and the closets had been thoroughly cleaned ;z— -,at disinfected only a short a time before his visit, tt,re was but a small quantity of liquid and that disinfected 15 days after) ; water supply bad—(it is good for its purpose, washing, and it is not as the master -ould have told him, used for drinking) ; measles b.d broken out—(he had taken no steps to verity ote report, and as a fact there was not a single case of measles in the parish). Other remarks upon that ncnool were simply an impertinance, and, as Dr. Adams report related to matters which did not concern him or the authority. So much for his report. Dr. Adam's report simply goes to show that the conveni- ences might with benefit be increased, or improved, but does not prove or assert that present arrangements are injurious to the childrens' health, and no one could say they are, looking at the faces of the scholars. Again I must take exception to your Inspector's action in pub- licly announcing the school as a disgrace to the village, etc., before making his report to the Authority. He visited the schools on the 16th of Nov., but not until the 30th of Nov. ,was any official intimation received by the managers. I wrote to the Authority on the 12th Dec., pressing for the re-opening of the school promising to do everything necessary to further secure the healthfulness of the school and wing and the fever had vertically dis- appeared some time before the school 'Was closed. No answer was given to my letter. I learnt privately that Dr. Adams would visit and report. He did not coma for more than a fortnight, in the meantime the Authority had met. It was reported that fever was prevalent still in Norley, and on this report the schools were closed yet another fortnight. I affirm that there was not then nor had been from some time before the school was closed on the 30th Nov., a single fresh case of fever nor any dan- ger from previous sickness. I requested p.oof to the contrary. No proof is forthcoming, the fact of the mat- ter is the officers were three weeks or a month behind their work to do any real good; the attendance at school was good, and the school work was interrupted at an important time ; children turned into the lanes to con- tract fresh sickness and to distract their parents without any real necessity against such methods. I beg to pro- test, the point of my last inquiry was whether the offices were to be put further from the schools.—' am yours faithfully, C. R. Nunn. When the Clerk had partly read the letter, the Chairman said, "I think we have had enough of that."

(atighter.)—The Clerk.' No, you passed a resolution that it must be read.—At the conclusion of the letter the Chairman remarked with a sigh of relief, "Is that the end ?" (Laugliter.)—Mr. randreth, who had opened the letter to Mr. Woodward, said Mr. Nunn asked Mr. Woodward to withdraw a certain statement. Mr. Hanby: I move that the Education Department be com- municated with.—Mr. Woodward : And that that letter be forwarded to the Education Department —Mr. Han- by : I think all the correspondence ought to go.—Mr.

Aaron : You will have to engage an extra clerk- to copy it. (Laughter.)—Mr. Heywood: Send the originals; don't keep them. (Laughter.)—Mr. Hanby : The Clerk can't do that. It must be dune in the usual orthodox style on foolscap, and foolscap will suit the case very well. (Loud laughter.)—Mr. Woodward seconded the motion.—lnspector Farrington : I still maintain the I accuracy of my report.—Dr.Adams said,after apologising I to Mr. Nunn for the delay, and explained to him that it I was caused through a three weeks' illness, he thought it ; was most ungenerous on his part to report it in a public I letter.—The motion was carried unanimously.—lnspec- -1 tor Farrington.—As Mr. Nunn states the water at Nor- ley School is not used for drinking purposes, I have, therefore, to report that the school is without water ; supply. (Laughter.) When there were 135 children ' without a supply of water, I think the Authority should know about it. I have to ask that notice be served upon Mr. Nunn to provide a water supply.—A Member: Well done, Farrington. (Laughter.)—The Chairman : Is it your pleasure that notice be served ?—There was a loud response of "Aye," and the motion was declared carried unanimously.

div.p: THE WESTON WATER SUPPLY.

NORLEY AND KINGSLEY SCHOOLS TO CONTINUE CLOSED.

In reply to Mr. Woodward, Dr. Adams said it would be advisable to keep the Kingsley Schools closed for an- other fortnight. In Norley no fresh case had been noti- fied for over a month.—Mr. Woodward &lid a number of the fever cases were directly on the border of Norley, and he believed nearer to Norley Sehools than to Kings- ley.—lt was decided that the schools remain closed an- other fortnight.

div.head: WHAT SHARKS CAN SWALLOW.
div.p: WHAT SHARKS CAN SWALLOW.

In respect of being able to dirst almost anything, the shark out rivals the ostrich. A lady's work-box, the papets of a slave ship, a horses head, whales' blub- bier in lumps of seven pounds.all kinds of ship appliancs these and a vast variety of odds and ends, hardly likely to be nourishing, have been found inside a shark. And it is even said to provide its young with a harbour of refuge by swallowing them, and keeping them in hiding ustil the danger is• past. A shark came alongside a ship that was lying some miles off the town of Panama. She was accompanied by a couple of dozen of sharklets,that swam around her head, and from her hungry looks, it was plain she had come to the vessel for a chance meal. The odd thing was that every time there was a splash in the water the sharklets vanished, as if they had taken shelter beneath their mother. The old sailors aboard, however, said mamma had swallowed them. Of course none of the land-lubbers believed them, and so it was resolved to catch the mother. A large hook was fastened to a strong chain, and baited with a nice piece of pork, and thrown over. In a twinkling the greedy fish seized the pork, discovered her mistake in another twinkling, and was lashing the deck in a third twinkling. She was beaten to death, and when cut open, twenty-three wee sharks were found, all alive and kicking. Placed in a large tub of salt water, they immediately began swim- min, about as briskly as if they were on the ocean wave. —" 'Little Folks "

div.head: NEW BOOKS, &c.
div.p: NEW BOOKS, &c.

The first list of a catalogue of portraits of authors,and artists wit() have contributerl towards the production of the volumes published by Messrs. Cassell and Co., was issued at the end of December. The portraits which are reproduced from photographs, are the Pest specimens of portrait printing that we have se -qt,anl in the list num- ber about forty, including some of the first artists and authors of the day. About the sawne time appeared the first monthly part of" The Dore Dante." (Cassell and Co.), embracing the Inferno, Purgatorio, and Para4iso. It is translated with critical and explanatory notes, by the Rev. Henry Francis Cary, M.A., and when complete will contain one hundred and thirty-six full page illustrations designed by Gustave Dore. As the author.the artist, and the pub- lishers have each and all attained a world-wide celebrity, there must be a demand for such a work as the Dore Dante." We know of no subject more suited to Dore's genius for depicting the weird and imaginative than the immortal cantos of Dante.

" The English Illustrated Magazine" for January is an excellent number for variety. " The Witch's Castle," a fairy tale, is contributed by Carmen Sylvia, Queen of Roumania ; "New Year's Day in Paris," by Emily Crawford •, " Indian Viceroys" (with portraits from photographs) by Sir Edwin Arnold ; "..Some Jewel Mysteries I Have Known," by MAX Pemberton ; in addi- tion to a number of other contributions equally good, including some verses by Robert Herrick, and illtistra- trations by Yeend King, Dudley Hardy. IL Caton Wood- ville, Leslie Wilson and others. The principal literary feature of "The Queen" just now is "The Manxman" by Hall Caine, with illustra- tions by Fred. Pegram. The opening chapters are ex- csedingly interesting, and characteristic of the dauthor's style and knowledge of INlanxland and its inh bitants. The Manxman" will certainly increase the circulation as well as the popularity of "The Queen," the lady's newspaper. "The Young Ladies' Journal" for February gives a cut-out paper pattern of a double circular mantle for a lady. The fashion supplement is issued in book form, a decided improvement on the large sheet previously given, and the coloured sheet illustrates some pretty knick-knacks with directions for making them, &c. The opening chapters of a new story promise it to be very interesting, in short the journal offers plenty of reading, both instructive and entertaining. One of the prettiest coloured designs we have seen for some time, for needlework, is a corner and border for table cover or bed-spread in Persian embroidery, pre- sented with " Sylvia's Journal" for January. The design is one for which three prizes are offered by the proprietors of " Sylvia's Journal" to the amount of ten guineas, for the best worked copy of it, particulars of which will be found in the journal. The latest of" The Lady" hand-books gives most explicit instructions, (with illustrations) how to cut and make tailor-made garments at home, To the uninitiated these hooks must be very useful and acceptable. The paper pattern of an evening cloak with the new butterfly collar, presented with " Weldon's Ladies' Jour- nat " will be greatly appreciated, as it is convertible into a day or evening wrap. There are several interest- ing articles in the number: how to Cress on £3O a year, articles on cooking, practical dressmaking &c. The " NeedlewotiT " number gives instructions how to crochet doll's clotung, toy animals, capes, d'oyleys, &c.

div.head: RUNCORN LIBERAL CLUB.
div.p: RUNCORN LIBERAL CLUB.

The annual meeting of members was held on Wednesday night, at the club premises, Regent-st. Mr. A. R. Norman presided, and there was a large attendance of members. The Chairman, in opening the meeting, congratulated the members upon the change they had made in the present meeting compared with the last Meeting ; which was held in temporary premises in Hi.:h-st. He was very glad to see that they were now settled in their new home, and he thought they would all agree with him that the change they had made was a very agreeable • one, and a very beneficial one to the club. At a special meeting a few months ago, the =Abers authorised the committee to purchase the building, and they did so on very favourable terms from their member, Mr. Brunner. (Applause.) Mr. Brunner had been very kind indeed to them throughout; he did not press them very hard for the money, and the fact of the matter was that it was only quite Tecently that the money had been paid, so that from the time of coming there they were practically living rent free. They therefore saw what a good thing it was to have a good gentleman to deal with in a matter of this kind. If they had had to pay the money down'. the club would have been three months' interest W 01843 off than they were. He was happy to say that they were now their own landlords—(applause)—, and he thought that the money that had been expended in purchasing that building was money well laid out,and money which they would be able easily to realise any time they de- - sired. (Hear, hear.) As regarded the conduct of the club, they had been doing their best to make the social side of it very attractive. They had provided several new billiard tables, and the returns they get for the out- lay in this direction were very satisfactory indeed, and the games could be much better enjoyed than was pos- sible in the old room. They had also been doing their best to improve the intellectual part of the club, and to cultivate the literary side of the club. They commenced this season with a determination to go in for some lec- tures. They had had two lectures, and there was a prospect of others to follow. Of course it would take some time to organise this branch of the club, but the committee would do their best, and he should be glad, far one, to see more of this kind of thing going on than had been the case in the past. (Applause.) Mr. A. Riley, the secretary, then read the report of the Committee as follows :—ln presenting the annual report we may congratulate ourselves that we no longer meet in a hired building, but in one that, for some time at least, may be regarded as a permanent home. It may be remembered that at the last annual meeting great anxiety was expressed by the members, a feeling equally shared by the Committee as to the future, and that the Committee were empowered and strongly urged to ob- tain permanent premises as soon as possible. This had happily been accomplished through the kindness and generosity of our President, J. T. Brunner, Esq., who at a considerable personal sacrifice has conveyed to the Liberal party of Runcorn, the building in which we are now assembled. Our gratitude is also due to those who freely consented to accept the onerous position of trus- tees and made themselves pecuniarily liable in order to advance the cause we all have so much at heart. That the step taken has been fully justified no one will doubt who glances over the balance sheet as although in addi- tion to the purchased price of the freehold building a sum of over two hundred pounds has been needed for alterations, new furniture, and new billiard tables, one hundred and forty pounds of that additional sum had been paid off at the close of the year.. At the present rate of progress a very few years will suffice for paying off tho whole of the purchase and the party will then possess a building as an evidence of the sturdy Liberalism of the Runcorn Polling District. It is pleasing to have to re- cord that since the occup -Lucy of these premises the membership-has so largely increased, an increase which is steadily added to month by month. At the last annual meeting reference was made to the need of lectures and discussions in connection with the club, and a desire ex- pressed that such work should be undertaken at the first possible opportunity. The Committee in their sympathy with that feeling have already arranged for several lec- tures, two of which have been deliver( d —one by the Rev. D. S. Prosser on "The Peers versus the People," the other by Mr. B. Kniveton on "S >cial problems." Both lectures were listened to by a large number of members and friends and the discussion which followed the delivery of the last one, was of a very interesting and educational character. A third lecture by Mr. W. S. Callie, the secretary of the Financial Reform Association under the auspices of the Peace Society, on " the French Revolution and What it cost us," is arranged to take place on the 14th February, and the Committee trust that their efforts in this directien will be appreciated not only by the atten- dance of the club members but of that larger number of Liberals who have not yet identified themselves as mem- bers, and thus help the Club to accomplish its true and full mission of not simply providing f.r the social intercourse of the members, but of spreading political knowledge. Turning to the finaucial part of the Club's operations, we may thus summarise the year's operations. The year commenced with a balance in hand of £45 125.11.,subscriptioas and sale of rapers, profit on annual excursion, hire of lecture room, and sundry re- ceipts, £46 Bs. lid. ; from billiard and handicap re- ceipts, £165 Os. 4d. has been received ; from sale of re- freshments £9 6s. Bd., a total of £266 Bs. 10d. The ex- • penditure has been :—Rent at Bank Chambers,£l3 155.; heating and lighting, £l92e. 4d. ; rates, taxes and in- surance, £4 12s. 3d ; newspapers, printine, stationery, advertising, and sundries, £l7- 16-. 3d. ; legal and lecture expenses. £3 3s. ; purchase of refreshments, £7 • 3s. 6d.; secretary and caretaker's salary and commission, £47 193. 7d. ; bank interest, £4 25. id. ; new billiard tables and refitting old ones,£ll3 4s. 41. ; purchase of Club, £4OO ; alterations and furnishing, £95 19s. 9d., a total expenditure of £726 1.5 Q. 4d., leaving a balance due to the bank •f £460 94. 6d. In drawing this report to a, close the Committee express the confident belief that the step taken during the year has been the right one, and hope the Club will gather in its membership not only,. those who are attracted by its social advaetages, but also those Liberals who sympathises and desire are that the Club may become the actual embodiment of the dis- semination of political knowledge in the surrounding district.

The Chairman said the report showed that they were in a very satisfactory-, condition. The trustees made • arrangements with the bank to provide the money to purchase the building and they got permission to over- draw £5OO. The condition was that this might remain for twelve months and at the end oi that time the amount was to be progressively reduced. He did note think they had ever reached that figure of £5OO. He hoped they would go on gradually and bring down that balance until they had wiped it away altogether and then the building and the whole property would be their own.

Mr. Harry Wright,, one of the auditors, said the accounts were placed before Mr. Holt and himself in a. very plain and straightforward manner and there was. very little trouble in auditing them. He was greatly in favour of the increase the Committee proposed to give to Mr. Riley.. (Applause.) He proposed the a loption of the report. Mr. B. Kniveton seconded.

Mr. T. Dean.moved that Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P., be- re-elected president and that he be thanked for his past services. He had been a very great friend to them dur- ing the past pear. (Applause.) Mr. J. liate seconded the motion; which was carried by acclamation. The folleming gentleman were nominated vice-presi- dents: Messrs. P. Speakman, J. P. , C.C. , Samuel Taylor, J.P., G. Bellamy, T. Dean, T. Lea, R. H. Posnett, S. Walton, A. R. Norman, John Bate, Samuel Coventry, H. Wright, W. M. Sowerby and W. Ockleston. Mr. W. Ocklnton was re-appointed treasurer on the motion cf Mr. John Clarke seconded by Mr. T. Lea. The Chairman referred to the great amount of work , connected with the office of secretary and the excellent manner in which Mr. Riley had carried it out. He had, performed his duties faithfully and well, and the Corn- , mittee recommended that his salary be increased from, £5 ss. to £7 10s. Mr. Kniveton move :1 and Mr. G. Bellamy seconded a motion increasing the secretary's salary as stated. Mr. Bellamy said it would be interesting to know what profit the club made during the past year. The Chairman said the Committee had reckoned it to be £l2O.
The motion was carried and Mr. Riley was unani- mously re-appointed secretary on the motion of Mr. W. Brimelow seconded by Mr. Dean.
The committee were constituted as follows :—Mr. J.

Clarke, W. Handley,J. Bate, J. Lea, S. Walton, J. Arden, J. Stanwav, J. F. Moulton, C. Stubbs, B. Kniveton, W. Page, G. E. Kirkham, W. Brirnelow. Several alterations and additions were made to the rules of the club and the proceedings ended. Messrs. Harry Wright and Holt were re-elected auditors.

There will, it is understood,be a slight reduction in the weekly wage by the adoption of the eight hours day. According to a London evening contemporary, infor- mation was received on Wednesday that Lobengula is retracing his steps southwards to surrender on the terms proposed by Sir Henry Loch. A shoplifter, recently convicted, carried a bogus baby with her during her predatory excursions. The infant had a wax face and a hollow leather body. It was the thief's custom to dexterously transfer purloined articles, such as gloves, laces, &c. to the spacious baby, which usually gained much in weight during these little excur- sions.

THE politicians have been largely Political in evidence this week. Mr. BAL- Speeches . FOUR has favoured his constituents in Manchester with several singularly colourless disquisitions on the polit;cs of the day, and Mr. ACLAND, at Rotheriarn, Mr. BRYCE, at Aberdeen, 1

and Sir Wm. HARCOURT, at Derby, have don° yeoman's service on behalf of the Government and its policy. Mr. BALFOUR'S speeches afford a curious and interesting revelation of the Tory mind when confronted with the pressing social and legislative problems which are at the present time calling for solution. Mr. BALFOUR does not deny the existence of these problems, but he has ' no solution of any one of them to offer. He seems to be disposed to admit that, in some respects, the "time is out of joint," but, unlike Hamlet, he does not claim that he "was born to set it right." In the world of politics there are many things want doing, and it would be well if they were done, but, clearly, Mr. BALFOUR is not the man to do any of them. He not only makes no suggestions of his own, but his objections to the proposals of others are simply multitudinous. The Parish Councils Bill,he admits in a condescending sort of way, makes a few necessary and desirable additions to our existing system of local govern- ment, but, really, on the whole the Bill is not worth talking about—at least not in Manchester. This was, to say the least, an extremely disin- genuous way of escaping a rather embarrassing task. It is easy to avoid a responsibility—for the time being at all events—by running away from it, and Mr. BALFOUR adopted this course. One would have liked to hear how this whilom mem- ber of the Fourth Party attempted to justify before a democratic audience, eves though the democracy was of the Tory type, the desperate and unscrupulous efforts of the reactionary party of which he in a leader to shut out the rural labourers from access to the soil and to withhold the administration of the poor law and public charities from popular control. " But," said Mr. BALFOUR, "on the Parish Councils Bill I mean to say nothing; it does not affect Manchester." A statement like this is surely one of the most glaring illustrations of what Mr. BRYCE aptly called the "New Unionism " of the Tory Party. Hitherto the "New Unionists" have, for the most part, confined themselves to denounc- ing Irishmen for exercising their full privi- leges of citizenship while denying them the right o managing their own affairs, but Mr BALFOUR goes a considerable step further. He assumes that because a person lives in a town or city he has no interest, or should have no interest, in what concerns those who live in the country. Sympathies with the weal or • the woes of others are not to extend beyond township or borough boundaries, and the workmen of Manchester, for instance, must not indulge in that fellow feeling which makes us wondrous kind towards the land- less peasantry of the country. So, in effect, says Mr. ARTHUR BALFOUR; but he is mistaken,and lie will doubtless live to learn that the artizans of the town are little less interested in the fate of the Parish Councils Bill then the labourers in the most obscure and out-of-the-way villages. At Derby, Sir WILLIAM HARCOURT was in a fighting mood and his speech contained many a shrewd thrust at his political opponents. Tory speakers would fain put the Government on its defence, but Sir WILLIAM HARCOURT does not deal with the work of the Ministry in an apologe- tic key. On the contrary, he carries the warfare into the enemy's country with all his well-known vigour. Mr. BALFOUR complained at Manchester that the majority in Parliament had resorted to unusual methods. But what, asks Sir WILLIAM MAROC:IIMT, has Mr. BALFOUR to say of the unex- ampled conduct on the part of the minority ? Mr. BALFOUR complains of the effect, but what has he got to say of the cause? The gag was, as Sir WILLIAM points out, a " pat ent " of the Tory party. It was invented for the furtherance of coercive legislation, and the same party which invented it have compelled the present Govern- ment to use it in order to pass beneficent measures which are demanded by the country. The CHAN- CELLOR of the EXCHEQUER amused his audience at the expense of that " ferocious friend" of his, Colonel SAUNDERSoN, who, discreet warrior that he is, still lives to fight another day, and Sir HENRY JAMES was playfully dealt with. Probably Mr. CHAMBERLAIN will find as little to be satisfied with in the speech as anybody. As a rule a politi- cian will regard it as an honour to have his speeches quoted from, as it goes to show that he is a man of weight, but it must now be a painful ordeal for Mr. CHAMBERLAIN to read passages from his own speeches of a few years ago. He figures at the present time as one of the most ardent defenders of the House of Lords, yet in an indictment of the here- ditary Chamber Sir William HARCOURT could find no stronger language than that formerly used by the member for West Birmingham. In this pas- sage, which istoo lengthy to quote in full, Mr. CHAMBIRLAIN eferred to their lordships as "an oligarchy which is the mere accident of birth," miserable minority of individuals; " " ancient monuments ; " and "antiquities." To these choice epithets he adds," The chronicles of the House of Lords are one long record of concessions delayed until they have lost their grace, of rights denied till extorted from their fears. It has been a his- tory of one long contest between the representa- tives of privilege and the representatives of popular rights, and during thistime the Lords perverted, delayed, and denied justice until at last they gave grudgingly and churlishly what they could no longer withhold." After this, Sir William HAR- COURT had little to do hut endorse the words which were used by Mr. CHAMBERLAIN in his Radi- cal days, but he added a few temperate words of warning. The Government are determined, he said, to press forwtird their policy as a whole. They would stand by their scheme as laid before the people at the last election ; "and they would stand by that scheme, the whole scheme, and nothing but the scheme."
THE Parish Councils Bill was read The Parish a second time in the House of Councils Bill.

Ler ls on Thursday evening, and a forecast of the treatment it is likely to receive at the hands of their lordships may be gained from the discussion that took place. It would appear that Lord, SALISBURY, who, of course, voices the sentiments of the majority, has no objection to the Bill, provided that it be divested of almost every feature and every provision that makes it of value. He has no objection to Parish Councils so long as they are only a name, and possess no real power. He is dead against public control of charities,and as f( r parish rooms he is full of fore- bodings that if they pass into the hands of the re- presentatives of the ratepayers Liberation meet- ings may actually be held in them. The leader of the Conservative party is evidently of opinion that freedom of speech is not a good thing for rural districts. The same dis- trust of the people is observable in the references to the allotment and poor-law clauses. That the majority of the residents in a parish should have the power of providing allotments, and that the adminitration of the poor-law ehould be pl.2ecci
Mt2'4

• the hands of those who best know the needs of the poor are regarded as very doubtful proposals by Lord SALISBURY, though his remarks upon these points are diplomatically vague. The Toryism even of Lord SALISBURY is tempered by that fear of the people which the possibility of a general election inspires. Throughout the whole debate the most bitter hostility to this democratic mea- sure was displayed by those who spoke on behalf of the majority of the Peers, but fortunately here- ditary legislators are in these days a timorous sort of people who shrink from bold and resolute actions. As the Dux° of DEVONSHIRE confessed with refreshing candour, the House of Lords can not always act upon its own sense of what is the wisest and the best course. He hopes, however, that they will indulge in a few "prudent and moderate amendments."

It can hardly be described as a An "l Inter"-healthy sign of the times that the tiona " Event. doings of prize fighters are chroni- cled with more minuteness than those of the most eminent statesmen or even of the most powerful monarchs. The daily papers of yesterday contained long and expensive telegrams from "Our special correspondents" anent the Mitchell- Corbett fight as though it were one of the decisive battles of the world, instead of a disreputable contest for money between two professional "bruisers." And the scene that was enacted at the obscure Florida town of Jacksonville has no ele- vating or edifying feature about it. It is a mere picture of brutal rivalry and hatred. We are told that the two combatants would not even comply with the usual preliminary formality of shaking hands, but that they stood regarding each other with "a scowl upon their features." What fol- lowed was a series of merciless Mows, till the end was reached by a blow in the face which knocked MITCHELL stunned and helpless to the floor. Yet the gladiatorial contest is spoken of as an" in- ternational" event, 'and the "defeat of the Eng- lishman." Fortunately none of England's hon- our was in MITCHELL'S keeping. This country suffers no discredit by his defeat, just as she would have gained no credit by his victory.

A HAYDOCK GRIEVANCE. Mr. John W. Green, solicitor, Sc. Helens, is on be- half of the tradesmen of Haydock getting up a peti- tion to the Haydock Local Board praying them to memorialise the Lord Chancellor to join Haydock to St. Helens for County Court purposes. At pre- sent the district is attached to Warrington, and suitors and defendants have a return journey of about sixteen mile, while if they went to St. Helens, the return journey would be reduced to six or eight miles.

CAUGHT IN THE ACT. At the Warrington Occasional Court on Saturday, before Mr.S.R. Armitage. James Hayes, was charged with night poaching at Golborne on the pre- vious night.—Samuel Watkins,a gamekeeper in the employ of Lord Newton, deposed that while be was in Park-road,Golborne,at two o'clock that morning, he saw the prisoner standing by a net set in front of a gate leading into a field. Two other men were in the field on the opposite side of the road driving game towards the net. Prisoner was on the point of picking up the net when witness came up and seized him. A sharp struggle ensued, the effects of which were to be seen on the prisoner's face, which was terribly bruised. Witness took him to the police station and handed him over to Sergeant Peters.—Corroborative evidence having been given, prisoner was remanded to the Newton Sessions, which will be held on Saturday. A tea 'meeting and social gathering of the mem- bers of the church and congregation was held on Thursday. An excellent tea was repared in the Lecture Hall. There was a large attendance, a second sitting being necessary. After tea an adjonrnment was made to the chapsl,w h ere a public meeting was held, under the presidency of the Rev. Owen Watkins. In opening the meting, the Chair- man delivered an interesting and appropriate speech, in which he expressed his pleasure at meet- ing the members of the Society, and their frieres. Ite,regarded the present and ft ture prospects of their church as most encouraging and hopetul. He theught they had good reason to tak) courage nnd , go forward, and exhorted all who were engaged in the work, to "labour with ber..h hands earnestly" , end success would be assured. Addresses we also delivered by the Rev. G. D. Mason, Messrs. A. H. Cann, E. Place, J. Johnson, 4 and W. Light. The choir, under the direction elf Mr. James Bennett, rendered a selection of music, Mr. E.S . Garland pre- siding at the organ. div.head: OBTAINING A PENSION- /CS' FALSE PRMENCES.
div.p: OBTAINING A PENSION- /CS' FALSE PRMENCES.

At the Warrington Occasional Court„ yesterday, before Mr. James Tinsley., Thomas Morton, alias Squire Wood, who for some years has resided at Golb orne, was charged with making a &else declar- ation for the purpose of .t btaining a pension, and was further charged with receiving a certain pen- sion with intent to defraud the commissioners of the Royal Hospital for soldiers at Chelsea. Mr. Edleston, solicitor. Preston, prosecuted on behalf of the War Department. .The evidence showed that on the Ist April, 1892, the prisoner wrhte under the name of Squire Wood, Applying for a pension; he received the same on the 18th August, 1892, and had been in receipt of it up to the end of 1893. Mr. William Henry Arnett, J.P., declared that the! signature, to a certain document produced an ' marked " 5.W.," was in the handwriting of him- self. He recognised the prisoner es the one who made the declaration therein referred to. The prisoner at that time signed his name as Squire ; Wood. Mr. T. Squire Wood, residing at Leeds, saidi he was formerly in the 41st Regiment of foot sol- diers. He was in the band, and at that tittle I prisoner served in the same regiment. The prisoner was known in the regiment as Thomas Morton. Witness applied for npension in the year 1892, but he received no reply from the War Depart- ment. He again applied in 1893. Inquiries were' then set on foot hy the War Department. He never authorised anyone to :make an applica- tion on his behalf for 41. pension. Patrick Alcock identified the last witness as the real Squire Wood.; Th 3 prisoner when arrested in North Shields by,. P.C. Robert Simpson pleaded guilty to the charge., The prisoner was committed to the Liserpeall Assizes.

THE WYCLIFFE KS.A.

Tif3 usual P.S.A. meeting at Wycliffe Church was held est 'Sunday afternoon. There was again a large attend- ance, and the membership of the brotherhood now totals )1,126. Mr. C. H. Bickford occupied the chair, and de- livered a brief address. Mr. William Gleave was the speaker, and he said he esteemed it to be a very great pleasure and honour to be asked to take part in a meet- ing of that description. He was glad the society had been so successful, and hoped that by this time next year the membership would have increasal to 2,000. The subject of his address was "Preparing for a rainy day," and the speaker urged upon his hearers the necessity of their providing for times of adversity. He also com- mented on Lite large sum of money spent anuually by the working classes in drihk. The Rev. 3. Yonge announced that the 18 members of the P.S.A. St. John Ambalance Class, who sat for examination, had passed in the first division. Mrs. Gleave contributed a solo, and Mr. W. H. Payton also played by request, an organ solo with his usual fine taste and judgement. Messrs. R. Atkinson and C. T. Owen also toek part ila the meeting.
THE REV. J. YONGE Al-sID ANGLICAN ShiI',ERDOTA- USK.

There was a large con lion in Wycliffe Church, Bewsey-st., on Sunday evening, when the Rev.J. Yonge preached a special sermon on "Evangelical Home Mis- siens—a necessary countess-action of Anglican Sacerdote- , limn." After referring to the claims of the Lancashire Congregational Union, in connection with the Church Aid and Home Missionary Society, which has for its object the supporting of Congregational Missions in Lancashire and in tirecountry where they cannot ade- quately support themselves, Mr. Yonge mentioned that the Congregational churches in the rural districts were gradually growing less able to support themselves, ow- ing to the trend of population being now from villages to towns. Mr. Yonge considered one of the chief claims for supporting their Evangelical home missions in the country was to be found in the interests of their reformed Protestant and Evangelical faith. The village and country churches of their own and other Evangelical denominations were rapidly becoming the latilwark of Protestantism in the land. No doubt many would re- member how that rather high sounding phrase " the bulwark of rrotestantisin" used in the past to be pi oudly applied by Episcopalians to the Church of England, as by law estehliSlie,d. Advocates of Free Church principles who asserted the unscriptura.lness of all State establish- ments of volitgion, and who therefore agitated for the disestablistrrnent of this Episcopal church were con- stantly met by the declaration that to disestablish the Church of England would be to destroy the bulwark of Protestantism:" 'the Anglican church was regarded as the great defence against the revival of Romanism in the country, itetthe great support and pre muter of the Pro- testant faith. How far was that the case to-day ? He sup- posed that the statements of Dr. Sinclair, Archdeacon of London, would not be disputed on that point. He had made a remarkable declaration concerning the spread of sacerdetalism in the Established Church. .lelr.Yonge gave several 'extracts from Dr. Sinclair's declaration which showed the spread of sacerdotalism to an alarming extent among the bishops, theological seminaries for training young clergymen, and in the ecclesiastical press. Your bishops and 1,600 clergy belonged to the "Corel'raternity of the Blessed Sacrament," whose great desire was to be permitted to take eemmunion in Roman Cathalic churches. Their leader told them there was no difference between them and the Church of Rome on Eucharistic adoration. In 326 Episcopalian churches masses were said for the dead every month. More than LON 'used Eucharistic vestments,,end they were advo- cating the restoration of the word 'Amass" and deplored the disastrous effects of the Reformation. Several other extracts were given of views held by Lord Halifax and Canen/iCnox Little, who advocated sacerdotalism in the Church ef England. Mr. Yong,' also quoted from two recently published Anelican workeeeone of which called Hoaevina " bade the children to creefully make the sign of •thweross, first on their forehead,rthen on their lips, and then on their breast. Mr. Yonge said let them not thinle that such teaching was so rare arid exceptional in rhe,Church of England that no nocice need be taken of it. he ilea very little doubt that there were clergy to be found within easy distance of thavepot who woald en- dersesweiat he had read concerning sacerdotalism, and adhoweuld teach and practice it so far as they dared. That it was the doctrine of many pulpits, of many paro- chial-eiasses, of much private instruction was beyond :question. He pointed to this growing development of ,prie'etieni in the Church of England with all its contra- diction and obscuration of " the troth as it is in Jesus" as a atrong reason why they shatild uphold and promote fEvaneedical Home Missions. The dwellers in their rural disttlete were in especial need, ard peculiar danger from this condition of things. The friest must be met by the prenetale The perplexing ritual of the Anglican church Tnast be contrasted with the sinvelicity of the Evangeli- cal faith. The pastors of their aural village churches -shod be so trained and sustained as to be able to pre- sent an educated and cultured'-resistance against that 'Romatising Anglicanism. Thesy must not let their wit- mess to the truth decay and decline. The evangelical 'Christians of England must awake. Their free churches .were-being distanced and outdone as shown in the cen- sus of a 631. Let them understand that the victory of the priest was the death of Christian liberty.

div.head: SOME NOTES FROM MY READING.
div.p: SOME NOTES FROM MY READING.

Br Mn. JOHN REERES. (With apologies to Laurence Sterne, A. 11.) "It would indeed.," said my Uncle Toby, knock- ing the ash out of his pipe and reaching over to the jar to refill, "it would indeed be very selfish." " What would ?" said the Corporal. Now my Uncle Toby had for some minutes been in a reverie, "a brown study," so he said, and had just come to the top again after being lost to the world and all his surroundings, and broke the silence by the forego- ing remark. "It's a matter of duty Trim," con- tinued my uncle—" Then it should be fulfilled," exclaimed Trim," without waiting for the word of command"—" a matter of duty,l say Trim, to spread the blessings of life over as wide an area and among as many people as possible.' "Quite so," put in Slawkenbergius, who had been a silent lis- tener of the'dialogue, "an excellent sentiment." "Then why don't you practise it," said my Uncle, "flow; I have few blessings to spread,except books, and them I cannot part with." "You area literary miser," retorted my Uncle Toby, "and, like other misers, you would be all the happier if you could bring yourself to divide your gains with others." Slawkenbergius moved uneasily on his seat and said, " What would you have me give away, my boeksr "No," replied my uncle, "What I would have you give, you would be none the loser for the giving of it." "Ay, 'twould be like the lighting of my pipe at the candle," said Trim, "a benefit to me without loss to either." "how so ?" interposed the bookworm. "Not by giving your books away, but the results of your reading," exclaimed my uncle. So thus it came about that Slawkenbergius brought to the nightly meeting, the notes, clippings, and jottings of his reading.

At the next meeting of this curious conclave, Slawkenbergius brought with him a newspaper and, flourishing it towards my Uncle Toby, exclaimed— "The very thing, the very thing Toby, to begin our session of Notes and Comments with " Let us have it" quoth my Uncle." "Present--Fire ' inter- jected Trim. "I have been reading The Warrington Examiner' and find therein something quite pat to your observations,Toby,at our last meetiug. It is the report of a speech by the president of a Working- men's Mission. Mr. John Crosfield told them he had been abroad in Switzerland. While there he found some narrow-minded bigot' had found fault with him for opening his grounds and conservatories to the people on Sunday afternoon. 'He had no patience with bigots who would close museums, picture galleries, libraries, and gardens on Sunday afternoons.' . One Sunday afternoon when in Switzerland with his wife, he took train to a place up in the mountains—We then walked five miles down to Vevey on the shores of Lake Geneva, a most beautiful walk through the woods with their autumn tinted leaves. It was exquisite, and I thought, when I read (that bit of sa,bbata.rian fanaticism) in the Warrington paper, that if I had the power, I would have had every Sunday school teacher and every Sunday school child with me to take that walk." "That's right said my uncle and emphasized his remark by his fist upon the table. "Yes," brother said my father, but it has the fault with the world of being more Christ-like than Christian." " Ay, Ay," said the Corporal," if not against the rules of the service, let some of the de- lights of life come down to the ranks." "These " said my uncle " are sentiments often in the months of the chaplains but seldom put into practice." "There are men," cried my father, " who bury themselves in their libraries, who"—" Scorn de- lights and live laborious days," interposed Hagen— " who"continued my father "hoard up their treasures of knowledge, information and amusement as the miser his gold." "Yea," said my Uncle," both would be the better for a freer circulation."

Here my father drew from his pocket a book called " Where three Empires meet," from which he read a few extracts :—" At page 48,1 tind a passage , that reminds me bow very widely spread is human nature among the inhabitants of this world. here is a specimen of oriental red tapeism '—According to dastar,' that is to commission or custom. It is a word that one soon comes to hate. Vain is it to try to 'have things done after your own ideas. You point out how some piece of work can be accom- plished in a more expeditious or satisfactory way, and the oriental to whom you address your remarks listens patiently, quite agrees with all you hue said, and then politely but doggedly replies, • Sir, that is net the dastur; that ends the argument.' Whoever succeeded in persuading an Asiatic to break' through the old traditional method, the sacred ,dastur? It is a fetish to him. Now we have the thing—if not the name in England. What is it but dastur that makes it possible to say,, when you ask a man what his 'screw' is- ‘So much, and pexquisites;' meaning pickings. In America they are more open and 'call it' so much, and steal- ' ings:' 'Dastur, like charity covereth a multitude of sins.; end its worshipunder other names is almost as prevalent in England,as with the less progressive Oriental. 'For it is easier to follow a lucrative pre- cedentAlian to adopt some impoverighing, albeit righteous, principle. The words—' It is customary,' cover a host of little peculations. Dastur is very respectable, it makes things pleasant all round— eticept•toits victims—let the galled jade wince."

Tie describes them thus—• On the sides of the gates by which we entered some large prayer Nvbeels werelixed. These were cylinders some 2ft. in a igtneter, containing rolls of prayers, and turning on.pivots projecting•from the wall. Each of the Inoriksoaslie enterel, gave one of these wheels a push wit)h his hand and so made it twirl round for a ,few seconds, vainly imagining thot,'by a constant repetition of revolutions, he would, at last escape from the 'trammels of earthly existence; like some silly captive squirrel that perpetually runs up the treadmill of•its turning cage, in the fond belief that it is hurrying to liberty:" "Very candid," remarked -Slawkenbergius "but how if one of the Lsdaki's mere to -come over here and write hi.; impressions Of ,our praying machiner Ile would ifind it to be little lessnnaechanical and rnuo more expensive." and this was mcromery 'in Tihet !" "No, your Itt-hour' said the Coworal, "surely-good inte,n- tions will avail something when the -lan muter- roll is called!" "It is all'," said my father--but what he said must appear in our next.
WARRINGTON LIBERAL CLUB READ-
ING ROOM.

The work ofcenovating and decoratingthis room has 11:5W been completed, and it must be • admitted that Mr. Fletcher, painter and decorator, deserves a word of commendation forthe skill and taste he has displayed it: the carrying out of the work. The room 'presents a,bright cheedful appearance, and is ,undonkedly one-of the best embellished rooms in the district. A censiderable amount of local interest clings to the roonvitself, for the.club has been, at one tkne or another, the residence of .the Blackburns, Bea- mont4, and Ryland, three name c long connected with Warrington history. The room it an excellent example ot what ffirst class workmanship was in the lost cen- tury, andthe occupants seem te have spared no ex- pense in making this.iparticular rocm the most Leauti- ful in thetkouse. Ike ceiling is elegantly enriched with composition ornament in the" Adams" style, and the decorator 'has now Dainted it in shades of czearn colour, ,picked out in .gold. The walls are paintxcl in panels and tivided by dines of colour and gold, support- ed by a &Co painted dull blue. But perhaps :the most interesting feature, and those which will be most noticed, are se historic pictures painted on the walls, and which pregiGus to to renovation, were almost ob- literated. They now, however, come .stzt in clear relief, and are worthy of inspection. The artiat is unknown. but we believe they were painted for the late Mr. William Beartont, during, his residence at the house. The whole 2 the picture'', represent famous women and are workg. of considerable merit. Entering the doorway the first picture on the right is a representation of the stealing of the youog Duke of York, from Isis mother, and the succeeding pictures following in rotation portray the undermentioned inci- dents. Grace Darling going to the rescue ; Queen Phil- lippa interceding with Edward 111 for the lives of the six burgesses of Calais ; trial of queen Caroline ; Ethel- hert being persuaded by his wife Bertha to profess Christianity : Jeannie beans supplicating for her sister Effie Deans (an incident in one of Sir Walter Sc tt's works). Cromwell's daughters interceding on behalf Gf Charles I ; Boadicea urgiug. her warriors to battle ; and Eleanor of Castile sucking, poison from the wound on the arm of Edward I. It should also be stated that the gas fitC.ngs have been renovated, and new globes put on. It has been decided to open the room on Tuesday when a tea will he held to which the leader,: of the party have been invited to meet the Committee, as well as Mr Thornton, who has generously defrayed the cost of the renovation. The prrs:dent of the club, Mr. J. H. Flem- ing will prcside.

ANNUAL MISSIONA RY MEETING AT ' THINGS HEARD AND SEEN SANKEY BRIDGES. AT WARRINGTON. INTERESTING REMARKS ON THE MATABELE WAR. The Foreign A.lisionary anniversary of the San- key Bridges Wesb-yan Chapel was held on Sunday and Monday evenings. The anniversary should have been held in October, but owing to the distress in cOnsequence of the coal dispute, it was decided to postpone it until more settled times. The pulpit was occupied on Sunday morning by the Rev.J.Kirtlan, and in the evening by the Rev. G. D. Mason, who took subjects suitable for the occasion. The chapel was crowded at the meeting en Monday nignt, when the chair was occupied by Councillor A. Bennett in the place of his father, Mr. Wm. Bennett, of Padgate,whose prolonged illness prevented him from being present. The Rev. G. D. MASON, in giving trio annual report of the Foreign Missionary Society,after reviewing the work accomplished in various parts of the world, said that the Warrington branch had contributed this year £251 63. 9d., and Sankey Bridges had contributed £7 155.9 d. The rev, gentleman laid great stress upon the offer of Mr. Hutchinson, of Liverpool,to contribute an equal sure to the increase upon last year's collections. He hoped there would be a large increase during the present year. The CIIAIRMAN said that he was rather ashamed to confess that he was almost a stranger to the missionary platferm, but when Mr. Watkins requested him to come to Sankey Bridges in place of his father, he could not refuse. Referring to loreign missions, he said that one objection which people raised against them that while people were spending their money abroad they were neglecting their own neighbourhood. That was not true at Sankey Bridges. The whole town of Warrington had been touched by the way in which the Sankey Bridges people had met the late distress consequent upon the coal strike. When people did so much good around them, they surely could have the privilege of , helping to do good abroad as well. He thought that it would be well to have broad principles upon which to send out the missionaries, and that would prevent a waste of energy which sometimes happened now, by there being missionaries from different societies in the same place at the same time. This led to fearful results in Uganda. He thought that if a general policy to pre- vent this was adopted, there would be many more sub- scribers to the funds. Mr. J. HORTON next spoke in favour of foreign mis- sions. They had been a grand success, and each year's report was better than the previous one. The Rev. OWEN WATKINS said that his field of labour had been in the Dark Continent. England owed a great deal to Africa. In the west coast to-day, they would find ruined towers which had been used for the abomin- able slave trade which wrought such fearful havoc among the inhabitants, and the debt which England contracted then,had not been repaid by all that they had done since. R-terring to the remarks of the Chairman with respect to the work of the different missionary societies, Mr. Watkins said that it was always the policy of the Wesleyan Society in Africa, never to send any missionary to a place in which there was already one from another society. For this reason, they had not sent a missionary to Mataheleland. In that country,the representatives of the London Missionary Society were holding their lives in their hands, and they had been there for many years. He went to Mashoualand two years ago, and was not above 50 miles from Buluwayo, the capital of Lobengula. Mushonaland was north, south, and east of the Matabele country, which wastinly a small country, and they who knew that part of Africa, were amazed at the nonsense which was written and spoken about it, anA its people. For seventy years the Matabele had been a scourge which God seemed to have permitted to come upon Mashonaland. The father of Lobengula overran the vast country called the Transvaal, and almost denuded it of its population. He then overran the part of the country now called British Bechuanaland, and cleared away almost every inhabit- ant. For seventy years the Mashona people had been as 'dogs to the Matabele, and when he went into the coon- try, more than half of the Mashonas had either been slain by the Matabele, or were carried away into hope- less captivity. When he and his colleague went into the country, they could not find any of the natives for a long time, until one day as they were passing by a mountain, there was an indescribable hum. Signs of life could be heard, and after some time, behind every rock, they could perceive the Mashonas. His colleague went up the mountain, and in a hollow at the top, he found a village. They had estanlished themselves here out of fear of the Matabele. Missionary work was com- menced here which had had great results. Mr. Watkins concluded with an eloquent appeal to help in the good work amongst the heathen. An offertory was then taken, after which a vote of thanks to the Chairman was accorded on the motion of Mr. W. Brough, seconded by Mr. J. Summersgill. The Rev.G.D. MASON announced that whereas the col- lection last year, including 203. collected by the children only amounted to £7 15. 7d., the collection this year was £0 ss. 4d., exclusive of the children's collections which had not yet CORI 9 in.—The meeting concluded with the pronouncing of the beirediction.

Alderman Harrison has no sympathy whatever with hawking, and he went tcr the extent of giving his mind about it on Nionday morning at the police court, during the hearing of a case. Hawking bootAl laces appears to him to bean effeminate occupation and quite unworthy of the stronger sex. I don't know whether Alderman Harrison's antipathy to hawking bootlaces had anything to do with the senteuee upon the prisoner in question or not, hut a mouth's imprisonment, without the option of a flue, for being drunk and disorderly seems to be a very harsh sentence. Of course it was stated that the prisoner had been trying doors of hotbes,but n the other hand he declared he was selling laces, and he had a genuine hawking license in his possession " Justices' justice " is often spoken of with scant respect,and, unfortuuately.sentences are sometimes out of all proportion with the offences that are proved. Selling bootlaces may be effeminate but effeminacy is Rot a legal offence, and, besides, some men may prefer to sell bootlaces to absolute unem- ployment.

I notice that the Warrington Debating Society are going to open the second part of their session on Tuesday evening. The syllabus which has beER prepared appears to be about the best I have yet seen in connection with the society. In addition to the subjects upon which papers are to be read being of great interest, socially and politically, the gentlemen who are to introduce them appear to be all well fitted for their tasks. The subject for Tues- day evening, for instance, is "The Socialism of the Church," by the Rev.E. C.E. Carleton. The coupling of socialism with the church, in name at least, is getting to be quite fashionable, and it •is ' a significant sign of the times. In the hands of the Vicar of Trinity, whwe faculty for debate is, very streng,the subject is bound to yield some inte- re-ting matter. Among those who, later on. are to- introduce subjects for debate, I notice the names a Mr. A. H. Crosfield and of the Rev. F. K. Freestof.-; formerly pastor of the Cairo-st. Unitarian Church, and his successor, the Rev. W. IL Drummond. Mr. Crostield has not yet signifed what his subject is to be, but Mr. Freeston will deal with "The faith of a heretic,' and the Rev. W. H. Drummond will cham- pion " The Social Questions Union." Mr. Joseph Dakin's name appears in connection with the sub- ject " How to stop the pollution of the Mersey." This subject will bear a great deal of discussion no doubr,and if Mr. Oakin can offer a practical remedy for ithe pollution he will be doing a very useful thing. The other papers will be con- tributed by Mr. J. C. Harrington ("Fair Trade"), Mr. Charles Plinston ("Disestablishinent"), and Mr. Wm. Silcock ("The Church of the Future").

A matter which is sometimes alluded to in the gymnastic circles is the apparent lethargy shown by schoolmasters and school managers in regard to physical exercises for the scholars. Warrington has within its borders a gymnastic institution of which it may well be proud, equipped with all the neces- sary appliances, and having a conductor who thor- oughly understands his business. There can be no doubt as to the beneficial results derived from phy- sical exercise, and Warrington youths would be healthier for it. Very advantageous terms, I hear, have been offered to several schools in the town and not accepted. It is, perhaps, not difficult to dis- cover the cause of the backwardness on the part of the managers. Pnysieial recreation at present brings no grist to the mill, and the time which might be occupied in such recreation is given to special subjects for which a government grant is given, But a better time is looming for those in- terested in physical recreation for scholarsjor an . . .
Act, is likely-to-be passed in the next sessip of Par- liament sanctioning the payment of grants for physicql training in schools

Speaking of youths reminds me of the temerity shown by one Warrington lad named Michael Burns, during the past week. He was a smart lai, in fact a "d:effi smart lad, but during his confine- ment in his fortified quarters he will undoubtedly find time to regret a recent irresistible attack of kleptomania. His adventures on Tuesday night and Wednesday would provide fruitful " c-opy " for writers of "penny dreadfuls." On Tuesday night this youngster decided to have a night out, and to keep himself from becoming drowsy be broke into a stable, aroused the donkey from his slum!iers,and harnessed him to a cart. He then approporiated a large dog from a neighbouring greengrocer's to keep guard. But a watchman's fire near Winwick-road attracted his attention and he went to warm him- self, leaving the dog in charge of his cheaply pro- cured donkey and cart. A man in blue now ap- pears on the scene, but this dees not disturb Michael's equanimity. With falsehood after false- hood he blandly told " Robert" how he had been delityPd in the selling of his goods in Warrington for his Widnes master,so that he was too late to puts up anywhere. The policeman was good enough. to show him the at-,arest way to Widnes, but Mich iel had got other business in Warrington, an& 'he loaded his cart with somebody's potatoes and herrings. Being sufficiently well freighted he- • made his way to Widnes. He was now a self-made• fish and potatoe dealer, and retailed his diverse goods to Widnesians, at a good profit, considering what he had paid for them. He regaled himself' and hisdonkey, and then a spell of ill luck fol- lowed. The donkey plavei sad havoc with a tradesman's window, the damage amounting to £4.. Michael was then taken into custody, and after- wards handed over to the Warrington police. ties is now serving ten days in gaol, previous to enter,- ing a reformatory.

div.head: MINERS' CONCILIATION BOARD.
div.p: MINERS' CONCILIATION BOARD.
ATPOINTMENT OF CHAIRMAN.
The Speaker has nominated Lord Shand to be chair- man of the Board of Conciliation established in accord- ance with the Rosebery agreement, and his lordship has accepted the office. _ _ _ _

Lo'-rd Shand is about sixtv-live years of age. He is an Aberdeen man.,with his full- share of the hardheadedness of the granite city. Proceeding south, to Edinburgh, he was called to the Scottish Bar in 1853. He soon marked himself out among his competitors, and in nine years he secure," the sheriffship of Kincardineshire' whence be was promoted, later on, to Haddington and Berwick. In 2872 he became a judge of the Court of Session,where he greatly distinguished himself by his keenness and legal lore; and the University a Edinburgh conferred on him the Doctorate of Laws. At the same time he served on various Commissions with much public advantage. In 18a0 Lord Shand retired from the bench, and was aro- inted a member of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, in which capacity he has served with assiduity and with marked distinction. His legal penetration and judicial balance of mind will prove most serviceable in the chairmanship of the Conciliation Board. We.trust that no untoward circumstance will intervene to thwart the hopes raised by his appointment, and that he will be frankly accepted by both parties.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
A FOWL CASE.

At the Occasional Court on Monday, before Mr. Tins- ley, Samuel Leigh, Warringten, was charged with hav- ing stolen seven fowl some time between the 18th and 20:h inst. at Great Sankey, the property of Ann Fair- dough. The prisoner was sent to gaol for 14 days with hard labour on Monday morning for assaulting a police -consPable.—P.C. Cooper stated that he saw the prisoner in Dallam-lane, and noticed something bulky in his pockets. Witness found that the man had three fowls -on him, which the prisoner said he had bought. He 'escaped ; but was recaptured afterwards, and on being charged with having stolen seven fowl admitted the offence, and said that he threw four into Sankey Brook. "The case was remanded.
ALDERMAN HARRISON'S STRICTURES ON HAWKING.

A man of no fixed abode, named Edward Scully, was charged at floe Warrington Borough Court on Monday, with being drunk and disorderly in Allen-st., on 'Satur- day lAght. Sergeant Smith said he received a complaint of men trying the doors of houses, and he noticed the prisoner try several. He was engaged hawking laces, and commenced to make a disturbance. Be was arrested by witness, and was very violent on the way to the police station. The Chiet Constable said that hawking in a great many instances was only a "stall.'" The licence which prisoner had however, was a genuine one. Alderman Harrison addressing the prisoner, said that he was surprised to see a man engaged in such an effeminate ocmpation as hawking laces. It was only a pretext for doing something wrong. Prisoner would have to go to gaol for one months' hard labour.

div.head: SUSPICIOUS CHARACTER.
div.p: A SUSPICIOUS CHARACTER.

Samuel Lee, 17, Watkin-st., was charged at the Warrington Borough Court. on Monday, with assaulting P.C. Frank Cooper, while in the execution of his duty in Dallam-lane, on Saturday night. The prisoner who is a la tourer on the London and North-Western railway, was ILIA in company with another man, on Saturday night, by P.C. Cooper, who stopped him, as his pockets were very bulky. The officer asked him what he had .got in his pockets, to which he replied he had got noth- ing. The legs of a fowl were, however, protruding out •of his pocket, and the officer drew his attention to this. He then said that he had bought the fowl from an old man at the railway crossing. Cooper was taking him t, the place indicated when a struggle ensued, during which the prisoner escaprd leaviry, his coat behind: The coat was examined at the police station, and there were found in it three fowls, a dog slip, and several other things A description of the man was given and he was arrested. During the interval between the struggle and the time he was arrested, he had shaved his moustache off, hut was nevertheless immediately identifir,d by Cooper. It was subsequently discovered that the fowls belonged to a farmer in Burtonwood, and were missed on Saturday night. The prisoner was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour for assault, and then ordered to be banded over to the county police on the charge of fowl •stealing.

div.head: SINGULAR AFFAIR.
div.p: A SINGULAR AFFAIR.

At the Warrington Borough Nlice Court, on Saturday 'before Mr. Burgess (in the chair), and other magistrates William John Roberts, a well-dressed man, was charged with stealing 3s. Bd. from Herbert Richards, Temper- ance Hotel, Sankey-st., by means of a trick.—Mr. Richards said that prisoner came to his hotel on Thurs- day night. He asked for a bed and tea. On Friday he had his breakfast and was going out when witness asked him to pay his bill. He said "I will be back some time this morning, I have no money but I will pay you to-morrow (Saturday) " Two letters were at this stage given to prisoner. He said he wished to make a statement before he opened them. He said" I walked from Liverpool on Thursday, and on arriving in War- rington, I went to the Central station to see which was the best way to get to Bolton, but found that was the wrong station for Bolton. I then went to the London and North-Western Station, where I sat down and rested, and shortly afterwards I saw a cabman, and asked him if he could recommend me to a good place to get a bed, and he directed me to Mr. Richa*.ds' hotel. I went there and asked Mr. Richards if I could have a bed for a couple of nights, and a 156 asked for some writ- ing paper and envelopes. I wrote two letters, had some thing to eat, and about 930 I went to bed. On Friday morning I had breakfast, and was going out for a walk when Mr. Richards asked me if I was not going to pay my bill, and I said "No, I have no money now, but I will have some t4)-morrow (Saturday), when I will pay you." Mr. Richards then called a police officer, and I was locked up. These are the answers No the two letters that I wrote, and I think they contain the money I was expecting." The prisoner thsn opened the letters,which contained two postal orders to the value of 10s. each. The bench spoke disparagingly of Mr. Richards' action and dismissed the case and the defendant discharged his debt.
SENT TO A REFORMATORY.-AN EXTRAORDINARY YOUNGSTER.

At the Warrington Borough Court Qn Thursday, a lad under eleven years of age. named Michael Burns,stepped into the defendants' hex to answer an unusually long and perhaps extraordinary charge against suck a youngster. He was ch, rged with stealing from a stable in Winwick- road, a donkey and cart, set of harness and four bags, valued at £B, the property of Samuel Sutcliffe ; from the premises of Michael Quinn, three hundred herrings, and two hags of potatoes ; and from the premises of Joseph Caldwell, Winwick-road, a harrow and bridle, value 15s. Michael was asked whether he pleaded guilty or not guilty, and after shedding a few tears, lie replied guilty. I\lr. Aunt (chief constable) statecl that Samuel Sutcliffe was a greengrocer in Turner-street, and kept a stable off Winwick-road, near to St. Ann's School. The defend- ant Michael Burns was the son of James Burns, brick- setters-labourer, living in Friars'-lane. Mr. Sutcliffe left his donkey, cart and harness in the stable about 8 o'clock °on Tuesday night. At 8 o'clock on Wednesday morning he found they had disappeared, and informed the police. D.S. Monaghan set out to look for the missing donkey and cart, when he was informed that two Ines of pota- toes had been taken from Quinn's-yard, and also 300 herrings. A telephonic message was sent to the Widnes police, and other places giving particulars as to the theft. The constables who had been (en night duty were informed, and P.C. Corbett recollected seeing the donkey and cart in Haydock-St., at 2.20 a.m.. with a savage looking dog in the cart. The prisoner was near too, and he told the officer that lie was a servant of Mr. Tilling, of Widnes, and he came to warrington on rues- day afternoon to sell potatoes. His answers appeared ' satisfactory and he told the lad to get off hack to Wid- nes. Before going to Widnes the lad got assistance to lift the stolen potatoes in his cart, and he also took the her- rings and sold them in Widnes. During his stay in nes he drove his donkey and cart in a plate glass window doing damage to the extent of £l.. The police detained him, and the Warrington police were communicated with. D.S. Monaghan brought the prisoner to Warring- ton. The Chief Constable further stated that on Nov., 21st,the prisoner took a chestnut pony and cart frem the Fairground and drove it to Widnes and back. The pony belonged to a Mrs. Lane, hut as the prisoner brought it back, she didn't prosecute him owing to his youthful- ness. The dog seen in the cart by P.C.Corbett belonged to Mr. Caldwell, grefaigrocer, and the prisener had taken it from his premises along with the other articles. Mr. Riley, School Attendance Officer, said the boy attended Butterrnarket-at., Catholic schools, but his father was summoned that morning for the boy's irregular atten-

dance. The Chairman, Major Ridgway, said the father didn't seem to have the lad under :proper control. They would send the lad to the Reformatory for five years on the first charge, and a conviction would be recorded against him on the second and third charges. The boy , would have to spend 10 days in prison previous to enter- ng the Reformatory.
LOCAL APPLICATION TO THE HOME SECRETARY.

Thomas Jackson, " The Rose," Dial-st., was sum- moned at the Warrington Borough court, yesterday, to show cause why an order should not be made upon him, to contribute to the maintenance of his son William on the ship " Clio." The magistrates' clerk said that Mr. Percy Davies had appeared a fortnight ago and obtained an adjournment of the case stating that an application was being made to the Home Secretary to obtain the release of the boy. Mr. Davies had not yet received a reply, and he (the magistrates' clerk) had received a letter simply asking under what act the bey was sent.— Mr. Davies applied for a further adjournment. He said claey certainly expected to have had a reply from the Rome Office before now. Another letter had been sent, and on this ground he asked for an adjournment. He was instructed that the boy had been sent to the" Clio" contrary,to his parents' desire, and he was informed that Mr. Riley led the magistrates to believe that the father was agreeable to the course being taken. The father did not attend the court when summoned because he had been told by Mr. Riley that he need not attend as the boy would not be sent to the " Clio." On that occa- sion, he had sent money to pay for a fine.—The magis- trates' clerk said that on a former occasion,when he had I been summoned, the father had said that he could not manage the boy.—After some consultation the magis- trates said that it would be better if Mr. Riley could te sent for. Mr. Riley was accordingly sent for, and on his arrival at the court, Mr. Davies bad a consultation with him after which he said that Mr. I Jackson must be mistakea in saying that he objected to Mr. Riley sending his son to the "Clio." He had how- ever changed his mind before the case was heard, and under the circumstances, he applied for a fortnight's adjournment. Should the Home Secretary's decision be against his client, he would undertake to pay for the fortnight.—The magistrates granted the application on this condition.

Defendant' pleaded guilty. From the chief constable's statement it appeared that the complainant missed the pigeons .on the above date and at once went to a pigeon dealer in Golborne- street where he found that only a few minutes previously two boys had been offering some pigeons for sale, and failing in their object, they threw up the pigeons when they got into the street.
