ALLEGED THEFT OF A MACKINTOSH AND A HORSE Bartholemew Welsh was charged with stealing from a funeral coach in Heath-lane, az. 4.15 on the afternoon. of November 29th, a man's tiLack mackintosh and a horse rug, valued 205., the property of Wm. Chritnes. Mr. Browne defended and pleaded not guilty. The Chief Constable stated that the defendant was a bricksetterfs labourer. Wm. Chrimes had been employed for some months as a 'bus driver for Mr. E. Connor. On Nov. 29th, he was ill, and his father, Thomas Chrimes, did hia work for him. On that date, the elder Chrimes was in charge of a funeral, and after his return from the ceme- tery he took his coach to Legh-st., where he left it for about five miautes, with the mackintosh and rug upon it,while he went to make room for it in the coach yard of Mr. Connor. When he returned,the articles were gone. In- formation was given to the polke hut no trace was found of the missing articles until Tuesday, this week, when the defendant came into the Talbot yard of Mr. Connor, and offered a mackintosh for sale. It was bought by one named Garvin, and was immediately identified by Wm. Chrimes. The police were informed, and the de- fendant was arrested by Sergeant Smith. On his house being visited, the rug was also found. He was charged with stealing the above mentioned articles, when he re- plied that lie had found them on Bank Quay Bridge.—: Thomas Chrimes, Wm. Chrimes, Garvin. P.S. Smith and Inspector Spinks each gave evidence, Garvin asserting that 'Thomas Chrimes was drunk when he lost the articles, which Chrimes, however, denied. Mr. Browne said that it was very unlikely that a man should steal the things from Mr. Connor's men, and afterwards go and try to sell them to the same men. It was far more likely that he had found them as he said on Bank Quay Bridge.--The magistrates thought it probable that de- fendant had found the things, but he ought at once to have reported the matter to the police. They would fine him ss.

THErr OF TlMBER.—Herhert Smith- a young tran residing with his parents at 91 Sharp-street was charged with stealing a quantity of timber from a building in course of erection in Scott-street, the property of Mr. Joseph Mounfield, jun.,builder, &c. From the Chief Con- stable's statement it appeared that Sergeant Smith from information received visited the house where prisoner lives,and on examining the house,foond the timber pro- duced, near the staircase. The timber WM new and was valued at 33. Sergeant Smith went in search of the privoner, and when arrested he admitted taking the timber from some new honses in Scott-street. The prisoner had been out of work about eight months, and latterly had been selling firewood. Mr. Mounfield said he didn't know anything of the prisoner, but he had missed a great deal of timber, and other builders com- plained of the same thing, The msgiitrates imposed a fine of 103. including costs, or seven days imprison- ment. Sergeant Smith deposed to stopping the prisoner in Manchester-road, and in reply to his questions the prisoner said he had been discharged from the army for misconduct. A Patrick Kelly was announced in the "Police Gazette" as being a deserter, but in anNther it stated he had been discharged.—Tlie prisoner was remanded until Saturday for further enquiries. , ST. ELPHIN'S V. WARRINGTON ASSOCIATION.—A large crowd witnessed the return match between these great rivals at Dalton's Bank on Saturday. Warrington were without Connor and Linaker, their places being filled re- spectively by Fairclough and Dendy. St. Elphin's won the toss and Hatton elected to play with a fairly strong breeze at the back of his colleagues. Phillips kicked off, and the Saints at once pressed- but Mather made them retreat. Warrington responded to this in good style, Fennelly taking up the running, and a fine centre was equally well saved by Jones. The home team were evi- dently on business intent, and were terribly hard to keep ovt, Forrest having to save in rapid succession. The defence was of a capital order, but the onrush was ir- resistible, and Taylor five minutes from the commence- ment of the game completely beat Forrest. Warrington then had another spell of pressure. but Marshall made a ~,plendid clearance. The home left then made tracks for Forrest* and from a pass by Taylor, Hiekinbottona sccr- ed the second goal. For a minute or two the game was more even, flatten by some pretty play gave the ball te 'raylor, and it was carried right on to the visitors' quar- ters, when Clarke was compelled to give &corner which was faultily placed. After some rather tame play Phce- nix threw into the goal mouth, and after a stiff tussle with Mather, Radford headed a beautiful goal. Half time soon afterwards arrived with the score St. Elphin's, three goals e Warrington Association, nil. After the in- terval the Saints' defence was subjected to aa vigorous onslaught, and as the result of a corner well placed by Fennelly an exciting scrimmage occurred round Jones, and Norman-cleverly took the gall from the feet of several opponents, and banged it through at a tremendous pace. After a brief visit to the opposite end,a returiawas made hy the visitors, and the ball was given to Fennelly, who made good progress, and Reid, who was playingea dash- ing game, nolthed the second goal. Hands were eiven against Clarkeeand pl ,ced beautifully in the goal mouth, the ball going Through, the Saints appealing for a goal, alleging that they touched it in its progress through. The referee, however, disallowed the claim. Jones saved a grand shot from Fennelly, and tha game now became mare of a give-and-take natnre. Final re- sult : St. Elphin'S, three. goals ; Warrington Association two goals. The locaDelubs have now met on eight occa- sions, St. Eiphin's being credited with six wins aud, War- rineton two. Ea riestown pressed somewhat,and after severe riempes they scored a third -time from a scrimmage in front of goale Some excitement new ensued and South •find- put forth every effore to draw level, and they ultimately succeeded with an easy shot in making matters even. div.head: LABOUR MEETING AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: LABOUR MEETING AT ST. HELENS.

At the Chemical and Copper Workers'Club, St. Helens, Sunday, a meeting of working men of vari- ous trades was lipid to consider a number of labour questions, including the eight hours'day, the aboli- tion of Sunday labour or double pay where work had to be performed, and the 7ayment of a living wage of „El is.. for labourers in Chemical and Copper Works. Mr. P. J. King, preside vit of the union, was supported by Mr. D. rilly, of Liverpool, end Dr. Bellew.

The Chairman said that in St. Helens, where the Chemical Union was atrong, they were going to have an eight hours' Jay without having anything less in wages. (Applause ) That was one of the best steps tbat had been taken for the prosperity of St. Helens, because it meant a third more eraployment, and a third more money would be put in circulation.. (Applause.) It might seem rather egotistic, hut it was nevertheless a feet, that through the activity of the Chemical and Copper Workers Unioni. the eight hours' day had now been brought within the range of practical politics. (Applause.) They had made the Secretary of a progres- sive Government promise that if the Crated Alkali• Co- mpany did not give them what they demandednamely, the eight hours' day, a leeislative enactment in the next session would force them 'to do it. (Hear, hear, and ap- plause.) Speaking on the abolition of Sunday labour, he said that in six months he hoped olead an attack against qunday labour. Be admitted' that some.work wawcontinuous, and required to be done on Sunda7 ; but let them have for every one hour's work on Sunday,. two hours' pay. (Applause.) Mr. Crilly said he was phased to fincilhat at Tact the chemical slaves of St. Helens-had awakened to their t7ue condition, and they now saw amend to.the inhumanity and cruelty which had been a disgrace to Lancashire:for so many years past. (Applause.) Be saw in the labour movement a far more significant sign, than the mere raising of men's wages andlthe lessening of hours of labour. It meant the uplifting of the whole of the.aace to whigher level of cornfora; . happiness, and prosperity than they had ever done before. (Applause.) Thefoilowing resolutions were carried unanimouely : "That we, the members of the Chemical and Copper Workers' and General Labourers' Uitibn, hereby pledge oursel-res to induce every man working in connection with these industries to join this union for the pur-se of accomplishing the onjects of.ourorganisation, and we emphatically condemn the action of the managers of the United Alkali Company in St Helene-for stopping from our wages and forcing ue ta become members of asick club in which we have lost confidence ;" and " That we hereby deelare our determination to fight for and to see that 'se claims of labour are not ignored im the selection of our next Parliamentary candidate., and, furthermore, we look with more than suspicion on any man whose political record is doubtful or shady, or candidatesee- commended by men whose previous and present attitude does not conform with trades union piinciples."

RUGBY. WARRINGTON v. TYLDF.SLEY.

At one time the Tyldesley team—and their supporters —were confident that they would not find any difficulty in climbing to the pinnacle of success in the Cup Com- petition. Indeed at the outset they showed signs of climbing the statistical ladder at a startling hand-over- hand rA te. But alas! " how the mighty are fallen!' Tyldosley are now removed by seven places from the lead- ing position. Indeed they seem to have quite lost their way—at least they appeared so on Saturday when War- rington paid them a visit and carried away a victory in exchange. About a thousand Warringtonians accom- panied their home team on their march to victory—and upon returning in the evening along Sankey-st., allowed the public to know the result of the struggle by proceed- ing very much in the manner of a triumphal march. There was cause to be happy however, because War- rington have forced their way to an interesting position in the competition and no one can prophecy "nay," to their chance of carrying if the cup—at least not with safety. Warrington had their best fifteen on the field, as had also the home team.

The composition of the two teams was thus :—War- rington : F. Heesom, back; J. T. Massey, J. W. Evans, C. Potts, and H. Barber, three-quarters; James Bate and John Bate, half-backs; Fair. Turner, J. Jolley, W. Nevins, J. Taylor. J. Buckley, J. T. Thorniley, T. Dono- hue, and J. Dakin, forwards. Tyldesley : J. Ashworth, full-back; F.Howarth, F. Shaw, E Evans,and H.Taylor, three-quarters; J. Berry and W. Berry, half-backs; a Woodward, j. Shepherd, J. Tucker, W. Sutcliffe, J. Fell, A, Smith, J. Worthington, and W. Roberts, forwards. Referee, Mr. E. Flower.

It was 3.15 before Turner gave the ball its initial touch in what proved a hard and vigorous game. Evans (Tyldesley) and Nevins exchanged, and play at the out- set ruled at half-way. Respective forward rushes by Jolley and Shepherd proved even, whilst an injudicious kick by Berry, saw Heesom save. From the drop-out ' the visitors passed the half-way flag, and their progress was checked by Shaw, whose kirk was met by Barber, but the return was charged, andWarrington had again to resort to defensive tactics. Warrington was next 'penalized, and Shaw essayed to lower the bottom goal without success. Nevins, Taylor; Jolley, and Buckley were the leaders in following up a kick by John Bate, and Ashworth was collared with the oval in his posses- sion.. The Warringtonians further improved their posi- tion. by passing between Massey, James Bate, Evans, and P'otts, and then a grand movement taken part in by nearly the whole line of forwards srser the Warrington skipper pulled up under the posts. A case of wilful obstruction saw Turner making a bold bid for a goal with a mag,nifirent kick, and although the. place was at the quarter /age the oval travelled almost between the posts the high wind carrying it back into play. div.head: LIBERATOR FRAUDS.
div.p: THE LIBERATOR FRAUDS.
ARREST OF JABLZ BALFOUR.

The Central News says it was rumoured early on Mon- day afternoon in Government circles that Jabez Spencer Balfour had been arrested in Argentina, but no news of a definite character was received until about four o'clock. Cablegrams then came to band both at the Treasury and at Scotland Yard, which left no doubt that the notorious absconder had been laid by the heels. This confirmation caused the greatest satisfaction both in Downing-street and Scotland Yard. The Central News is informed that Balfour cannot possibly be sent to this country by the mail steamer leaving Buenos Ayres on Saturday. Such a proceeding would be entirely without precedent, and no informalities will be allowed to im- peril the prospects of bringing Jabez Spencer Balfour be- fore an English tribunal. It should be understood that the man has been arrested purely out of courtesy to the British Government and as the result of patient and persistent efforts on the part of our Foreign Office. The warrant for Balfour's arrest will be taken to Buenos Ayres by an official deputed by the Treasury to act in such a matter. We understand that a distinguished officer of Scotland Yard will take over the prisoner from the Argentine authorities. On the arrival of this officer Balfour will be placed on board an English steamer, and then, and not till then, the warrant will be executed in the usual manner. It is probable that quite two months will elapse before Jabez Spencer Balfour finds himself within the safe walls of an English prison. His capture Is considered such an important matter that special ar- rangements will be made for his sate custody on the voyage home. HOW BALFOUR WAS TRACED.

Some details regarding the flight-ina-s-ul-s;equent dis- covery of Jabez Balfour are published by the "Daily Telegraph." It appears that after Balfour had absconded the Senior Official Receiver found in his cash book an entry of £5OO, which sum appeared to have been drawn out of his Croydon Bank for personal use two days be- i fore he left England. 'Fire cheque, it was ascertained, was chequed in live £lOO notes. One of these notes was presented at the Bank of England before the attention of Mr. Wreford was drawn to the item; but the Bank authorities were requested to take note of thepresenta- don of the remaining four. In the early part of Feb., 1893, the four £lOO notes were tendered for payment by , the agents of an Argentine bank. The numbers corres- i pondeel with the notes which had been given to Balfour by his Croydon bankers; but the endorsement was not that of Jabez Balfour. He had selected an alias, but with a singular want of ingenuity, had chosen one with the same initials, " J. 8.," and these initials on com- parison with the scores of signatures in the Senior Official Receiver's possession, left no doubt that Balfour had endorsed the notes: The Argentine bankers had insisted that he should not only en- dorse the notes, but supply his address, and, curiously enough, Balfour had written upon the- notes themselves his correct address in Buenos Ayres. The Senior Official Receiver lost no time in apnlying to the Registrar for an order to prosecute, under the 12th section of the Debtors Act, which provides that a debtor absconding with his property to the amount of £2O and upwards is guilty of felony, punishable with imprisonment, with or without hard labour, not exceeding two years. Balfour was charged by the Official Receiver with having left the country with,roperty belonging to his. creditors—the evidence relating to the notes having been obtained. The order was granted and it was placed in the hands of the Public Prosecutor, who directed the Official Receiver to attend at Bove-st. Police Court and lay the information, upon which a warrant in the usual course was granted. While these proceedings were in progress Mr. C. J. Stewart, in the liquidation of the Balfourgroup of com- panies, assisted by Mr. Wheeler, who is now the liquida- tor of the Liberator, obtained other evidence, upon which some six or seven other warrants were granted, for offences alleged to have been committed in contraven- tion of the Public Companies Acts. It appears that none of these warrants have been executed. The Trea- sury officials preserve great reticence as to their past policy or their future action, and decline to give in- formation as to the causes of the delay which occurred in the arrest of the absconder. It would seem, adds the journal, that, the newspaper stories which have ascribed to Jabez Balfour abroad a life of luxury must be ac- cepted with reserve. in view of the fact that,.so far as has been ascertained, he did not appropriate any large sum to his personal use from his private purse o.: other known sources shortly before his departure. It is hinted that Balfour's return will not be welcomed by some people. It is stated that some of Balfoqr's fellow directors show every willingness to aid the Public Friosecutor,and have communicated to him important statements which will materially strengthen the case for the prosecution. For some months the Public Prosecutor, has. been on the point of applying for warrants for the arrest of two directors of the Liberator Building Society and the House and Land Investment Trusts, but after considera- tion it was deemed advisable to abandon the idea and to wait the further. development of events. A strong point is to be made in the indictment of the valuation of the estates at the sum of £358,000, whereas in the next balance sheet the properties were estimated at £483,000. being E. 1.50,00 more than the ngures of the valuation.

It was ascertained on Wednesday at the Ftireigni Office that all the preliminaries for the extradition of Balfour had been completed between Mr. Welby the British Secretary of Legation at Buenos Ayres, and the foreign Minister of the Argentine Republic. It was stated that from the first day of the landing of Balfour in,the• Ar- gentina,Mr. Weiby Imo done his utmost to dragthe bank- rupt to justice, and pointed out to the FoTeign•Minister of the Republic, that Balfour should not be allowed to remain in the country, because, to use Mrt.Welby's own words, "The frauds with which this individual is charged amount to the sum of a million,, and have caused the ruin of many families in England." Steps are being taken at the. Foreign Office to secure not only the handing over of Balfour to the English GOvernment but of other notorious persons who for some time have found a safe hiding-place in the Argentine Republic.

Jabea Spencer Balfour is in his fifty,first year. He was born in London,. his father. Mr. Junes Balfaur, be- ing a marine st.ro- dealer in Chelsea, but much more widely known as a•teatotaller and an advocate of tem- perance, not only in this country but in the Channel Islands, and among English navvies me Fiance and in the South of England ; while his mother,.Mrs. Clara Lim' Balfour, earned no small reputation both as a speaker and writer on temperance and religion, He en- tered Parliamentias a Radical, sitting:- first for: Tam- worth from 188 C to 185, was subsequfently unsuccessful', at Croyden and lewington,and then returnedunopposed for Burnley at a by-election in 1889,. and,, lastly, by a larae majority headed the poll for the same borough in 1892. He had in the meantime been electedas the first Mayor of the new borough of Croydon, and-when he en- tered the House of Cern-mons it was the "champion director," having, &seat on the boards of no fewer than thirteen companies.. The shareholders and depositors were largely of the middle and lower-middle- class, who had trusted the savings of a lifetime in these rotten so- cieties. Thousands of these have been absolutely im poverished, and havoanpliGd for relief from the funds generously ra,Eecl for the purnose. Of these, 1,414 were women, 161 being married, 652 single.andthe rest (601)i widows. An analysis of the ages of these applicants for charity showed that; 1,070 of them,were under sixty years of age, 538'were between sinty. andi seventy. 37'14 between seventy and eighty, and fifty-sew* upwards of, eighty. The total Jess of these victims for relief was £598,345, and these,. it is to be remembered, represented only a twelfth of the, total savings engulfed in the corn,- panies financed and managed by Me. Jab,s/ Spencer al- four.

CLOSING INSANITARY HOIJS ;S AT
RUNCCqiN.

At Runcorn Potty Sessions on Monday, beforelfr John Brundrit and Mr. Henry Reynolds, Mr. Fred A. Lake, law clerk, appeared on behalf of the Run- corn Board of Improvement Commissioners, ;and applied for an order to close 18 houses in Zion Place, Mill Brow, the property of John Stringer, grocer, Mill Brow and his sister-in-law, Hannah Stringer. Mr. Stringer said he could not do what the Commission- ers desired—he could neither remove the top soil nor make a sewer.—Mr. Lake said the application was made under the Housing of the Working Classes Act 1890,and this was the first time that the Act hal been put into force in this neighbourhood. Section 3lstated that it was the duty of every local authority to make an annual inspection of their district with a view of ascertaining whether any dwelling-houses were in a state dangerous or injurious to health, and unfit for human habitation, and if on the representation of the medical officer or any other officer of the authority any dwelling4iouse appeared ti the authority to be in such a state, that they take proceedings against the owner or occupier for closing the dwelling-house. Mr. Lake pointed out that this Act was to be worked in conjunction with the Ptiblic Health Act.—Mr. E. Marshall secretary to the Commissioners produced the original report of the medical officer as to the state of the property, and produced the minute bo-lt of the Board containing a resolution passed on Nov. 2nd last ordering service of notices upon the owners of the property in accordance with the Act.—Mr. Brundrit inquired whether the closing was to be permanent or temporary.—Mr. Lake : It will be necessary to get rid of the subsoil.—Mr. Brundrit : If the owners do the things set forth by the Commissioners minute can this.property be opened afterwerds.—Mr.Lake : Yes, if your worships are satisfied that it is habitable. If he makes it habitable he can come to you and ask for another order making the property habitable.—Mr. James Percival,. the nuisance inspector proved serving notices upon the defendants to abate the nuisance. Theproperty remained as it was.—Mr. Strineer How la it possible for me to make a sewer or remove the topsoil from the land.—Wit- ness : As far as the sewer is concerned it could be done from the cesspool.—/Ir. Stringer :The land is as dry. now . as in any part ef Runcorn. The cesspool had not been emptied for six weeks.—Witness said it cost 63. per-time' to empty the cesspool.—Mr. Stringer:lt doeseit take much longer than an laour—Dr. MacDougall, Medical officer of. Health, said he had inspected this property repeaclly. The property consisted of 18 houses and formed two sides of a square. One end of the square "dipped" into a pit 14 or 15 feet below the level of the soil above. The e - drainae of the place had been conducted for years by percolation. The houses had evidently been built upon the remains of an old quarry and a great amount of Quarry debris formed the basis of the soil, and the bottom part for a considerable time- was capable of carrying away the drainage. The whole of the houses were in a dilapi- dated condition, and the soil was saturated with sewage matter, and gave of a gas of an offensive and dangerous character. On the 10th October he reported upon the property and he then expressed the opinion that the property was not fit for human habitation. During the past year there had been 13 cases of fever reported from this place and one case of erysiplas. There had also been two deaths, one from typheid fevere—Joseph Stringer—and one frone erysipelas. The latter disease - was certified as due to the insanitary condition of the locality. The propertycould not be ventilated satisfac- torily and it was very damp. The sanitary offices were too close to the houses, and unsuitable and owing to the eauation of the property it was impossible to have water' carriage or any other system.—ln reply to Mr. Brundrit Dr. MacDougall said he did not think it impossible to ,make the property fit forehuman habitation. Answer-- ing further questions, Dr. MacDougall said the subsoil was saturated six or seven feet down and it was as black as a soot bag. Because-of the offensive smell it was dam cult to get any man to do the work of testing the depth of the saturation.—MaStringer said he thought it was ee very great hardship upon both Mrs. Stringer and him- self-. Each of the tenants lead been served with notices similar to the one handed to their worship. Since that time he has got no rents- from them. He had a ground rent charge of £2O 11. e: a-year and still for all that he could not do anything with the property. The ground landlord would not allow him to sell the propeete, nor take back the land. All his tenants were out but one. RI the magistrates made the closing order., he would be placed in a very queer predicament. He did not think there were 18 cottages in the town which had a lese ' death rate than Zion-place. There had, never been • typhoid fever In the cottages before this year of all the forty years the propezby had been in Strineers' family. elf it had been of any use he could have called a witness who had lived in one of the cottages for sixty years.-- Mr. Brundrit said fie-art-the evidence before the magis- trates there was only one conclusion they could arrive at and that was that the property was unlit for human habitation, and therefore it must be closed. It might, come hard upon the owners,but that was not what the," had to consider at aeh It was the working of the Act ' :they must look at, and under its provisions the magiS" trates were bound to make an order, and that was that the property must be-closed. If they could restore it to anything like decent order they had the right to ask for it to he opened again-.—Mr. Stringer: Nees have not land ,sufficient to do that. Brundrit : That increases the' , necessity why it should he closed.—At the request of Mr. Stringer, the order was made to take, effect in four- teen days—Mr. La lre said he did not make any appliestion for costs in the case. The Commissioners thought the loss had been quite sufficient for the defendants.

WESLEYAN FOREIGN MISSIONS. . The annual sermons in aid of the above Missions were preached in the Wesleyan Chapel, on Sunday, by the Rev. J. Fielding, of Didsbury College. Special Missionary hymns were sung. On Wednes- day evening the annual meeting was held, when ! there was a large attendance, Dr. Valentine presid- ing. After the usual opening, Mr. P. Parr, secre- tary, read the report for the past year, showing that the juvenile and adults were doing much bet- ter this year than last. Miss Spencer, late of Africa, said she had done very little in Missionary work,but her father was a Missionary and her sister was in charge of a school in Africa at the present time. The speaker had resided in Africa and she gave some particulars of the life of the Kaffirs, and showed the progress they were making in education. The Rev J. R. Ellis spoke of the work in India, in the Madras circuit, and alluded to the success gained there, although the difficulties they had to contend with, were very great. The Rev T. Wynne-Jones also spoke, and after a vote of thanks to the speakers, the meeting closed.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
HARD TIMES.
About 60 working people were on Monday summoned at St. Helens for nen-payment of water rates. The general excuse was the hard times consequent on the coal strike.
NICELY CAUGHT.

The St. Helens police have recently had a large number of reports of door mats having been stelen,and on Saturday night Police-constable Tomlinson met John Wilson,of New- castle-on-Tyne,carrying one in Li verpool-road,St. Helens. He ascertained that it had been stolen from the lobby of Mr. Grimshaw's offices, in Hardshaw-st. The prisoner was on Monday committed for fourteen days.

div.head: ALLEGED THEFT FROM THE PERSON.
div.p: ALLEGED THEFT FROM THE PERSON.

On Monday, John Caldwell, a rough-looking fellow, living in Sandfield Crescent, was charged before Mr. H. S. Oppenheim and Mr. J. B. Leach with stealing a purse containing 10s. or 12s. and a pawnticket, also is. Bd. in loose coppers, from the person of Hugh Cassidy, a labourer, as he was leaning against a window near the Lorne Hotel, Parr-st., on Saturday night. Prisoner, who had been in prison for theft, was now committed for two months with hard labour. THE REFORMATORY FOR INCORRIGIBLES.

At St. Helens, on Tuesday, two boys, named Lawrence Smith and Rickard Collins, of Greenback, who had each been several times convicted of larceny, were found guilty of stealing two tins of beef,value 65., from the shop of Ann Ward, in Liverpool-street. Chief Constable ood said Collins's mother died some time ago, and his father left him. He had really no home. Smith's par- ents could do no good with him. The magistrates (Alderman M4Bryde, Mr. W. J. Thomson, and Mr. B. B. Glover) ordered the lads to be imprisoned for seven days, and tt.en. to be sent to a reformatory for three years.

div.head: MIDNIGHT SHOP ROBBERY.
div.p: MIDNIGHT SHOP ROBBERY.

On Monday night the prevision shop in Church-street, St. Helens, belonging to Messrs. Voce and Ditclifield, was broken into. The thieves scaled a back wall, and forced an entrance by breaking away the support of a side door. The till, which was fastened t, toe counter, was taken into the yard, and there smashed up. About half-a-crown in copper was taken. 'Me thief or thieves do not appear to have extend -d their operations further than the till, and a safe in another portion of the shop remained untouched. A large slater's hammer was found in the yard near the broken till.
CORPORATION LOANS: DECISION OF THE LOCAL GOVERN-
MENT BOARD.

The Local Government Board have sanctioned the borrowing of £15,000 by the St. Helens Corporation for the extension of the main sewer from Ashcroft Bridge to the site of the proposed outfall works at Double Locks, and also £3,000 for the purchase of 14121. The question of a further sum of £lO,OOO asked for to construct works is deferred, and the Corporation will after the comple- tion of the sewer make experiments as to the best methods of dealing with the sewage. The chairman of the Health Committee (Councillor Forster) wrote from London hoping the committee would decido to do the work themselves, and not call in any outside contrac- tors.

div.head: EXELOSION IN AN FIOTEL.
div.p: EXELOSION IN AN FIOTEL.

An alarming explosion occurred at the Raven Hotel, St. Helens, on Tuesday. In escape of gas had been no- ticed for some days, owing to a defective tap in the cooking stove in the kitchen, and a man was sent to re- pair it. He left, telling the cook, Miss Webster, that everything was right, hut when she applied a light to one of the jets of the stove a lona explosion occurred. The front of the stove was blown out, the articles in the kitchen shaken,, and two large squares of glass in the window were broken. Mrs. Parkes, wife of the land- lord, Mr. William Parkes, was in the kitchen at the time, and she and the cook narrowly escaped injury. The explosion caused much alarm, and was heard all over the building.

div.head: Sr. HELENS TECHNICAL SCHOOL COMPETITION.
div.p: Sr. HELENS TECHNICAL SCHOOL COMPETITION.

The following resolutions were unanimously passed at a special council meenting of the Manchester Society of Architects, held on Tuesday :—"That the council, hav- ing perused the copies of the correspondence which has taken place between Messrs. Woodhouse and Willough- by and the authorities of the St.llelens Technical School regret that., contrary to the assessor's award, the com- mittee should have decided to allow the authors of the second premiated design to carry out the work in prefe- rence to the authors of the first, a decision which they consider to be opposed to the true spirit of competi- tions." "That copies of the foregoing resolution be stint to the Royal Institute of British Architects and the various allied societies, and to Messrs. Woodhouse and Willoughby."

div.head: OUTBREAK OF TYPHUS FEVER.
div.p: OUTBREAK OF TYPHUS FEVER.

During the fortnight ended January 20 there were 130 births and 58 deaths at St. Helens. The birth-rate was 44-25 per 1,000, or 4 above the average, and the death- rate was 19 7 per 1,000, against 17-5 the previous fort- night, and 25.72 in the corresponding period of last year. The medical officefs (Dr. MiNicoll and Dr. Robertson) reported on Wednesday that there had been three cases of typhus fever in the Green bank district. The house in which the fever broke out was one in which every condi- tion was fulfilled for the propagation of the fever. There were want of food, filth, and dirty habits and over- crowding. From the number of neighbours who had been in contact with these persons, it was highly pro- bable that other cases might occur. The medical officers were not able to trace whence the cases had been im- ported. There had been no case' in St. Helens 2ince a doubtful cne in 1890. NEW LIBRARY AT ST. HELENS.

At noon, on Thursday, the Mayor of St. Helens (Mr. Arthur Sinclair, J.P.) formally declared open the new Parr Branch Library and Healing-room. St. Helens. This is the third branch library and reading-room in the borough. The Central Library in the Town-hall was opened on the 20th august, 18.87, the Sutton branch on the 3rd February, 1877, and the Thatto-heath branch on November 3rd, 1891. The residents of the outlying dis- tricts of Parr have long been agitating f.,r a branch library, and ex-Councillor Brown was one of the first to moot the thing in the Council, and persistently advanced it until its adoption. The new library. which. has been erected at a cost of £B5O, is considerably larger than the Thatto-heath one. The building has been erected by Mr. Peter Tickle, the joinery work being carried out by Mr. Wm. Harrison. As on the occasion of the opening of the Thatto-heath library the Mayor was presented with the complete catalogue of the libraries, full-bound in scarlet morocco, with gilt edges.
TIII3 NEW RAILWAY.

Mr. J. P. Mearns, solicitor, appeared at the St. Helens Police Court on Monday, to make an application on be- half of Mr. John Walker, of 33, Derby-st., Prescot, who carries on the business of a 'Arse slaughteterfat boiler. and bone dresser, near the line of the new Liverpool, St. Helens, and South Lancashire Railway, as it runs near Park-road, St. rielens. Mr. Walker alleges that without any notice the company blocked up Lathorn-st.,the only way by which he had access to his works, and that the obstruction was a permanent one, as it consisted of the new line from Haydock to St. Helens. The application was for a special bench of magistrates to fix the amount if any, of compensation for the loss and injury he had received. The magistrates present were Mr.H.S.Oppen- helm and Mr.J. B. Leach. As both those gentlemen are interested in the new railway,the magistrates' clerk (Mr. Brewis),undertook to arrange fora bench of disinterested Justices on the 9th February.

ALLEGED NEGLIGENCE OF THE UNITED ALKALI Co. At St. Helens Town Hall on Saturday, Mr. S. Brig- house held an inquest on the body of Henry Vincent Dewar aged fourteen years, son of the late Air. Peter Dewar, wholesale tobacconist, Westfield-street and Bridge-street, St. Helens, who met with a violent death in the Hardshaw Brook Works of the United Alkali Com- pany, Limited, on Thursday morning. Mr. Richmond, inspector of factories, was present. Mr. J. 0. Swift represented the company, and Mr. Mearns appeared for the relatives of the deceased. John Johnsen, 131,Peasley Cross-lane, said he was a chemist at the works, and the deceased assisted him. On Thursday morning at half past eight he sent deceased to fetch samples. In order to get to vats Nos. 1,2,an(1 3 he had to go up a ladder with a rail on the left ha. d side,and at the top he would get on to a platform of three planks,which allowed him to take samples from Nos. 2 and 3. To get to Nos. 4 and 5 he would have to get on another platform about 31t high, on to which he would pull himself. The Coroner. The theory is that while climbing from the plank to the up- per platform he fell into the pan. Was it the right way to go? Witness.—lt was the way I had taken myself, and I could not chastise anyone else for going. There was another way, but this was the nearest. It was not the right one. The Coroner.—lf you had seen him, and said nothing, I don't see how we are going to find fault with deceased for going that way. Why was there not a rail on the righthand side of the ladder? Witness.— I cannot answer. Mr. Richmond, Government inspec- tor, while of opinion that the ladder should have two rails, and that no planks should be placed across danger- ous spots, did not see they were connected with this accident, as the boy fell from above. He, however, thought the gangway should be entirely fenced. The jury found a verdict of "Accidental death," but were of ( pinion that the United Alkali Company had been negligent in not providing sufficient protection.
DEATH OF A SCHOOLBOY AT ST. HELENS.
SERIOUS ALLEGATION AGAINST A TEACHER.

An inquest was held on Saturday, at the Railway Hotel, Garswood, near St. Helens, by Mr. S. Brig- house, on the body of William Cunliffe, aged nine years, son ot a collier named James Cunliffe, living in the brickyard near Garswood Station. Inspector Ryder and Sergeant Williams, of the Lancashire County Constabulary, were present, and the Rev. Austin Powell, of Birchlev, watched the proceed- ings on behalf of the managers and teachers of the Birchley Roman Catholic Schools. The Coroner opened the proceedings by saying that that was a case which would perhaps take some time o consider, because it was suggested—he did not say it was so—but it was suggested that the boy had Med frcm blood-poisoning caused by injuries received by caning. Mrs. Ann Cunliffe said she sent her son to Birchley Roman Catholic Schcol at Billiuge. He had a gathered finger before ha was caned by the teacher—had had it about a fortnight. It was the fitst finger of the right hand. A week last Monday the boy came home lion school about half-past five, and said the teacher had hit him on his sore finger. At this point the coroner called in Miss Mary J. Sum- ner, the teacher referred to. Witness (continuing) said she remarked to her boy, "Surely the teacher would not cane you on your sore finger.' He said, "She was caning me over my knee, and I was putting my hand across to save my knee, and I caught it." The lad, she admitted. required a lot of caning, because he was what they called a dunce. The boy did not go any more to the school. She called in Dr. Lathom, of Ashton-in-Makerfield, on the 16th. He died on the 18th. He never complained about the teacher being cruel; in fact, he was very fond o! her, and was particularly fond of going to Birchley School.

Dr. William Lathom, of Ashton-in-Makerfield, said he was called in to see the deceased on Wednesday last. The boy was in a very low csndition, consequent on fe- brile disturbances. There were marks of injury on his left leg, with contusions on various parts of the leg and loins which were very painful. Witness's attention was not called to the finger. The boy was in a semi- conscious condition when witness first saw him. On Saturday he made a post mortem examination. Dr. Mason was present on behalf of the achool autherities. Witness was of opinion that death was dna to septicce- mia, a particular form of blood-poisoning. In reply to questions, witness said that he considered the blood-poisoning to have been set up by the contu- sion below the knee.; there were no signs of it having been set up by the finger. A small sharp rap with the cane would be sufficient to cause the contusion. Some of the discolcuration was inflammatory following the injury. A fall and coming in contact with some hard substance would cause it. Dr. John Masson agreed with the last witness that the boy died of septiocemia, but said that he did not think that the contusion was the original site of the introduc- tion of poisonous matter. Miss *Sumner, who did not object to be sworn, said she was an assistant mistress at the Birchlev Ibman Catholic School. William Cunliffe was a scholar. She remembered hitting him on Friday with a ruler on the hand. She did not know which hand she hit, but it was not his sore hand. He had had his hand plastered all week, and she was very particular. She did not hit him on the knee. He was very lazy over his lessons,and his mother had given her permission to cane him. About four o'clock in the afternoon he began to cry, and said his heel was very painful. She was busy, and did not take any more notice of it, because •he was a boy who cried for very little. The coroner suggested as a verdict, owing to the dlff- erent opinions expressed by the doc_tors, " Death from septiocemia, but how caused or set up they were unable to say," and then the police could think it out. He must further say, although it was a side issue, that he was strongly opposed to any school assistants having the power ;liven them to inflict corporal punishment. He had had several cases of a similar description to that. He was very much interested in education, having chil- dren of his own, being a manager of a school,and gover- nor of a grammar school ; but he strongly objected to assistants having th 6 right to inflict corporal punishment. They were all liable to err. They were not always in a calm and judicial state of mind, and when something happened it was better to have the matter considered by some person at the top of the tree. When both sides had been heard, and it had been definitely decided that an offence had taken place, let the head master or mis- tress, after careful deliberation, inflict the punishment. When the power was given to assistants, and they inflicted punishment, it very often happened that the power was abused (the Jury " Hear, hear.") The jury then considered the matter, and found that the child died from septiccernia, but bow set up they were unable to say. They presented that the caning should be done, if required, by the head master or mis- tress, and that assistants should be forbidden to inflict corporal punishment.

div.head: 31 AZZINPS WRITINGS.
div.p: 31 AZZINPS WRITINGS.

Sir,—ln your short report of my address on Mazzini given at the Wlcliffe P.S.A., which appeared in your last issue, a slightly wrong impression is conveyed as to the book I urged my audience to buy. I took for my " text" the delightful volume of selections from Mazzini called "God and the People," for which we are indebted to the Rev. C. W. Stubbs, of Wavertree. This volume alight well e beyond the means of many,though strongly to be recommended to all who can get it. Fortunately, however,Mazzini's finest utterances can be purchased for next to nothing. There is a paper-backed volume (pub- lished I believe by Alexander and Shepherd), which can be bought for 6.1. It contains his "Thoughts on Democracy in Europe," and his" Duties of Man," and in addition Madame Venturi's well-known account of his life.. If I have led six men out of the hundreds who lis- tened to me to read and take delight in this book I shall feel that t have done a good deed. If this letter turns the six into seven I shall be glad I have written it, for I agree with Arnold Toynbee that in many things Mazzini is the true teacher of our age. lam almost inclined to thank you for your mistake as it gives me a fresh oppor- tunity of drawing attention to his message. Those of us who believe that Religion and Democracy hold the keys of the future can tave few more congenial tasks Ulan that of urging men to read and ponder his writings, —Yours, &c.,

i. dom.; PEERS AS A CONTROVERSIALIST. certal..? class of controversialists when they ,have been worsted u. -1 an argument throw the blame upon the wandering pmelilections of their opponents and magnify their own skill N keeping to the point. To this class belongs Mr. John Feel.. I have engaged him in controversy since the second week in November, and he has suddenly discovered that his original contention was that Mr. S. Woods had been guilty of intimidation. This statement is disingenuous and significant; disingenu- ous because he would have readers believe that his quar- rel lay only with Mr. S. Woods ; significant as a form of admission that all his other contentions have been turned inside out. When I entered the lists it was not as a special champion of Mr. S. Woods, I can assure you. I certainly would not have wasted my time and your space in discussing whether a miners' agent had a right to say boo to a goose. The game would not have been worth the candle, and I have besides a little more respect for the intelligence of yblur readers. I need not carry them again through the various arguments, exposing the want of logic and sense in Mr. Peers' description of the Miners' Federation as a body of " tryants," because, some few individual indiscretions had been committed. Nor need Ido more than point to his failure to show how a miner was to obtain the highest price for his labour except by Ceasing to work. His defence, too, of industrial ethics which sanction the further enriching of the moneyed man by lowering the standards of living among the workers, is obviously antagonistic to the golden rule,and needs no further exposure. These and other incidental issues, and the way in which they have been treated, are familiar to all who havo followed the discussion. I am glad that these matters have ;been ventilated in some degree in your columns. They are of vital import- ance to all workers, and will absorb more public atten- tion in the future. Men of the Peers' type will doubtleAs rush in to stem the advancing tide of democracy, and seek to uphold conditions which give the most to those who do the least,and the least to those who do the most, but they must be taught the futility, if they cannot see the injustive, of their action. It is quite evident, Show- ever, from Mr. Peer's remarks on Mr. Whitham's letter that he has not yet perceived the "true inwardness " of the labour movement. The underlying principles upon which it is based he fails to grasp,and deals only with the ,t-am and jetsam on the surface. In theology he is heterodox, delighting in thrashing old theological carcases, and in this pursuit heis eminently successful. In sociology he is orthodox, and he fails because he ignores the fact which is true in coo as in the other that "the old order changeth and giveth place unto the new.' —Yours, &c.,

div.head: COMMON JUSTICE.
div.p: COMMON JUSTICE.
RATIONALISM VERSUS REASuN.

Sir,—! note Mr. Peer's stricture on my letter of the 12th inst., and can only characterize it as unreasoning, and irrational (in the right sense of the word). Mr. Peers, the exponent of latitudinarianism, posing as the dogmatic Pope of Science is truly an instructive spec- tacle. The problems of a hereafter, of immortality, and of physical science may be(as he says)simple matters for one of your correspondent's calibre; but he must pardon the majority of the ignorant laity around hitn,including my humble self, if we refuse to accept,without adequate reasons, the ex-cathedra decisions both of Prof. Huxley and himself ! Words, Mr. Peers, take up a lot of space, but (per Sc) prove nothing, and other readers, as well as myself, would be much obliged if you would condescend to come from the realms of abstractions to that of fact. I dare champion "the primeval fall of man," also its " consequence," without its adjective Let Us look at it closaly—to use the words of Cardinal Newman-- I look out of myself into the world of men, and there I see a sight which fills me with unspeakable distress . . the sight of the world is nothing else than the prophet's Scroll, full of " lamentations, and mournings, and woe." To consider the world in its length and breadth, its various history,the many races of men, their starts,their fortunes,their mutual alienation,their conflicts ; and then their ways, habits. governments, forms of worship,their enterprises, their aimless courses, their random achieve- ments and acquirements, the impotent conclusion of long standing facts, the tokens so faint and broken of a superintending design, the blind evolution of what turn out to be great powers or truths, the progress of things as if from unreasoning elements,uot toward final causes, the greatness and littleness of man, his far•reaching aims, his short duration, the curtain hung over his futurity, the disappointments of life, the defeat of good, the success of evil—the prevalence and intensity of sin —that condition of the whole race, so fearfully yet exactly described in the Apostle's words " having no hope, and without God in the world," all this is a vision to dizzy and appal (not to make jokes of). What shall be said to this heart-piercing, reason-bewildering fact." I answer that this living society of men is in a true sense discarded from the intimate presence of its Creator. The world is implicated in some terrible aboriginal calam- ity. It is out of joint with the purposes of its Creator, and thus the doctrine of what is called original sin becomes to me almost as certain as that the world exists and as the existence of God. Did I see a boy of good make and mind, with the tokens on him of a refined nature, cast upon the world wiehout provision, unable to say whence he came, his birth-place or his family connexions, I should conclude that there was some mystery conercted with his history, and that he was one, of whoui, from one cause or another, his parents were ashamed. Thus only should Ibe able to account far the contrast between the promise and the condition •of his being. fore Air. Peers has his answer—l have :given him Plenty of rope, as the saying, is—and hope he -will be careful with it. As to Dr. Mivart, Mr. P. is incorrect both in fact and • theory, notwithstanding my blindness! Dr. Mivart did not recant anythkg in his articles, nor was he compelled or even asked to do so. Ills article was simply placed on the index without giving reaaons, and may be 'removed in the same way, when opportune. Having been both Agnostic and Socialist, I may, perhaps, be ,aredited with knowing something about them. All how- saver I would point out to your correspondent and others, iA the importance of not confusing terms, or to quote Cardinal Manning "Socialism is to Society, what rationalism is to reasoning. It denotes an abuse, an excess, a de-ordination in human society, as rationalism denotes a miSUSP and an abuse of reason. All reasoning must be rational that is in conformity with laws of reason, and all legislation for human society must be both human and social by the necessity and nature of man- kind. Inhuman and anti-social law is not law, hut tyranny or anarchy," but neither postulate Itationaliam Jr Socialism.-1 am,sir, yours faithfully, JOHN S. HOWELL, 9, Montgomerv-road, Chiswick, London. W. January 20, 1894.
