div.head: OUT WITH THE GEN.
div.p: OUT WITH THE GEN.
ADVENTURES OF A SHOOTING PARTY.
BY LUKE BLUNT.

" TO BE Sold, a bay mare; 17 hands high, indefinite; a little the worse for wear, but can be thoroughly recommended as a quiet, sagacious, and unvicious animal. As the owner is going out of the country and the animal has been in family some time, will sell to good master at 15s.—Apply---" Yes, there was no doubt that was the animal we were lookirig for, and so our little meeting of four, which had assembled to consider the advertisement, decided to repair to the address named—not a hun- dred miles from Sankey-street—and complete the purchase. We had arranged to set out from War- rington upon a four days' shooting expedition. Three days were to be spent on land adjoining a neighbouring, canal, and the fourth day was to be spent in wild fowl shooting at Frodsham Marsh. Benzon had procured the loan of a crude sort of house boat, and we unanimously agreed that this would provide famous lodgings for us during the three days at least. It was not a steamboat, nor was it a boat which could be sailed, hence the nec- essity for the services of our four-footed friend. te,mithson, who was studying as a veterinary sur- geon, agreed eventually to caary out the purchase alone. One could always tell that he was in the horse business because, for three years, both in winter and in summer, he was never seen out with- out a pair of cloth leggings. This was about the ' extent of his progress in the business, I was corn- pelled to think, on the memorable morning upon which the remainder of U 8 saw the horse for the ' first time. It was in a leld near the canal bank, hard by where our boat was moored. The previous evening we had stowed away in the lockers of the craft, what food and clothing we intended to take along with us, and now there was nothing to do but harness the horse, make the towing line fast, and proceed on our journey. So we adjourned to the field to help Smithson catch the horse. We crept quietly round the hedge until we reached a gap near where the horse lay ; because we were afraid to let it see us, lest, as Smithson had said, it should get galloping and prancing about the field and refuse to be harnessed. Steathily we stole into the field, steathily we crept up to the reposeful quadruped, and then,swift as lightning, Smithson had fastened a halter about its head. But it did not move. Oh,it was a callous horse! It slowly turned the eye that wasn't blind upon us,and stared with a calm,peaceful look,which plainly showed that the animal was innocent, now, of getting on its legs without strong and ample pro- vocation. By and by, after several futile attempts, it got up, and then what a disappointing spectacle it presented! The legs were bent at the knees, as though they had been stricken stiff, whilst gallop- ing, perhaps in some by-gone period of youthful levity. He had no tail that it would be safe to brag about—the decaying hand of Time, or a hatchet, had shortened it to a stump, like a rabbit's. Ho had the usual number of ribs and other jeints, I know, because we counted them. Although his age was unknown to the last owner, Benzon said that he thought that if Noah were here now, he could have told us, because the horse looked like one of the animals that strayed away from the Ark. But that maybe, was one of Benzon's little jokes.

In time, we commenced our journey,and then, for me set in quite a chapter of unpleasant experiences. Mine was the first" watch" which had to be taken with the horse—the duty:of guiding and persuading it. Passers-by used to turn round and jeer me about the brute; I was accused of robbing a veterinary surgeon's hospital, and of doing many other equally unpleasant things. Soon, however, the climax came. What the antiquated quadruped was about I cannot say. One said that be was going to prove his sagacity, by showing us how he could think, but, being blind in the nearest eye, had fallen over into the water by trying to lean against some- thing ; Smithson said it was an attempt at felo de 8e ; whilst I believe the animal was reaching for a fly on its top lip, with its hind leg, and lost its balance, in the act. At any rate, our struggles to get the brute out of the water were futile, and we eventu- ally had to procure the assistance of a farmer's horse, which we coupled to our half drowned brute and then lashed until he dragged the antiquity from the water. Even then, this thing of "indefinite " age would not stand, until, having thrown the coupling line over the strong bough of a tree we caused the farmer's horse to begin to haul. Thus our animal was lifted on to his lees, when he allowed just the least look of surprise to invade his eyes 89 though he had awakened from slumber. After this noth- ing of note occurred until we reached the first shooting ground. The sport was rooks—young ones for it is a waste of time and shot to try to kill old ones. Now, one of the party, W illotson, had never handled a rifle before, and, being a little afraid of him, we had taken the precaution to order blank cartridge for his use. It mayappear mean,but then he would enjoy himself we thought quite as well as with ball cartridge. True, a novice with a rifle, if he be filled with the usual enthusiasm and energy for slaughtering. will,if fair facilities are given him, quickly succeed in shooting some of his friends or himself. But Willotson is not ambitious, so we thought he would not miss very much such a treat. When we were sufficiently near to hit, operations were commenced. The first bird that fell was appa- rently from Benzon's gun, but Willotson said: "Not so bad for a beginner," and appropriated the bird. By and by, after taking deliberate aim, the sub- scriber brought down a fine young rook. Wino tson had fired his gun off into the air about the same time, and now he gleefully ran for the fallen bird. "I believe I shot that bird. Mr. Willotson," I re- marked. " But I don't believe you did, sir," he replied with indignation,and stalked away with the prize. This sort of thing continued for some time, and we all more or less began to feel annoyed, because the credit of having killed is always a sportsman's chief reward. By the time Wil- lotson had appropriated some ten birds, we others had in our possession two or three. Ile had endeavoured "to make up " the little difference between us. He said, "Blunt,old ruan,an old shootist like you shouldn't be jealous of the especial luck of a young marksman." Then he slapped me on the shoulder and said,"Come, cheer u,). OM feel quite happy. You know my wife had prophesied that I should blow ray head off : you know she thought I'm a bit of a mug at this sort of thing. But then when one's done this sort of thing when yonne, and doesn't admit it—the secret will out itself." And he winked significantly. I said "Yes there is no doubt you are a clever marksman; the cleverest among us." "Oh f draw it mild," he said with a gic.r.ele. "But there isn't a man amongst 11A who could , have killed that number of birds under the cirenra- I stances."
"Why?" "Simply because--

Yes." - "-- because we are not steady enough shots to kill more than an odd one or two—with Mank cart- ridge." He vrarked up a ghastly, corpQe-like smile, to accompany a look of interrogation which searched my face for a look to belie my words.. And finding it not, his head sank on his breast—he 'WWI like a man who. had lost the realization of his fond- est dream—or his watch and chain!

Shortly after this little incident a police sergeant came along—an officer whom Benzon and I knew very well. Now Smithson, who had no gun of his own, had borrowed one of a friend naraA Alfred Edward Willox-, and of course he was carrying it without a license. We informd the sergeant of this, and arranged that he should come round later on and ask to see our licenses, just to frighten • Smithson. By-and-by the officer came npon us and made his demand. Bennn and myself had left our licenses at home, so he took our names end ad- dresses. Then he came to Smithson, who said he had left his license at home.
" Name please?" " Alfred Edward Willox." "But I hear your friends calling, Nou Jack." Smithson went very red and very confused. stammered'
"Ye—yes. It's John Alfred Edward Smi—f mean "John Alfred—what an extraordinary name!"

"Yes. von see it's sort of family affair. Feller named John, grandfather Alfred, mother's brother named Edward—see ? " " it unoph ! "and the sergeant left but hung about, the fields. We rated Smittv.on soundly for t,ivincr his friend's name, as it would now .get him into trouble. This was the cruelest cut of all. Smith- son was almost beside himself—he would never for- give himself if Willox were dragged into the mat- ter lie desisted from shooting and fell to worrying

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 27, 1894. TIM SHIP CANAL. I NOTES ON GAMES AND
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 27, 1894. TIM SHIP CANAL. I NOTES ON GAMES AND

fretting. We assured him that he couldn't . it now; it would mean 203. and costs. He ...ew the danger he was rbinning and ought to put up with the results; but it wasn't generous to let tne owner of the gun in. "That's just it," he would say—" Oh! 808. and:costs,l9 kee_p_his name nut."

Sometime afterwards we were surprised to I see Smithson acting in a most facetious fashion with the sergeant; he was laughing loudly and anon he would poke the officer in the ribs—and then he would join in the laugh. During the remainder of the afternoon he simply swam in a sea of contented boyish happiness. He would hop about and sing snatches of songs—but never a word about the ser- geant did he utter until the return to the boat was being made. Then he made a speech. He said he had it various times been out with thickheaded company—with "mugs "—but never anything to equal the company present. This was very flatter- ing, and quite unexpected. He was asked to explain. He said: ' Explain! Bah !You will appear before the mag- istrates. I won't." "Oh!"
"That's it. I took the trouble to tip the sergeant 108. My name was crossed off the book. Yours remain.

In a bit I broke it to him gently; I told him how sorry we were, but the fact was we never would have carried out the joke had we known he was going to lose 10a. He said very distinctly and deliberately that Benzon and I were a couple of asses—and that mau Willotson, after all our per- aonal kindness went over to him.

It is quite possible however that with the judic- ious use of contriteness—and whisky—Benzon and I would have overcome this animosity, had it not been for an unforeseen occurranct. As we neared the boat there was espied sitting on the water keg, a man in uniform. Raving hurried up I should have demanded boldly, what he wanted of us. But I was checked by the appearance of R.S.P.C.A. on his hat. A suspicion darted across my mind that there was something wrong with that steed of ours. And so it proved. The officer said it possessed quite a number of things we couldn't account for—spavins, ring-bone, &c. &c. It would be necessary to account for its possession of these to the Runcorn Bench, the following day. So he took our names and told us what time to be at court. Our little party broke up and returned home to do several things besides consulting a solicitor.

THE TRADE AT SALTPORT. The tiade is increasing at Saltport. The steamer Cyprus has just discharge-I a cargo of inn pYri,ee fez Mpimm .thempson, Loitock, at the rate of 600 tons per day. Tne steamer Bittern arrived at Salt- port en Friday, and she left during Saturday with a cargo of saltcake for Antwerp, from the United Alkali I Company's Works, Weston. ALLEGED SHEBEENING ON TISE CANAL. The Cheshire police have mada a raid upon a hut at Saltport, Frodsham Marsh on the Manchester Ship Canal Works, where they had suspicions that drink was being sold without a licence. Superintendent Meredith, of the Eddisbury division, and several officers visited the premises occupied by John Taylor, alias Peg Walker, and on searching the place found an 18-gallon cask of beer nearly full, one empty cask, several drinking mugs, and some bottles containing a little whiskey. 'These were seized, and conveyed to, Frodsham Police Station. The summons has been issued, to be heard at the monthly petty sessions next week. A STEAMER TWICE IN COLLISION. The steamer Gorgi, a vessel of 1710 tons gross register belonging to the Persian Gulf Steamship Line, London, bad an eventful voyage from Eastham to Runcorn on the Ship Canal on Saturday afternoon. An attempt was made to navigate the canal with one small tug at the stern, but this method did not answer very well, and slow progress was made. At Ellesmere Port the vessel collided with the pontoon, and both received some dam- age. In proceeding attross themouth of the Weaver, at Weston Point,the ship ran sten: on into the piles there, and was then sent by the wind broadside against the Weaver sluices and could not move away until she was turned round by means of a rope fixed to the sluices. On reaching Runcorn Lay-by at half-past four, the cap- tain determined to attempt to get no further that night, and he completed the journey on Sunday. THE ASSESSMENT OF THE CANAL. At Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority on Tuesday, J. Mclntyre, the chairman, stated that fast week a meet- ing of the clerks of the various unionte bordering on thr Ship Canal had been held at Warringten to consider the best method of assessing the Ship Canal for rating pur- poses, and the meeting had fortnula.tedla scheme which had been submitted to the assessment committee that day. The object was to obtain uniformity of assessment throughout the whole length of the canal,. and a meeting of representatives from the various unions' assessment committees affected, was to be held in Manchester early in next month to deal further with the subject. The assessment committee had appointed the chairman (Mr. Charles Reynolds, J.P.) and the clerk (Mr. John Ash- ton), who had taken the initiative in the matter, to re- present the Runcorn Union. The sanction of the guar- I dians was required, and also permission to charge the expenses incurred.—Mr. Handley moved that the ex- penses incurred be paid, and remarked that he hoped some satisfactory basis of assessment would be arrived at.—The Rev. J. W. N. Tanner seconded the raotien, which was carried unanimously. THE NAVIGATION OF THE CANAL. The fine sailing ship Curzon 1,860 tons,. laden with nitrate from Iquique, the total value of the ship and cargo being placed at £50,000, arrived in the Mersey at ' Liverpool on Tuesday with the intention of proceeding via the Ship Canal to Manchester. The owners of the vessel, being also owners of the cargo,pffered to proceed to Manchester if the Canal Company would!make good any damage sustained by the vessel owing to the diffi- culty of navigating the canal to and from Ea.stham Locks the owners on their part undertaking to lower the ves- sel's masts, and lose a month's time on the canal in put- ting the ship in order and refitting her at Eastham or Ellesmere port, ready to go to sea again. They also • undertook to pay a month's demurrage, which meant £9OO, besides lightening the ship so far as was necessary • to facilitate a safe voyage to Manchester and the clear- ance of the bridges. After some negotiations the Canal Company refused to give a guarantee of safety, and the owners finding the practical difficulties of the navigation ' of the canal such as they could not encounter, ordered I that the Curzon be discharged in Garston Docks, Liver- pool, instead of proceeding to Manchester.

THE TUGGING OF VESSELSi 6 IMPORTANT SUGGESTION. The steamer Finsbury,which caaried the first cargo o cotton to Manchester along the canal, had a somewhat rough passage on her return, and narrowly escaped sus- taining serious injury. She left the docks light at 11.30 on Friday morning to go to Cardiff for cargo. After passing Latchford locks a south-westerly gale sprang up, and being so much out of water she experienced the utmost difficulty in keeping off the banks, being swung from side to side in consevence of not having sufff, ciently powerful tugs. She had her propeller injured. For safety's sake Captain James determined to proceed no further than Runcorn lay-by, where she was securely moored. Here she remained during the night,and until Sunday morning. Captain James contended that the Ship Canal Company should have strong steam tugs,and this especially in the case of large vessels- when light: Without this the waterway will not be :Oavigable ,aith safety. Ho acknowledges that the canal is a great en- gineering achievement, but joins in the opinion that it has been prematurely opened. He recommends the pro- vision of lay-bys or " gares " at various stations be- tween Eastham and Latchford locks; and especially in the neighbourhood, so that there will be no serious damage caused by ships passing each other. He also suggests that means should be supplied en route whereto ropes could be fastened in case a vessel ran ashore, so that she might be the more easily released from the awkward position. He also commented upon the ab- sence of telegraphic or telephonic communication along the banks in case of accident, &e. THE CHESHIRE POLICE AND THE OPENING OF THE CANAL. A meeting of the Standing Joint COmmittee for Ches- hire was held on Saturday under the presidency of Colonel C. H. France Hayhurst. One of the questions raised was that of charging the Manchester ship Canal Company for the services of the police on duty on the Company's property at the openinc, of the canal from Latchford to Manchester on the let January—The Chief Constable stated that in consequence of the large con- course of people witnessing the opening ceremony on New Year's day, he had to send down 69-policemen to protect the public, and 19 of the officers were employed' on the Canal Company's own property.—Mr. Ralph Bates asked at whose request the police were sent, and the Chief Constable stated that the secretary had requested him to arrange regarding the disposition of the police on the Cheshire por- tion of the canal.—Mr. Killick pointed out that a large number of the Manchester .and Lancashire police had been similarly employed, and he wanted to know whether they had charged the Canal gompany for the service. The police were present for the protection of the public and not in the interests of the Company.— Mr. Sykes moved that no charge be made upon the Company for the use of the police, because they were there simply for tbe safety of the public, and it was very creditable no accident occurred.—Mr. C. H. Booth seconded.--The Chairman remarked that if any private Person called in the police on the occasion of a fete he would have to pay the county.—Mr. Smith (Liscard) said when the local authority at New Brighton required extra police to deal with excursionists it had to pay the county.—Dr. Hocleson (Crewe) remarked that when the Corporation of Crewe required additional police even on the occasion of a burial they had to reimburse the county authority. The Ship Canal Company expected a large crowd, and he did not know whether the occasion was the burial of the hopes of some other port or not —(Laugh- ter.)At any rate the'Canal Company ought to pay for the police.—Mr. Killick submitted that the cases were not analogous. When private persons gave a fete the peo- ple were there by invitntien, but at the Canal opening the people invited themselves.—Dr. Hodgson retorted that the assembly of a crowd was never by invitation.— The Chief Constable explained that the Ship Canal Com- pany had made no application for a remission of the ex- pense, and he had raised the question himself.—Dr. , Hodgson moved an amendment that the ordinary charge be made upon the Canal Company.—.lr. Ralph Bates asked how much the Duke of Westminister was charged for extra police when the Shah visited Eaton and Chester on a Sunday.—The Chief Constable could not reply off hand how much his Grace paid, but he always paid,when he required special constables to regulate the traffic on his own grounds.—Mr. Beckett (Belvidere) seconded Dr. Hodgson's amendment, which was carried by eleven to nine votes.

ATHLETICS. --- Rucurr Fop [BALL. Another mark has been made against the Warrington Football Club ! But it is not in the Lancashire Eugby 1 Cup Championship ; it is simply in the memory of a team on whose threshold Warrington have placed deep, unutterable woe and disappointment. Tyldeate)" were sure of safe and certain victory, even up to the time that the" Warrington lads " waltzed en te their little lawn. The Tyldesley men are yclept " Bongers." for what reason I cannot say, nor can anyone enlighten me as to this thusness.' Warrington enthusiasto, indeed were far too jubilant to spend any time in, making in- quiries.

Warrington's improved form was maintained again, and to advantage. Although the exposition given was devoid of those scientific tactics by which Warring- ton have earned fame,- yet the game was full'of sharp earnest individual endeavours and occasional Ashes or individual brilliancy. Warrington were in every respect superior, but markedly SD at threequarter positions. The forwards, toe, made a splendid show. There was no shirker to be found in the whole eight,aad whether in scrimmages or loose tactics, they displayed form which was high' creditable. There is no " hifalutin " about this ; it is." truthful truth," to the core. Heesom played a good game and as usual was very safe, whilst the two Bates made the Tyldesley men watch their actions with breath very much bated. At threequarters Barber, the acquisition from Stockton Heath,blayed with commend- able spirit and alertness,and the Committee cannot very well regret introducing a little " new blood "so it be of the quality of this acquisition.

We may now quote that familiar paradox, "Let us, live in hope, if we die in despair." There is still hope that Warrington may get its gentle paw upon that silver drinking gobleK Our team are showing wonderfully im- proved form. If they will only maintain it they may yet retrieve their shady prospects. They hold a very in- teresting position in the statistical table. For an in- speotion of which perpend :

div.head: WARRINGTON FARMERS' CLUB. -- RAILWAY v. SHIP CANAL TRANSIT.
div.p: WARRINGTON FARMERS' CLUB. -- RAILWAY v. SHIP CANAL TRANSIT.

A meeting of Cheshire and Lancashire farmers was held under the auspices of the Warrington Far- mers' Club, at Cornhill, Warrington, on Wednesday. Captain Rodgers, Ds.resbury, presided, and there wore also present Messrs. D. L. Stelfox (sec.), J. Baxter, C.C.. J. Marsh, J. Derbyshire, Henry Cotton, and Edward Cotton.

div.head: AGRICULTURAL COMMISSION.
div.p: THE AGRICULTURAL COMMISSION.
The SECRETARY mentioned that he had now forwarded the names of the gentlemen who had been chosen as witnesses to give evidence before the Ryal Commission on Agriculture.

div.head: TUE ADD'LTERATION OF FOODS.
div.p: TUE ADD'LTERATION OF FOODS.

Mr. BAXTER, C.C., stated that the Weights and Mea- sures Committee of the Cheshire County Council had proposed the appointment or Dr. Carter Bell as analyst to the County Council, under the Foods and Drugs Acts. The fee to be paid to the analyst for each analysis would be one guinea, 16s. of which would be paid from the county rate and 53. from the person causing the analysis to be made, It would only be necessary for any person suspecting adulteration in his foods to com- municate with the inspector of the district, and then any prosecutions which might follow would be carried through by public authorities. A resolution supporting the Committee's action was passed unanimously.

THE MILK TRAFFIC QUESTION. The next business was to consider the recent altera- tions in train services whereby farmers have suffered tom and inconvenience through the termination ot milk contracts ; the loss and inconvenience in farmers other- wise being unable to reach in time the local markets ; to approximately fix the annual carriage value of the milk and other local farm produce traffic, and to ascertain whether a cheaper and more efficient service cannot now be had by the Manchester Ship Canal or otherwise.— The Chairman said he learned that the London and North-Western Railway, finding that their dividends were running rather small, thought they would try to meet the falling off in the traffic by reducing the num- ber of trains. In some cases milk trains had been knocked off, or instead of the milk being sent by pas- senger train it was tacked on to luggage trains.—Mr. John Marsh said he had been sending milk by the Lon- don and North-Western Railway for upwards of twenty- five years. Ile had sent very considerable quantities to Manchester ; a great deal more than he was sending now! Some six weeks ago the company took off the milk train in the morning, and now sent the milk by luggage train. He felt the inconvenience very much, as this train was sometimes from half an hour to an hour late. The consequence was that the Pendleton Co- ' operative Society, who were supplied from six to seven dairies in WarriNgton neighbourhood, had now knocked them all off except one. It would mean the milk traffic being put an end to altogether on the Warring- ton side of Manchester. They did not care by what train it was carried if it was in time, but if it was carried by luggage train he thought they ,were entitled to luggage rates. He believed the milk traffic from Warrington to Manchester brought in from £1,200 to £1,500 a year to the company, and in addition to this there was the farm produce. If the company treated them badly with respect to their milk, i)e did not see why the farmers should send their pro- duce by them, especially as they had now other facili- ties at hand by waterway. He would as soon support the shareholders of the Ship Canal as the shareholders of the railway.—Mr. Edward Gibbons, Lymm, who formed one of a deputation to Mr. Shaw and Mr. Neale, of the London and North-Western Railway on the matter of taking off the early milk train, said it was to be sub- mittA to the directors of the company at their next meeting. He (Mr. Gibbons) had, through the taking off of the train lost a customer who had paid him from £2OO to £3OO a year. Others had also lost customers.— Mr. Steltox, secretary of the Warrington Farmers' Club, said in trying to economise, the railway were striking at their very best customers. It was now necessary for the farmers to look out what was the best for themselves. A

light steamer either on the Bridgewater Canal or the Ship Canal would carry the milk at almost the same rate of speed. This means would perhaps pay carriers very handsomely, because in addition to the milk there was bound to be a large amount of subsidiary traffic. He had been in communication with Mr. Collier, manager of the Bridgewater Canal, who seemed to think the diffi- culty in running a light steamer 'would be the time difficulty, as he feared that the steamer running too fast might injure the banks. If a deputation, however, waited upon Mr. Collier, they might be able to convince him that no danger or difficulty would attach to the pro- posal. The Ship Canal had landing accommodation all alone the route.—Ultimately a resolution was adopted to approach the railway company to put on the early train again, arni the understanding was come to that if the result was unsatisfactory formal negotiations would be entered into with the Ship Canal Company for the carriage of the milk and produce by their route.

div.head: FRAUDS ON A SAVINGS BANK.
div.p: FRAUDS ON A SAVINGS BANK.
A MISSING ACTUARY.

" Mr. Cyril Dodd, Q.C., has completed his inquiry into the affairs of the Sudbury (Suffolk) Trustee Savings BAnic. He states in his report that owing to the miscon- duct of Pratt, the missing actuary, there is a deficiency of £17,000, and that the liabilities of the bank amount to £35 000. He refers to Pratt's former popularity, te,, his adroit bookkeeping, to the ease with which he de- ceived the trustees ; and says that one of the lessons of the bank's collary.e is this—that where there is only one paid official in the bank that official will', if he is a man of ability, be almost certain to obtain at dangerous ascen- dancy in the management. The existing rules, he con- siders, are strong enou,gh to safeguard the bank, and inasmuch as a dividend of 17s. 61. in the pound has been offered, and accepted by the depositors, he does not think it needful to present a petition for the winding 'up of the institution.
NONCONFORMISTS AND PUBLIC POLICY.

The annual meetings of the Manchester District Con- gregational Union were held on Thursday at Levens- hillme. under the presidency of the Rev. J. Hirst ' Uollowell. Speaking on the rights and duties of Non- ' confhrmists as to education and public policy, the President said the mere wirepulling politicians sometimes trifl,l with Nonconformisis on the supposition that they had no rights, conscience, or conviction in their Noncon- formity. Whoever was re:ponsible for it, the Horncastle el,ction was an insult to them. Party managers would find that Nonconf,irmists would nrat take a Liberalism with r equality struck out of it. Disestablish- ment was as necessary to liberty as self-government to Ireland. The new attempt to seize the rates for Anglican and eitholir, teaching and t') sectarianise Board schools would he stoutly oponSed. They would meet this list I reaction with the same resistance with which they had opposed all like attempts in the past.

div.head: WEEKLY REPOET ON THE REALTa 01
div.p: WEEKLY REPOET ON THE REALTa 01
WARRINGTON.

During the week, which was the 3rd of the current year, the following births and deaths were registered 7—Births : Warrington, 49; Latchford 7 ; t0ta1.56. Deaths : Warrington. 26; Latchford, 1 ; total 27. The excess of births over deaths was 29. The death-rate from all causes was equal to 25 per 1.000, against 21.2 the average of the previous four weeks, and against 28.2 the corresponding week of last year. The death-rate from the seven chief zymotic diseases was equal to 4.6 per 1.000, against 2.5 the average rate of the four previous weeks, and ngaintt 2.8 the corresponding week of 1893. The ages of mortality were :-0 to 1, 7 ; 1 to 5,6; 5 to 15. 1; /5 to 25, 1 ; 25 to 60, 7; 60 5 ; total, 27. The deaths included 1 from measles; 3 from whooping cough; 1 from scarlet fever ; 2 from tubercular disease ; 2 from cancer ; from plithisis ; 3 from old age; 4 from brain disease; 3 from lung disease ; 1 from liver disease. The following cases of infectious disease have been reported during the week 7—Scarlet fever, 7. METEOROLOGY.—The mean temperature was 45.2 Fah., and therefore 10 degrees higher than the pre- ceding week. The maximum temperature 52 P., was recorded on the 18th inst., and the minimum temperature 36 P., on the 15th inst. 7132 rainfall measured .54 inch. The general direction was S.W. the reading of the Anemometer denoting 800 miles.—JOHN 11. GORN4LL, Medimk Officer of Health.

The following is the Warrington team which will do duty to day against Wigan :—F. Heesont, full back, P. Carey, C. Potts, J. W. Evans, and Barber, three quarter hacks ; James T. Bate, and John T. Bate, half backs ; F. Turner, J. Jolley, W. Nevins, Dakin, Taylor, Thorniley, Bailey, and Buckley, forwards ; Donoghue, reserve. The match is creating considerable interest and special trains will be run from Wigan and neighbour hood to Warrington. At the present time Wigan hold third place in the cup competition and Warrington fourth, but should the match of to day result in a vic- tory for Warrington the places will be reversed.

The committee of Lancashire County Football Club I met on Tuesday evening in Manchester, and selected the following team to represent Lancashire against Devon- shire at Swinton on Saturday, the 3rd February ;—T- Foulkes (St. Helens), full back; W. M'Cutcheon (Old- ham), S. Lees (Oldham),, A. Barrett (Salford), and J.. Valentine (Swinton), three-quarter backs; A. Varley (Oldham), and James T. Bate (Warrington), half backs ; J. Simpsan (Rochdale Hornets), G. Woodward, (Tyldes- ley). H—Case (Swinton),. J. C. Goold (Liverpool Old Boys), J..;blley (Warrington), W. Rigby (Wigan), T. Whittaker (Walkden), and T. Dixon (Askam), forwards. Reserves W. Winterbottom (Swinton), full back ; J. Hurst (Oldham), T. Anderton (Leigh), R. Lewis (Ulver- ston), and R. Holmes (Morecambe), three-quarter backs ; ,W. Halliwell (Wigan),„ and J. Drummond (Widnes), half backs ; w. Unsworth (Wigan), T. Butterworth (Rochdale Hornets), and G. H. Murray (Swinton) for- wards.

I see that Runcorn has had adequate honour done it so far as the selection of a team by the Cheshire Commit- tee, for the match with Yorkshire, goes. S. Houghton ha 3 been selected as back, S. Abrams and J. Faulkner as halfbacks;. J. Davies has been 'selected as a forward, whilst there have been placed on the reserve T. Warder and P. Stubbs.

The " A " team have nraw fairly got into their stride, and very easily beat the Tyldesley " A " by two goals and two tries to nil. This is the second successive week in which Warrington have won by this result. The club who rejoice in the euphonious name of " Bongers " thus on Saturday suffered defeat in b)th first and " A" teams the total • result being two goals, five tries, to a try, Which must be anything but comforting to the said " Bongers." Stockton Heath is a prolific place for excellent feotballers, and while they have supplied the first team with Barber, who has never yet failed to score on each occasion he has played for Warrington, in the "A " team, Broady has shown himself almost, if not equal to his brother " heathen." Should the first team require another three-cyarter,they would not have much difficulty in choosing one.

div.head: ASSOOIzITION FOOTBALL,
div.p: ASSOOIzITION FOOTBALL,

The two loading Association teams in Warrington played their return.match on Saturday at Daltons Bank, before a good muster of spectators. The St. Elphin's team have not been so successful this year as last with their local rivals for they have been beaten already by both Warrington and Penketh, and the Warrington sup- porters were pretty confident that their champions would again lower the S. Elphin's colours. They were, how- ever, doomed to disappointment, for St. Elphln's won by three goals to two, after having unquestionably the best of the game..

The St. Elphins were undoubtedly lucky in having alm(st a gale at their backs during the first half,but they did not maim the most of their chances, for instead of three goals they ought to have scored more than double the number. In the second half, when the atmospheric advantagos were•reversed, St. Elphins were anything but overplayed, , although Warrington got through twice. Warrington were undoubtedly off form on Saturday, and missed Connor very much. St.Elphin's had a great advantage in the total number of matches played be- tween them and Warrington, for whereas they have won six,. the. Warrington team have only won two. Among the Warrington players on Saturdays Reid and Fenaelly were the pick of the forwards, while among the backs Mather and Williamson shone out most pro- minently. The•St.Elphins players are a very equal lot, and,it would be very difficult to individualize them. Tickle as left half was about the best. The respective goalkeepers, Forrest and Jones, are about on par.

div.head: PAAR'S, BANKING COMPANY AND THE
div.p: PAAR'S, BANKING COMPANY AND THE
ALLIANCE BANK.
ANNUAL MEETINGS

Mr. Alfred Turner, who was supported by nearly the whole of the twenty directors, presided•on Thursday at the twenty-ninth annual ordinary general meeting of the company held at the Cannon-st. Hotel, London.. There was a good attendence of shareholders. In mov- ing the adoption of the report which was given in last week's." Examiner," the chairman, said that they had had an increase in the number of their shareholders, and their accounts had been steadily increasing. The past six months, commercially speaking,. had not been a good one, and they had heard many sound reasons why that had been so. But in spite of those reasons they has been able to earn a dividend at the.usual rate of 19 ;per cent. for the past three months,, and the same rate:for the present three months ; they had carried for-, ward £5,000 to the property account, and were carrying forward £35052 to the next general account, so that he thought they had no reason to complain. No doubt there was great uncertainty and restlessness abroad. As regards other countries. they could only watch carefully,and so far as they were con- cerned at homeall fear might be removed if the Govern- ment would do its duty. They had the money- in the City, but they wanted the men and the ships,, and he hoped that the Government would realise that men-of- war were not made in a day, and that armed, cruisers could not be built in a month. (Hear, hear.) i If confi- dence was restored to the country they would shew a great improvement. They luad had a lamentable contest between capital and labour—he meant the coal strike. He trusted that commonserise would now prevail, and that both sides would recognise the folly of killing the goose that laid the golden egg. (Hear, hear.) If such a state of th'ings as they had had were to continue, it was net improbable. that capital , would seek investment in other countries, He hoped that would not be so. (Hear, hear.)- He hsd lately heard in the North • and also in Londr.n. that there had been some improvement in trade, and if nothing unfore- seen should happen, to sweep that way he trusted that when they next met the directors would have even a more favourable state of accounts to present. (Hear, , hear.) Mr. Cecil F. Parr seconded the motion, which was unanimously agreed to. The directors who retired by rotation, Messrs. H. W. Nix, E. Banbury, A. Hewlett, F. H. Dixon, Alfred Tur- ner, H. W. Meade-King, and Cecil F. Parr, were duly re-elected ; Messrs. Turquands and Co., and Stead, Taylor, and Stead (of Liverpool) were re-appointed ! auditors.
Cordial votes of thanks were passed to the erirectors and Mr. Dun and the othor principal ofliCials of th company.

div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.

The House of Lords met on Thursday, and the second reading of the Local Government (Parish Councils) Bill was moved by the Marquis of RIPON, who stated the main provisions of the measure, and said he hoped that the Earl of KINBBRLEY would be in his place in time to take charge of the bill in Committee. The Marquis of SALISBURY said he thought the parish councils would on the whole be an advantage, and certainly could do no injury. But he did not see why it was necessary to deal with the question of charities, and feared that if Parlia- ment passed the bill as it at present stood they would inflict a heavy blew on public benevolence. The clauses which permitted the hiring of land would most injure the tenant farmers, and he should strongly oppose any proposal which conferred judicial functions on persons whose official existence depended on the will of a politician. The noble Marquis expressed his disapproval of the poor law portion of the measurer and concluded by asking that at lea‘t a week might be allowed for the preparation 0 amendments to be moved in committee. The Archbishop of CANTE/TISURY said no protectien was afforded for parish rooms built for social purpcses. Lord MONKSWELL spoke in support of the bill. The Duke of DavoNsmira, while declaring that amendments in Committee would be necessary, said he believed they all desired that the bill should become law before long. Lord CARRINGTON said that after the re- ception given to the principle of the bill he hoped it would pass through the House without substantial al. teration. The bill was read a second time and the Com- mittee stav axed for Thursday next.

div.head: ST. JOHN AMBILANCE ASSOCIATION RUNCORN BRA,./TCII..
div.p: ST. JOHN AMBILANCE ASSOCIATION RUNCORN BRA,./TCII..
The annual concert and distribution of certificates in connection with the Runcorn branch of St. John
Ambulance Association, were held in Gireenw—ay-road schobl on Wednesday evening. There was a large attendance of members and friends. Mr. J. Brun- _ _

drit, J.P., the president of the branch, occupiedithe chair, and Miss Barclay of Chester, occupied a seat by his side. The programme was as follows :e—Quartitte,. "The Clang of the Hammerrquartette party; song, "1 fear no foe," Mr. Branch ; song. "She wore a wreath of roses," Mrs. Temperley ; song, "Sailing across the sea," Pownell ; song, " Waiting." Madame Meunier;. musical sketch, "The Village Choral Society," Mr. L, Harris, (by special permission of Mr. Grossnaith) ;:duet, "The Fisherman," Messrs. Littler and Branch;. song, "The Wishing Cap," Mrs. Temperley ; • song, "The Fly- ing Dutchman," Mr.. Branch ;* song, "Te'Reccacio," Madame Meunier ; . song, "The Longshorensan,r Mr.. NicksoD; Humorous sketch, Mr. Leslie HarriB. Accom- panist, Mrs. W. B. Kay.. Madame Mounisr and Mr. Harris were highly successful in each of their efforts and were twice tenthusiastically encored. During the interval Mr: Brundrit said he was glad to see so raany present to support and encourage their efforts. The St. John Ambulance Associathn was created for the purpose of forming classes for ladies and gentlemen to go through a courseof study under a medi-- cal man to-enable them to render first aid to the injured. In these days of hurry-scurry when everthing was done at electric speed so many accidents occurred, and pre- cautions were not so great as in years gone by. It had been said that "Accidents will happen in the best regulated families." Many accidents may occur and a medical man could not be got instantly. Thus if a mem- ber of their society was on the spot, they could render their assistance,and so alleviate the sufferings of the un- fortunate person. It was not all enere theory, they had proof of the very valuable aid which had been rendered in cases of accidents. They sometimes had cases of fractured heads, broken bones, stopping of profuse bleeding.and the rescue of the drowning,occurrences that might prove fatal- but for the assistance of some meme ber of the Association. The Assosiation, although of recent growth had spread all over the kingdom, and was one of the foremost of societies.. The patronage was of the highest in the land, dukes, marcinises, and actors clergy and others. Runcorn had been accused of being nearly a century behind the times,but at any rate,no one could accuse them of that in the present case. Some four or five years ago, classes were formed for instruction and certificates had been given to 224:43ersons. 90:per cent had passed in their examination. They themselves felt that the town had greatly benefited by such work being carried on and which would still go on in the future. Other classes would be formed before very:long and the work would still go forward.. Many of the Runcorn people had emigrated and there could be no more useful knowledge than that of first, aid to the. wounded,whet,her !n the backwoods of Canada,or in the far west of America, or any other past of the world. Dr. MacDougall (applause) deserved the highest apprecia- tion fcr his kindness and voluntary services. It was very gratifying to the members to be instructed by so able a. preceptor. It was not necessary for him to say anything to introduce Miss Barclay. She had spentithe greater portion of her life in Runcorn and had devoted much of, her time to parochial work. He then asked Miss Barclay to kindly distribute the certificates. Miss Barclay who on rising was greeted with laud ap- plause handed the certificates to the following :---First examination in Ist aid : Mrs. Abel, Mrs. Allen, Mrs.Bos- worth, Mrs. Marshall, Miss E.Dobson, Miss Littler,.Miss Millington, Miss Mainley,Miss Rogerson, Miss E.Setibbs, Miss A. Statham, Miss Edith Tatters and Miss Ethel Tatters. Gentlemen : Messrs. W: Busball, W. Bartlett, H. Branch, J. Bosworth, W. J. Davenport, R. FOulkes, John Gates, Thomas Grounds, William Grounds,. John W. Hardy, R Lea, A. Morris, R. Newall, F: Olives, R. Rosenberg, L. Rosenberg, S. Riley and J. D.p Smith. Gentlemen, /st aid, re-examination : Messrs. .J; Clark, F. W, Clark, R. R. Clark, H. Davenport, William R. Richards, D. Smith, R. Taylor, Police Sergeant Woolley, P.C. J., W. Juett, P.C. G. Beckett and Mr. Isaac North. Ladies' Nursing Club : Mrs. Ann Bankes, Mrs. Boyle, Mrs. Homphreys, Mrs. Imison, Mrs. Kay, Mrs. Marshall, Mrs. Moore, Mrs. Norman, Mrs. Partington, Miss Acton, Miss Burton. Miss Dobson, Miss Fisher, Miss Heaton, Miss He-Pd, Miss Joyson, Miss Kilburn, Miss Savege,Miss M. A. Smith, Miss Statham, Miss Stonnore, Miss,Stubbs, Miss Edith Tatters, Miss Ethel Tatters, Miss Wilton and Miss Litticr, (Applause.)

The Ghairman -remarked that besides the certificates, there were nine gentlemen whe were entitled to gold medals, having passed their final examination. They had hoped to have been able to have presented them upon that, occasion, but they had not come from head- quarters, so they would have to be deferred till some other time. The gentlemen were as follows :.W. Bankes, J. H.Close, W, Epps, S. Henderson, T. Peirpoint, Henry Tarleton, J. Rhodos, P.C. G. Benfield and Inspector Cooper. (Applause.) D. McDougall said thathe was surie‘ they would all agree that the most cordial thanks of the meeting were due to Miss Barclay, for coming to distribute the certifi- cates to those who were so much entitled to them. She was :the distinguished daughter of a more distinguished father. (Applause.) They had had on various occa- sions much difficulty in getting ladies to come forward and identify themselves with the good work, that Miss. Barclay had willingly c..nsented to come r,nd extend to, them, her kindness and. sympathy. No women in the- county would be better received in Runcorn than the daughter of their ever to be beloved friend, the late Canon Barclay (Applause.) He proposed that the thanks. a the meeting be given to Miss Barclay for honouring: them with her presence. Heatherington seconded the vote-of thanks, and, said they were all very thankful to Miss Barclay for the manner in which she had responded to their invitation. The vote was carried by _acclamation.
The Chairman responded on behalf of Miss Barclay, Mr. Rhorles stepped forward and mid that there,was,.)

. , another certificate far more important than the certi- .ftates which had been distributed. It was a certifiteate, for valuable servicee rendered to the St. John's Ambul- ance Association, and constituting the person, an, honorary life member of the society. Miss Barclay amid ,deafening cheers and applause pre- Rented certificate, which was nicely framed, to Dr. Mac-- 'Dougall. Mr. Bushall on behalf of the lady and gentlemen mem:- ! bar of the St. John Ambulance Association Runcorn, branch, said he had much pleasure in presenting Dr.. MacDougall with the silver dish for the manne!yin which, he had tau.,gh;Y. them during the past year, and as.a. , token of respect and esteem. In acknowledging the crift,D% MacDougall 2,aid he did not know how to thank7them, for the honour they had done him. During the last fear or five years,. he had) been the recipient of so many presents that, it was really difficult to find words to exlmess himself. The, greatest honour they could him. Yves to give attention to. the work in which be was so much interested. He enumerated instances. in which members of the branch had been enabled to. render valuable aid to suffering persons,.and said they had formed two corps, of 25 or 26 men and their servie9.4 would be placed at the com- mand of everybody in the district, an ambulance litter of the most approved kind. (Applause.), Oa behalf of the rneraers Dr. MacDougall then handed to Mt. Epps a cruet stand and silver toast rack in recog- nition of his valuable services to the Association, and to, his4,rood qualities as. secretary. The cruet was int-- s,nihed "Presented to Mr. William Epps by the mesa-. hers of the St. John Ambulance Association Runcorn Branch on the occasiem of his marriage% and as a marl of ~esteem for his disinterested services, to the above branch,. 2511,/E93." Mr. Epps said he was deeply grateful for the admin. able present the members had given him. It wes;qpite unexpected. When he became secretary of the society, the number of members was about 30, and now it was 230. On behalf of himself and his wife he begged to think them most heartily for their gift. Subscriptions are invited towards the purchase of the hand ambulance. The latest contributions are Sir R. M. Brooke. -£2 : Mr. James Reynolds, j.P., I ; Miss Barclay, 104. 6d.

div.head: SHIELD COMPETITION.
div.p: SHIELD COMPETITION.
WARRINGTON GYMNASIUM AND TILE

The Warrington Gymnasium eight met Stock- port eight, at Stockport. on Thursday, in the second round of the 200 Guineas Shield Competition, held under the auspices of the N.P.R.S. The result was a signal victory for the Warrington eight, who are considered to have shown better all round form than in any previous competition. Accompanied by some 15 spectators, the eight left Warrington at five and reached their destination in ample time to "enter the lists "at 7.30. There was not,however, a very warm reception awaiting them,for the total number of specta- tors in the Wellington-street Gymnasium, did not exceed 50, including the 15 persons from Warrington. The building itself is a very inferior one and bears no com- parison to the excellent institution in Palmyra Square. It is of a triangular shape, and about 21 feet wide, a disadvantage which was felt considerably by the War- rington men in the jumping exercises as it hampered those who are given to "side jumping." The only exer- cise in which Warrrington did not excel was rope climbing. Stockport are very expert at this exercise, whilat Warrington are somewhat defective. Conse- quently the latter were beaten by 29 points. In vault- ing only one of the Stockport men reached the height of five feet 17. n., whilst five of the Warringconians cleared six feet and some itches, and the points-141 to 113-.- show how vastly superior they were in this direction, though, as we mentioned above, the room was not favourable to the performances of several. In high jumping there was &similar result, the visitors scoring 74 against 2. Among the Warringtonians J. Podinore was the leading scorer, and was closely followed by J. Morzam G. N. Vernon,and A. Dickens. Podmore scored 9' points more than any individual in the Stockport eightt It was considerably after ten o'clock when the competition was concluded the result being that the Warrington eight missed their train home, and were compelled to wait about Stockport Station until four o'clock next morning,-without refreshment. That they enjoyekthernselves whilst in this predicament, may be surmised from the fact that the stationmaster said to them on leaving "Lam very pleased to have seen you— but lam much more pleased to see you go." The judge was Mr. Renshaw, of the Manchester Y.M.C.A. Mr. Kinsley, the Warrington conductor, accompanied the visitors. The following is a list of the individual points scored :

THEFT OF TIMBER.—TWO yeomen named Johanna Quinn, Peter-st., and Mary Glinn, of Peel-Bt., were charged with stealing a quantity of timber from Hut- chinson's works, valued at 31—P.C. Murray stated that he saw the defendants on Friday night coming from the cooper's shop at the works in question, carrying the timber produced.—Quinn,who had been previeusly con- victed for a similar offence, was fined V., or 14 days ; and Glinn was fined 10s. or seven days in default.
